## Preface

The stories in this volume are transcribed from extensive illustrated diaries which I have kept for about twenty years spent traveling and hunting <note>original: "sport"</note> in many lands—the last nine of which were spent almost entirely in Japan while I was collecting natural history specimens for the British Museum. I spent my time trawling and dredging in the Inland Sea—sometimes with success, sometimes without—but ultimately contributing about fifty discoveries new to science to the national collection. According to Sir Edwin Ray Lankester <note>A prominent British zoologist and director of the Natural History Museum in London from 1898 to 1907.</note>, these efforts "added greatly to the knowledge of Japanese <term>Ethnology</term>." <note>Ethnology: the study of the characteristics of different peoples and the relationships between them.</note>

As you might imagine, such a life has brought me into close contact with the people—the fisherman, the farmer, the priest, the doctor, the children, and all others from whom there is a possibility of gathering information. I have been told many strange and supernatural tales. In this volume, the publishers preferred to have a mixture of subjects: stories of mountains, trees, flowers, historical places, and legends. For the general results recorded in my diaries, I must thank our former Minister in Tokyo <note>original: "Tokio"</note>, Sir Ernest Satow; the

<summary>In this preface, the author explains that the following stories were gathered during his nine years in Japan while collecting natural history specimens for the British Museum. He highlights his close interactions with the Japanese people as the source for the diverse legends and tales included in the volume.</summary>
<keywords>Japan, natural history, British Museum, Inland Sea, Sir Edwin Ray Lankester, Japanese Ethnology, Tokyo, Sir Ernest Satow, folklore, diaries</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the author's preface, continuing the list of acknowledgments for those who assisted in the collection and translation of these tales.</meta>

# Ancient Tales and Folklore of Japan

...Ministers and Vice-Ministers of Foreign Affairs and of Agriculture, who gave me many letters of introduction; my dear friend Mr. Hattori, Governor of Hyogo <note>original: "Hiogo"</note> Prefecture; the translators of the original notes and manuscripts (which were often roughly written in Japanese), including Mr. Ando, Mr. Matsuzaki, and Mr. Watanabe; and Mr. Mo-No-Yuki, who drew and painted the illustrations from my own sketches. These sketches must have often clashed with his artistic sensibilities, keeping him awake as he reflected on the perceived lack of refinement in the European sense of art.

I also owe my thanks to my faithful interpreter, Yuki Egawa, for her constant efforts to find what I wanted, and to many Japanese peasants and fishermen, whose good nature, kindness, and hospitality have endeared them to me forever. It is fitting that such a worthy people have such a worthy Sovereign <note>A reference to Emperor Meiji, who ruled Japan from 1867 to 1912.</note>.

->**R. GORDON SMITH.**<-

*June 1908.*

# ANCIENT TALES AND FOLKLORE
# OF JAPAN

## I

### THE GOLDEN HAIRPIN¹

Up in the northern city of Sendai, from where the best Japanese soldiers come, there lived a samurai named Hasunuma.

Hasunuma was rich and hospitable, and consequently highly esteemed and well-liked. Some thirty-five years ago, his wife gave him a beautiful daughter, their first child, whom they called "Ko," which means "Small" when applied to a child, much as we say "Little Mary" or "Little Jane." Her full name was actually "Hasu-ko," which means "Little Lily"; but here we will call her "Ko" for short.

On exactly the same date, "Saito," one of Hasunuma’s friends and also a samurai, had the good fortune to have a son. The fathers decided that, being such old friends, they would marry their children to each other when they were old enough to wed; they were very happy with the idea, and so were their wives. To make the engagement of the

---

<note>1. This story resembles "Botan Dōrō," or the Peony Lantern story, told by both Mitford and Lafcadio Hearn. In this instance, however, the spirit of the dead sister passes into the body of the living one, assumes her form, leaves her sick and ill for over a year, and then allows her to reappear as if she had never been ill at all. It is the first story of its kind I have heard.</note>

<summary>This page introduces Chapter I, "The Golden Hairpin," set in Sendai. It describes the birth of two children to samurai friends, Hasunuma and Saito, who decide to betroth their children to each other.</summary>
<keywords>Sendai, samurai, Hasunuma, Ko, Saito, betrothal, Japanese folklore, Botan Dōrō</keywords>

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of the betrothal between the children of the samurai Saito and Hasunuma. It details the exchange of a golden hairpin as a token, Saito's sudden departure from Sendai, and the eventual tragic death of Hasunuma's daughter, O Ko San, who remained faithful to her missing fiancé.</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>Ancient Tales and Folklore of Japan</header>

babies more binding, Saito handed Hasunuma a golden hairpin that had been in his family for a long time and said:

> "Here, my old friend, take this pin. It shall be a token of betrothal from my son, whose name shall be Kōnojō, to your little daughter Ko; both are now only two weeks old. May they live long and happy lives together."

Hasunuma took the pin and handed it to his wife to keep; then they drank sake to each other’s health, and to the bride and bridegroom of some twenty years later.

A few months after this, Saito somehow displeased his feudal lord and, being dismissed from service, left Sendai with his family—to where, no one knew.

Seventeen years later, O Ko San was, with one exception, the most beautiful girl in all Sendai; the exception was her sister, O Kei, who was just a year younger and as beautiful as herself.

Many were the suitors for O Ko’s hand, but she would have none of them, remaining faithful to the engagement her father had made for her when she was a baby. True, she had never seen her betrothed, and (what seemed even more curious) neither she nor her family had ever once heard of the Saito family since they had left Sendai over sixteen years before; but that was no reason why she, a Japanese girl, should break her father’s word. Therefore, O Ko San remained faithful to her unknown lover, though she grieved greatly at his failure to appear; in fact, she secretly suffered so much from this that she became ill and died three months later, to the grief of all who knew her and to her family’s serious distress.

<vocab>Saito, Hasunuma, Kōnojō, O Ko San, O Kei, Sendai, betrothal, sake</vocab>

To make the bond more binding, Sanai handed over the golden chrysanthemum hairpin which had long been in his family and said:
> “Here, my old friend, take this pin. It shall be a token of betrothal from my son, whose name shall be Kōnojō, to your little daughter Ko, both of whom are now only two weeks old. May they live long and happy lives together!”

Hachizaemon took the pin and handed it to his wife to keep; they then pledged each other's health for a marriage to take place some twenty years later.

A few weeks later, old Sanai somehow offended his Lord and, after being dismissed, went away and had his head closely shaved to <unclear>become</unclear> <unclear>a</unclear> <unclear>priest</unclear> dressed in white <unclear>garments</unclear>.

To make the bond more binding, Sanai handed over the golden chrysanthemum hairpin which had long been in his family and said:
> “Here, my old friend, take this pin. It will be a token of betrothal from my son, whose name will be Kōnojō, to your little daughter Ko, both of whom are now only two weeks old. May they live long and happy lives together!”

Hachizaemon took the pin and handed it to his wife to keep; they then toasted to each other's health for a marriage set to take place some twenty years later.

A few weeks later, old Sanai somehow offended his Lord and, after being dismissed, went away and had his head closely shaved to <unclear>become</unclear> <unclear>a</unclear> <unclear>priest</unclear> dressed in white <unclear>garments</unclear>.

## The Golden Hairpin

On the day of O Ko San’s funeral, her mother was attending to the final rites for the deceased and smoothing her hair with the golden pin given to Ko San—or O Ko<sup>1</sup>—by Saito on behalf of his son Kōnojō. When the body had been placed in its coffin, the mother thrust the pin into the girl’s hair, saying:

> ‘Dearest daughter, this is the pin given as a memento to you by your betrothed, Kōnojō. Let it be a pledge to bind your spirits in death, as it would have been in life; and may you enjoy endless happiness, I pray.’

In praying this way, no doubt O Ko’s mother thought that Kōnojō also must be dead, and that their spirits would meet; but it was not so, for two months after these events Kōnojō himself, now eighteen years of age, arrived at Sendai, calling first on his father’s old friend Hasunuma.

> ‘Oh, the bitterness and misfortune of it all!’ said the latter. ‘Only two months ago my daughter Ko died. Had you only come before then, she would be alive now. But you never even sent a message; we never heard a word from your father or your mother. Where did you all go when you left here? Tell me the whole story.’

> ‘Sir,’ answered the grief-stricken Kōnojō, ‘what you tell me of the death of your daughter, whom I had hoped to marry, sickens my heart, for I, like her, had been faithful, and I hoped to marry her and thought of her daily. When my father took my family away from Sendai, he took us to Yedo; and afterward we went north to

After the palanquin had passed, he picked it up without paying much attention to it.

It was the golden hairpin; but of course, although Kōnojō’s father had told him about the pin, Kōnojō had no idea that this was it. Therefore, he thought nothing more of it other than that it must belong to *O Kei San*. "Though you have not seen me, I have seen you several times, and I have fallen so madly in love with you that I can think of nothing else but you. When you picked up my golden pin tonight on our return, I had dropped it to serve as an excuse to come to you and knock. You must love me in return; for otherwise I must die!"

This heated and outrageous declaration scandalized poor Kōnojō. Moreover, he felt that it would be doing his kind host Hasunuma a great injustice to be receiving his younger daughter at this hour of the night and making love to her. He expressed himself forcibly in these terms.

"If you will not love me as I love you, then I shall take my revenge," said O Kei, "by telling my father that you got me to come here by making love to me, and that you then insulted me."

Poor Kōnojō! He was in a difficult mess. What he feared most of all was that the girl would do as she said, that the samurai would believe her, and that he would be a disgraced and villainous person. "Do not joke, sir! My daughter, O Kei San, is not a subject for jokes and untruths. She has been like one dead for over a year—so ill that we have with difficulty forced gruel into her mouth. Moreover, she has spoken no word and shown no sign of life."

The samurai and Kōnojō stared at each other, and the mother stared at both. Neither knew what to think, or what to say or do. Imagine the general surprise when the sick O Kei walked into the room, having risen from her bed as if she had never been ill for a moment. She was the picture of health and beauty.

"How can this be?" asked the samurai, almost shouting. "How is it, O Kei, that you have come from your sickbed dressed, with your hair done, and looking as if you had never known a moment of illness?"

"I am not O Kei, but the spirit of O Ko," was the answer. "I was most unfortunate to die before the return of Kōnojō, for had I lived until then, I would have recovered and married him. As it was, my spirit was unhappy. It took the form of my dear sister O Kei, and for a year has lived happily in her body with Kōnojō. It is appeased now and about to take its final rest."

The old samurai, his wife, and Kōnojō were all amazed at this. The girl appeared to be O Kei, but her voice and manners were those of O Ko. Furthermore, the golden hairpin served as additional proof. The mother knew it well. She had placed it in O Ko's hair just before the tub coffin <note>A traditional circular Japanese wooden coffin.</note> was closed. No one could convince her otherwise on that point.

"But," said the samurai at last, "O Ko has been dead and buried for more than a year now. It puzzles us all that you should appear to us. Why do you trouble us so?"

"I have explained already," the girl resumed. "My spirit could not rest until it had lived with Kōnojō, whom it knew to be faithful. It has done this now and is prepared to rest. My only desire is to see Kōnojō marry my sister."

Hasunuma, his wife, and Kōnojō held a consultation. They were quite ready for O Kei to marry, and Kōnojō did not object.

With everything settled, the ghost-girl held out her hand to Kōnojō, saying:

"This is the last time you will touch the hand of O Ko. Farewell, my dear parents! Farewell to all of you! I am about to pass away."

Then she fainted and seemed dead, remaining so for half an hour. The others, overcome by the strange and eerie things they had seen and heard, sat around her, hardly saying a word.

## The Golden Hairpin

At the end of half an hour, the body came to life and, standing up, said:

"Dear parents, do not fear for me anymore. I am perfectly well again; but I have no idea how I came down from my sickroom in these clothes, or why it is that I feel so well."

Several questions were asked of her, but it was quite evident that O Kei knew nothing of what had happened—nothing of the spirit of O Ko San or of the golden hairpin!

A week later, she and Kōnojō were married, and the golden hairpin was given to a shrine at Shiogama, where, until quite recently, crowds used to go to worship.

### II

## THE SPIRIT OF THE WILLOW TREE

About one thousand years ago (though according to the dates of the story, it was 744 years ago), the temple of San-jū-san-gen Dō was founded. That was in 1132. "San-jū-san-gen Dō" means "hall of thirty-three spaces," and it is said that there are over 33,333 figures of the Goddess Kwannon, the Goddess of Mercy, in the temple today. Before the temple was built, a willow tree of great size stood in a nearby village. It served as the playground for all the village children, who swung from its branches and climbed on its limbs. It provided shade for the elderly in the heat of summer, and in the evenings, when work was done, many young men and women of the village vowed eternal love under its branches. The tree seemed to be a good influence on everyone. Even weary travelers could sleep peacefully and stay almost dry under its branches. Alas, even in those times, people were often ruthless toward trees. One day, the villagers announced their intention to cut it down and use it to build a bridge across the river.

# The Spirit of the Willow Tree

Heitaro, a great favorite who had lived near the old tree all his life, just as his ancestors had done, was strongly opposed to cutting it down.

"Such a tree should be respected," he thought. Had it not braved the storms of hundreds of years? In the heat of summer, what pleasure it gave the children! Did it not provide shelter to the weary and a sense of romance to the love-smitten? Heitaro impressed all these thoughts upon the villagers. "Rather than approve of you cutting it down," he said, "I will give you as many of my own trees as you require to build the bridge. You must leave this dear old willow alone forever."

The villagers readily agreed. They also had a secret veneration for the old tree.

Heitaro was delighted and easily found the wood needed to build the bridge.

Some days later, Heitaro, returning from his work, found a beautiful girl standing by the willow.

He instinctively bowed to her. She returned the bow. They spoke together of the tree, its age, and its beauty. They seemed, in fact, to be drawn toward each other by a shared sympathy. Heitaro was sorry when she said that she must be going and bid him good day. That evening, his mind was far from being focused on the ordinary things of life. "Who was the lady under the willow tree? How I wish I could see her again!" he thought. There was no sleep for Heitaro that night. He had caught the fever of love.

The next day he was at his work early; he remained at it all day, working twice as hard to try to forget the lady of the willow tree; but on his way home in the

There was not a moment of their spare time in which either Heitaro or his wife was not playing with the child, whom they called Chiyodō. It is doubtful if a happier home could have been found in all Japan than the house of Heitaro, with his good wife Higo and their beautiful child.

Alas, where in this world has complete happiness ever been known to last? Even if the gods permitted it, the laws of man would not.

# The Spirit of the Willow Tree

Once the retired Emperor Toba’s wish became known, the authorities gave orders to collect timber for the construction of the vast temple. And so it happened that the days of the great willow tree were numbered, for it was needed, along with many others, to form the roof.

Heitaro tried to save the tree again by offering every other tree he had on his land for free; but his efforts were in vain. Even the villagers became eager to see their willow tree built into the temple. They thought it would bring them good luck and, in any case, would be a fine gift from them toward the great temple.

The fatal moment arrived. One night, while Heitaro, his wife, and their child had retired to rest and were sleeping, Heitaro was awakened by the sound of axes chopping. To his astonishment, he found his beloved wife sitting up in her bed, gazing earnestly at him, while tears rolled down her cheeks and she sobbed bitterly.

‘My dearest husband,’ she said with a choking voice, ‘please listen to what I tell you now, and do not doubt me. This is, unfortunately, not a dream. When we married, I begged you not to ask about my past, and you never did; but I said I would tell you someday if there were a real reason to do so. Unfortunately, that time has now arrived, my dear husband. I am none other than the spirit of the willow tree you loved and so generously saved six years ago. It was to repay you for this great kindness that I appeared to you in human form under the tree, hoping that I could

A little later, at the break of day, Heitaro took Chiyodō by the hand and led him to the tree. Upon reaching it, they found it down, and its branches were already lopped off. Heitaro’s feelings can well be imagined.

Strange! Despite their combined efforts, the men were unable to move the trunk a single inch toward the river, where it was to be floated to Kyoto.

On seeing this, Heitaro spoke to the men.

# The Spirit of the Willow Tree

‘My friends,’ he said, ‘the dead trunk of the tree you are trying to move contains the spirit of my wife. Perhaps, if you allow my little son Chiyodō to help you, it will be easier for you; he would also like to help show his last respects to his mother.’

The woodcutters fully agreed, and, much to their astonishment, as Chiyodō came to the back of the log and pushed it with his little hand, the timber glided easily toward the river while his father sang an ‘<term>Uta</term>.’¹ There is a well-known song or ballad in the ‘<term>Uta</term>’ style said to have originated from this event; it is sung to this day by men pulling heavy weights or performing hard labor:—

> Muzan naru kana
> Motowa kumanono yanagino tsuyu de
> Sodate-agetaru kono midorigo wa
> Yoi, Yoi, Yoito na !²

# III

## GHOST OF THE VIOLET WELL¹

<margin>¹ Told to me by Shofukutei Fukuga.</margin>
In the wild province of Yamato, or very near its borders, is a beautiful mountain known as Yoshino-yama. It is not only known for its abundance of cherry blossoms in the spring, but it is also celebrated for more than one bloody battle. In fact, Yoshino might be called the staging ground for historical battles. Many say, when in Yoshino, "We are walking on history, because Yoshino itself is history." Near Mount Yoshino lies another mountain, known as Tsubosaka; and between them is the Valley of Shimizutani, where the Violet Well is located.

<margin>² Valley.</margin>
As spring approaches in this *valley*², the grass becomes a perfect emerald green, while moss grows luxuriantly over rocks and boulders. Toward the end of April, great patches of deep-purple wild violets appear in the lower parts of the valley, while up the sides, pink and scarlet azaleas grow in a way that defies description.

About thirty years ago, a beautiful seventeen-year-old girl named Shingé was making her way up

Shimizutani, accompanied by four servants. All were out for a picnic, and all, of course, were in search of wild flowers. O Shingé San was the daughter of a Daimyo <note>A powerful feudal lord in pre-modern Japan.</note> who lived in the neighborhood. Every year she was in the habit of holding this picnic and coming to Shimizutani at the end of April to hunt for her favorite flower, the purple violet (*sumire*).

The five girls, carrying bamboo baskets, were eagerly collecting flowers, enjoying the activity as only Japanese girls can. They raced in their rivalry to have the prettiest basketful. Since there were not as many purple violets as they wanted, O Shingé San said, "Let us go to the northern end of the valley, where the Violet Well is."

Naturally the girls agreed, and they all ran off, each eager to be there first, laughing as they went.

O Shingé outran the rest and arrived before any of them; and, spotting a huge bunch of her favorite flowers, of the deepest purple and very sweet in scent, she threw herself down, anxious to pick them before the others came. As she stretched out her delicate hand to grasp them—oh, horror!—a great mountain snake raised its head from beneath its shady retreat. O Shingé San was so frightened that she fainted on the spot.

In the meantime, the other girls had given up the race, thinking it would please their mistress to arrive first. They picked what they most liked, chased butterflies, and arrived fully fifteen minutes after O Shingé San had fainted.

### Ghost of the Violet Well

...filled them with the fear that she was dead, and their alarm increased when they saw a large green snake coiled near her head.

They screamed, as most girls do in such circumstances; but one of them, Matsu, who did not lose her head as much as the others, threw her basket of flowers at the snake. The snake, not liking the bombardment, uncoiled himself and slid away, hoping to find a quieter place. Then all four girls bent over their mistress. They rubbed her hands and threw water on her face, but without effect. O Shingé’s beautiful complexion became paler and paler, while her red lips took on the purplish hue that is a sign of approaching death. The girls were heartbroken. Tears coursed down their faces. They did not know what to do, because they could not carry her. What a terrible state of affairs!

Just at that moment, they heard a man’s voice close behind them:

"Do not be so sad! I can restore the young lady to consciousness if you will allow me."

They turned and saw a remarkably handsome youth standing on the grass not ten feet away. He appeared like an angel from Heaven.

Without saying more, the young man approached O Shingé's prostrate figure and, taking her hand in his, felt her pulse. None of the servants wanted to interfere in this breach of etiquette. He had not asked permission, but his manner was so gentle and sympathetic that they could say nothing.

O Matsu San forced the medicine, along with a little water, into her mistress's mouth, and in a few minutes, she began to recover.

Shortly after this, the doctor returned, carrying the dead snake on a stick.

"Is this the snake you saw lying by your young mistress?" he asked.

"Yes, yes," they cried; "that is the horrible thing."

"Then," said the doctor, "it is lucky I came, for it is very poisonous, and I fear your mistress would soon have died had I not arrived and been able to give her the medicine. Ah! I see that it is already doing the beautiful young lady good."

On hearing the young man's voice, O Shingé San sat up.

"Please, sir, may I ask to whom I am indebted for bringing me back to life this way?" she asked.

The doctor did not answer, but in a proud and manly way, he satisfied himself by smiling and bowing low and respectfully in the Japanese fashion. He departed as quietly and unassumingly as he had arrived, disappearing into the sleepy mist that always appears on spring afternoons in the Shimizu Valley.

done her much good, and she felt quite recovered. O Shingé's father and mother were very grateful for their daughter's recovery; but the name of the handsome young doctor remained a secret to all except the servant girl Matsu.

For four days O Shingé remained quite well; but on the fifth day, for some reason or another, she took to her bed, saying she was sick. She did not sleep, and did not wish to talk, but only to think, and think, and think. Neither her father nor mother could make out what her illness was. There was no fever.

Doctors were sent for, one after another; but none of them could say what the matter was. All they saw was that she became weaker every day. Asano Zembei, Shingé's father, was heartbroken, and so was his wife. They had tried everything and failed to do the slightest good for poor O Shingé.

One day O Matsu San requested an interview with Asano Zembei—who, by the way, was the head of his whole family, a <term>Daimio</term> and a great nobleman. Zembei was not accustomed to listening to servants' opinions; but, knowing that O Matsu was faithful to his daughter and loved her almost as much as he did himself, he consented to hear her, and O Matsu was ushered into his presence.

> “Oh, master,” said the servant, “if you will let me find a doctor for my young mistress, I can promise to find one who will cure her.”

> “Where on earth will you find such a doctor? Have we not had all the best doctors in the province and some even from the capital? Where do you propose to look for one?”

O Matsu answered:

> "Ah, master, my mistress is not suffering from an illness which can be cured by medicines—not even if they were given by the quart. Nor are doctors of much use. There is, however, one person I know of who could cure her. My mistress’s illness is of the heart. The doctor I know of can cure her. It is for love of him that her heart suffers; it has suffered this way since the day when he saved her life from the snakebite."

Then O Matsu told the details of the adventure at the picnic which had not been told before—for O Shingé had asked her servants to say as little as possible, fearing they would not be allowed to go to the Valley of the Violet Well again.

> "What is the name of this doctor?" asked Asano Zembei, "and who is he?"

> "Sir," answered O Matsu, "he is Doctor Yoshisawa, a very handsome young man of most courtly manners; but he is of low birth, being only one of the <term>eta</term>.<note>The eta were the lowest people or caste in Japan—skinners and killers of animals.</note> Please think, master, of my young mistress’s burning heart, full of love for the man who saved her life—and no wonder, for he is very handsome and has the manners of a proud samurai. The only cure for your daughter, sir, is to be allowed to marry her lover."

O Shingé’s mother felt very sad when she heard this. She knew well (perhaps by experience) of the illnesses caused by love. She wept, and said to Zembei:

> "I am completely with you in your sorrow, my lord, at the terrible trouble that has come to us; but I cannot see my daughter die like this. Let us tell her we will make—"

inquiries about the man she loves, and see if we can make him our son-in-law. O Shingé San was told by her mother that her father, though he had not consented to the engagement, had promised to make inquiries about Yoshisawa.

O Shingé ate and regained much strength upon hearing this news; and when she was strong enough, some ten days later, she was called into her father’s presence, accompanied by her mother.

‘My dear daughter,’ said Zembei, ‘I have made careful inquiries about Dr. Yoshisawa, your lover. Deeply as it grieves me to say so, it is impossible that I, your father and the head of our whole family, can consent to your marriage with one from such a lowly family as Yoshisawa, who, in spite of his own goodness, has come from the <term>eta</term>. I must hear no more of it. Such a contract would be impossible for the Asano family.’

No one dared to say a word to this. In Japan, the decision of the head of a family is final.

Poor O Shingé bowed to her father and went to her own room, where she wept bitterly; O Matsu, the faithful servant, did her best to console her.

Next morning, to the astonishment of the household, O Shingé San could not be found anywhere. A search was made everywhere; even Dr. Yoshisawa joined in the search.

### IV

## GHOST STORY OF THE FLUTE'S TOMB¹

LONG ago, at a small and remote village called Kumedamura, about eight miles to the southeast of Sakai city in Idsumo Province, a tomb was built called the Fuezuka, or Flute's Tomb. To this day, many people go there to offer prayers and to worship, bringing with them flowers and incense sticks, which are left as offerings to the spirit of the man who was buried there. All year round, people flock to it. There is no season at which they pray more particularly than another.

The Fuezuka tomb is situated on a large pond called Kumeda, some five miles in circumference, and all the places around this pond are known as being of Kumeda Pond, from which the village of Kumeda took its name.

Whose tomb can it be that attracts such sympathy? The tomb itself is a simple stone pillar, with nothing artistic to recommend it. Neither is the surrounding scenery interesting; it is flat and unattractive until the mountains of Kiushu are reached. I must tell, as well as I can, the story of whose tomb it is.

->1 Told to me by Fukuga.<-

<meta>This page continues the "Ghost Story of the Flute's Tomb," introducing the main character, Yoichi, and the circumstances leading to the legend.</meta>

Between seventy and eighty years ago, there lived near the pond in the village of Kumedamura a blind <term>amma</term><note>shampooer or massage therapist</note> called Yoichi. Yoichi was extremely popular in the neighborhood, being very honest and kind, besides being quite an expert in the art of massage—a treatment necessary to almost every Japanese person. It would be difficult indeed to find a village that did not have its <term>amma</term>.

Yoichi was blind, and, like all men of his profession, carried an iron wand or stick, and also a flute or ‘<term>fuezuka</term>’—the stick to feel his way around with, and the flute to let people know he was ready for work. Yoichi was such a good <term>amma</term> that he was nearly always employed and, consequently, fairly well-off, having a small house of his own and one servant who cooked his food.

A short distance from Yoichi’s house was a small teahouse, situated upon the banks of the pond. One evening (April 5; cherry-blossom season), just at dusk, Yoichi was on his way home after working all day. His road led him by the pond. There, he heard a girl crying piteously. He stopped and listened for a few moments, and gathered from what he heard that the girl was about to drown herself. Just as she entered the lake, Yoichi caught her by the dress and dragged her out.

“Who are you, and why are you in such trouble that you wish to die?” he asked.

“I am Asayo, the teahouse girl,” she answered. “You know me quite well. You must also know that it is not possible for me to support myself on the small pittance paid by my master. I have eaten nothing for two days now, and I am tired of my life.”

## Ghost Story of the Flute’s Tomb

"Come, come!" said the blind man. "Dry your tears. I will take you to my house and do what I can to help you. You are only twenty-five years old, and I am told you are still a fair-looking girl. Perhaps you will marry! In any case, I will take care of you, and you must not think of killing yourself. Come with me now; and I will see that you are well fed, and that dry clothes are given to you."

So Yoichi led Asayo to his home.

A few months later, they were married to each other. Were they happy? Well, they should have been, for Yoichi treated his wife with the greatest kindness; but she was unlike her husband. She was selfish, bad-tempered, and unfaithful. In the eyes of the Japanese, infidelity is the worst of sins. How much more, then, is it against the country’s spirit when advantage is taken of a husband who is blind?

Some three months after they had been married, and in the heat of August, a company of actors came to the village. Among them was Sawamura Tamataro, who had some reputation in Asakusa.

Asayo, who was very fond of plays, spent much of her time and her husband’s money going to the theater. In less than two days she had fallen violently in love with Tamataro. She sent him money, which had been hard-earned by her blind husband. She wrote him love letters, begged him to allow her to come and visit him, and generally disgraced her sex.

Things went from bad to worse. The secret meetings of Asayo and the actor scandalized the neighborhood. As in most such cases, the husband knew nothing about—

The ghost then told all that had happened since he had been established in the house at Kumedamura. Tamataro and his wife tried to get up and run out of the house; but they found that their legs would not support them, so full of fear were they.

Tamataro seized a lamp and threw it at the ghost; but the ghost was not to be moved. The lamp passed through him and broke, setting fire to the house, which burned instantly, with the wind fanning the flames.

# V

## A HAUNTED TEMPLE IN <term>INABA PROVINCE</term>¹

Around the year 1680, an old temple stood on a wild, pine-covered mountain near the village of <term>Kisaichi</term>, in the <term>Province of Inaba</term>. The temple was located far up in a rocky ravine. The trees were so tall and dense that they blocked out nearly all daylight, even when the sun was at its highest point. For as long as the old men of the village could remember, the temple had been haunted by a <term>shito dama</term> and what they believed was the skeleton ghost of some former priest who had lived there. Many priests had tried to live in the

---

<note>¹ In many stories in manuscript volumes, I have told of <term>shito dama</term> or astral spirits. I have received so much evidence from personal acquaintances regarding their existence, and even their frequent occurrence, that I almost believe in them myself. Some say that there are two shapes—the roundish-oblong tadpole shape, and the more square-fronted shape with eyes. Priests declare the shapes and sexes to be all alike, indistinguishable from each other and square-fronted, as in No. 2. My hunter, Oto of <term>Itami</term>, who, with his son, saw the old barber's wife's <term>shito dama</term> after she had died, declared that the shape was like an egg with a tail. At <term>Tsuboune</term>, near <term>Naba</term>, two or three dozen people who had seen the <term>shito dama</term> of a deaf man and that of a fisher-girl there declared both to be square-fronted. Again: At <term>Toshi Shima</term>, the old men declare that there was a carpenter whose <term>shito dama</term> appeared five or six times about fifteen years ago, and that it was red instead of having the ordinary phosphorescent smoky-white appearance. <term>Shito dama</term>, I take it, is the astral form that a spirit can assume if it wishes to wander the earth after death. This is the story of a dissatisfied spirit which haunted a temple and also showed itself as a ghost.</note>

At last, in the winter of 1701, a priest who was on a pilgrimage arrived at the village of Kisaichi. His name was Jogen, and he was a native of the Province of Kai.

Jogen had come to see the haunted temple. He was fond of studying such things. Although he believed in the <term>shito dama</term> form of spiritual return to earth, he did not believe in ghosts. As a matter of fact, he was anxious to see a <term>shito dama</term>, and, moreover, wished to have a temple of his own. In this wild mountain temple—with a history that fear and death prevented people from visiting or priests from inhabiting—he thought that he had (to put it in common English) "a real good thing." Thus, he had found his way to the village on a cold December night and had gone to the inn to eat his rice and hear all he could about the temple.

Jogen was no coward; on the contrary, he was a brave man and made all inquiries in the calmest manner.

"Sir," said the landlord, "your holiness must not think of going to this temple, for it means death. Many good priests have tried to stay the night there, and every one has been found dead the next morning, or has died shortly after daybreak without regaining consciousness. It is no use, sir, trying to defy such an evil spirit as the one that comes to this temple. I beg you, sir, to give up the idea. As much as we want a temple here, we wish for no more deaths and often think of burning down this old haunted one and building a new one."

Jogen, however, was firm in his resolve to find and see the ghost.

"Kind sir," he answered, "your wishes are for my safety; but it is my ambition to see a <term>shito dama</term>, and, if prayers can quiet it, to reopen the temple, to read its legends from the old books that must lie hidden within, and to be its head priest."

The innkeeper, seeing that the priest could not be dissuaded, gave up the attempt and promised that his son would accompany him as a guide in the morning and carry enough provisions for a day.

The next morning was one of brilliant sunshine, and Jogen was out of bed early, making preparations. Kosa, the innkeeper’s twenty-year-old son, was tying up the priest’s bedding and enough boiled rice to last him nearly two full days. It was decided that Kosa, after leaving the priest at the temple, should return to the village, for he, as well as every other villager, refused to spend a night at the eerie place; but he and his father agreed to go and see Jogen the following day, or (as someone grimly put it) "to carry him down and give him an honorable funeral and decent burial."

Jogen fully appreciated this joke and shortly after left the village, with Kosa carrying his belongings and leading the way.

The gorge in which the temple was situated was very steep and wild. Great moss-clad rocks lay strewn everywhere. When Jogen and his companion had reached the halfway point, they sat down to rest and eat. Soon they heard the voices of people ascending, and before long the innkeeper and some eight or nine of the village elders appeared.

# A Haunted Temple in Inaba Province

"We have followed you," said the innkeeper, "to try once more to dissuade you from running to certain death. True, we want the temple opened and the ghosts appeased; but we do not want it at the cost of another life. Please reconsider!"

"I cannot change my mind," answered the priest. "Besides, this is the chance of my life. Your village elders have promised me that if I am able to appease the spirit and reopen the temple, I shall be the head priest of the temple, which must hereafter become famous."

Again Jogen refused to listen to advice and laughed at the villagers’ fears. Shouldering the packages that had been carried by Kosa, he said:

"Go back with the rest. I can find my own way now easily enough. I shall be glad if you return tomorrow with carpenters, for no doubt the temple is in great need of repairs, both inside and out. Now, my friends, until tomorrow, farewell. Have no fear for me: I have none for myself."

The villagers bowed deeply. They were greatly impressed by Jogen's bravery and hoped that he might be spared to become their priest. Jogen, in turn, bowed and then began to continue his ascent. The others watched him as long as he remained in view and then retraced their steps to the village; Kosa thanked the good fortune that had not required him to go to the temple with the priest and return alone in the evening. With two or three people he felt brave enough; but to be here in the gloom of this wild forest and near the haunted temple alone—no, that was not for him.

At first glance, Jogen recognized that the temple was large; but neglect had caused it to fall into great disrepair. Cautiously, Jogen entered the temple and saw that there was a remarkably large and fine gilded figure of Buddha, besides figures of many saints. There were also fine bronzes and vases, drums from which the parchment had rotted off, incense-burners, or <term>koros</term>, and other valuable or holy things.

Behind the temple were the priests’ living quarters; evidently, before the ghost’s time, the temple must have had some five or six priests always present to attend to it and to the people who came to pray.

The gloom was oppressive, and as the evening was already approaching, Jogen thought of lighting the area. Unpacking his bundle, he filled a lamp with oil and found temple-sticks for the candles which he had brought with him. For about two hours, he heard nothing. The wind—what little there was—sighed around the temple and through the trunks of the tall trees. An owl hooted from time to time. Bats flew in and out. A smell of fungus filled the air.

Suddenly, near midnight, Jogen heard a rustling in the bushes below him, as if someone were pushing through. He thought it was a deer, or perhaps one of the large red-faced apes that are so fond of the area around high and deserted temples; perhaps it might even be a fox or a badger.

The priest was soon proven wrong. At the place where the sound of the rustling leaves had come from, he saw the clear and distinct shape of the well-known <term>shito dama</term>. It moved first one way and then another in a hovering and jerky manner, and a voice like distant buzzing came from it. But—horror of horrors!—what was that standing among the bushes?

The priest’s blood ran cold. There stood the glowing skeleton of a man in loose priest’s clothes, with glaring eyes and skin like parchment! At first, it remained still; but as the <term>shito dama</term> rose higher and higher, the ghost followed it—sometimes visible, sometimes not.

The ghost stood at the base of the great figure of Buddha and was facing Jogen.

Cold beads of sweat stood out on the priest’s forehead; the marrow seemed to have frozen in his bones; he shook so much that he could hardly stand. Biting his tongue to prevent himself from screaming, he dashed for the small room where he had left his bedding and, having bolted himself in, proceeded to look through a crack between the boards. Yes! There was the figure of the ghost, still seated near the Buddha; but the <term>shito dama</term> had disappeared.

None of Jogen’s senses failed him; but fear was paralyzing his body, and he felt himself no longer capable of moving—no matter what might happen. He continued, in a lying position, to look through the hole.

The ghost remained sitting, turning only its head, sometimes to the right, sometimes to the left, and sometimes looking upward.

For a full hour this went on. Then the buzzing sound began again, and the <term>shito dama</term> reappeared, circling and circling around the ghost’s body, until the ghost vanished, apparently having turned into the <term>shito dama</term>; and after circling around the holy figures three or four times, it suddenly shot out of sight.

The next morning Kosa and five men came up to the temple. They found the priest alive but paralyzed. He could neither move nor speak. He was carried toward the village, dying before he got there.

## VI

### A CARP GIVES A LESSON IN PERSEVERANCE ¹

Between the years 1750 and 1760, there lived in Kyoto a great painter named Okyo—Maruyama Okyo. His paintings were such that they fetched high prices even in those days. As a result, Okyo not only had many admirers, but also many pupils who strove to copy his style; among them was one named Rosetsu, who eventually became the best of all.

When Rosetsu first went to study at Okyo’s, he was, without exception, the dullest and most stupid pupil that Okyo had ever dealt with. His learning was so slow that pupils who had entered as students under Okyo a year or more after Rosetsu soon overtook him. He was one of those plodding but unfortunate youths who work hard—harder, perhaps, than most—and yet seem to go backward, as if the very gods were against them.

### A CARP GIVES A LESSON IN PERSEVERANCE¹

->ROSETSU WATCHES THE CARP<-

Around the years 1740 and 1750, there lived in Kyoto a great painter named Okyo—Maruyama Okyo. His paintings were of such quality that they commanded high prices even in those days; as he grew old, he consequently became wealthy. After all, who was more popular than Okyo? Among his many students was Rosetsu, who eventually became the best of them all.

As a youth, Rosetsu went to study at Okyo’s; in the beginning, he was the dullest and most foolish pupil that the great Okyo had ever dealt with. His progress was so slow that, despite the best efforts of Okyo’s other students to help him along, he was overcome by despair. He was one of those persistent but unfortunate young men who work hard, have great desire, and do their utmost, yet seem to go backwards as if the gods themselves were against them.

I read this story about him, along with many others about Japan’s greatest artist, whose name I have already mentioned. It concerned a certain event that occurred some years ago. I told my good friend in a Louis XV style, for I was as interested as those at Okyo’s studio. I wrote to my friend, the critic of the *London Art Magazine*. His answer was, “You know your friend is a real artist—perhaps the best.”

# A Carp Gives a Lesson in Perseverance

I have the deepest sympathy for Rosetsu. I myself became a bigger fool day by day as I worked; the harder I worked or tried to remember, the more clearly I became a fool.

Rosetsu, however, was successful in the end, having been greatly encouraged by his observations of the perseverance of a carp.

Many of the pupils who had entered Okyo’s school after Rosetsu had already become quite good painters. Poor Rosetsu was the only one who had made no progress at all for three years. He was so discouraged, and his master offered so little encouragement, that at last, dejected and sad, he gave up the hopes he had of becoming a great painter. He quietly left the school one evening, intending either to go home or to kill himself on the way. He walked all that night and halfway into the next, when, exhausted from a lack of sleep and food, he threw himself down on the snow under the pine trees.

Some hours before dawn, Rosetsu awoke, hearing a strange noise not thirty paces from him. He could not make it out, but he sat up, listening and glancing toward the place where the sound—of splashing water—was coming from.

As day broke, he saw that the noise was caused by a large carp, which was persistently jumping out of the water, evidently trying to reach a piece of <term>sembei</term> <gloss>a kind of biscuit made of rice and salt</gloss> lying on the ice of a pond near which Rosetsu found himself. For three full hours the fish must have been jumping unsuccessfully in this way, cutting and bruising itself against the edges of the ice until it bled and many scales had been lost.

<summary>Rosetsu, a discouraged painting student who has made no progress in three years, flees his school in despair but stops to observe a carp's tireless efforts to jump onto ice for food.</summary>
<keywords>Rosetsu, Okyo, perseverance, carp, painting, struggle, sembei, Japanese art history</keywords>

--- Page 94 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of Rosetsu, who has been observing a carp's tireless struggle to reach a piece of food on the ice.</meta>

Rosetsu watched its persistence with admiration. The fish tried every imaginable tactic. Sometimes it would make a determined attack from underneath on the ice where the biscuit lay by charging directly upwards; at other times it would jump high in the air, hoping that by falling on the ice, bit by bit would be broken away until it was able to reach the <term>sembei</term>. Indeed, the carp did break the ice in this way until at last he reached the prize—bleeding and hurt, but still rewarded for his brave perseverance.

Rosetsu, deeply impressed, watched the fish swim off with the food and reflected.

"Yes," he said to himself, "this has been a moral lesson to me. I will be like this carp. I will not go home until I have achieved my goal. As long as there is breath in my body, I will work to carry out my intention. I will work harder than ever, and no matter if I do not see progress, I will continue in my efforts until I reach my end or die."

After this resolution, Rosetsu visited the neighboring temple and prayed for success. He also thanked the local deity that he had been able to see, through the carp’s perseverance, the path that a man should take in life.

Rosetsu then returned to Kyoto and told the story of the carp and his determination to his master, Okyo.

Okyo was very pleased and did his best for his struggling pupil. This time, Rosetsu progressed. He became a well-known painter, the best student Okyo ever taught—as good, in fact, as his master—and he ended up as one of Japan’s greatest painters.

Rosetsu took the leaping carp as his crest.

<summary>Inspired by a carp's successful struggle to break through ice for food, Rosetsu returns to his studies with a vow of absolute perseverance. He eventually overcomes his previous failures to become one of Japan's most celebrated painters under the master Okyo.</summary>
<keywords>Rosetsu, Okyo, perseverance, Kyoto, Japanese painting, leaping carp, sembei, moral lesson</keywords>

# VII

## LEGENDS TOLD BY A FISHERMAN ON LAKE BIWA, AT ZEZE

While fishing up on Lake Biwa, and later shooting in the vicinity (shooting is not allowed on the lake itself, as the water is considered a holy place), I often made Zeze my headquarters. At the edge of the lake, right there, stands the cottage of a very old fisherman and his sons. They have made a little harbor for their boats, but they cultivate no ground; their cottage stands in wild grass near a solitary willow tree. The reason for this is that they are rich, or relatively so, being the owners of an immense fish trap which runs out into the lake for nearly a mile and is a disgrace to all civilized ideas of conservation. They bought the rights from the <term>Daimyo</term>, who owned Zeze Castle a hundred years or more ago (this is my own guess at the date, as I never asked or noted it). The trap catches enough to keep all four families comfortable.

“From that time, in rain or in rough weather, a fireball, six inches in diameter or more, has come from the castle. It comes to wreak vengeance on fishermen and causes many wrecks by leading boats out of their course. Sometimes it comes almost into the boat. Once a fisherman struck it with a bamboo pole, breaking it up into many fiery bits; and on that occasion, many boats were lost.

“In full, it is called ‘The Spider Fire of the Spirit of the Dead Akechi.’ That is all, sir, that I can tell of it—except that I have often seen it myself and feared it.”

“That is very interesting,” said I, “and quite what I like. Can you tell me any more?”

“Perhaps, if <term>Danna San</term> <note>Master/Sir</note> found interest in that simple story, he would like to know the reason why we always have such a terrible storm over the lake on February 25; so I will tell of that also.”

## Legends told by a Fisherman

' At last the 25th of February arrived. O Tani had taken care that the best and largest washing tub had been left near the borders of the lake. After dark she embarked in her frail craft, and without the least fear, she started.

' When she was about halfway across, a fearful storm broke over Hiyei Mountain. The waves rose, and the wind blew with blinding force. Moreover, the light that usually burned on the Hiyei San side of the lake, which the priest had promised would be especially bright this night, had been blown out. It was not long before poor O Tani's tub was capsized, and in spite of her efforts to keep afloat, she sank beneath the waves to rise no more.

' It is said by some that the priest himself put out the light, so as to cut off the last possible chance of O Tani reaching the shore, being over-zealous in his thoughts of good and evil.

' Since the night that O Tani was drowned, every 25th of February has been wild and stormy, and fishermen fear to be out on that day. People say that the cause is the dissatisfied spirit of poor O Tani, who, though she did not fear death, died disconsolate at being deceived by the monk she loved.

' The washing tub that O Tani used drifted ashore at Kinohama village, in Eastern Omi. It was picked up by Gensuke, a matchmaker, who split it up and made matches from it. When this became known to the villagers of Kinohama, including Gensuke himself, they resolved that every 25th of February should be a holiday, and that a prayer should be said at their shrine for the spirit of

Then they went to the Hotaru Dani, and, after embracing each other for the last time on this earth, they each wrote a prayer on a piece of paper, twisted it into a piece of string, and fastened it in a double knot with their thumbs and little fingers through a small hole bored in the soft black rocks. Their ability to do this successfully was taken as an omen that all would be well with them after death, and was an answer to their prayer.

Their spirits passed away together, just as the leaves of fragrant flowers blown off by autumn winds pass together under Seta Bridge.

# VIII

## A MIRACULOUS SWORD

Around the year 110 B.C., there lived a brave prince known in Japanese history as Yamato-dake no Mikoto. <note>Yamato-dake no Mikoto, one of the eighty children of the Emperor Keiko, was a great hero of the prehistoric age. While still a youth, he was sent by his father to destroy the rebels of Western Japan. To achieve this goal, he borrowed the gown of his aunt, who was the high priestess of Ise; thus disguised, he made the rebel chieftains fall in love with him while they were feasting in the cave where they lived. Then, suddenly drawing a sword from his robe, he struck them dead. He next conquered the province of Izumo and finally subdued Eastern Japan, which was a wild wasteland at that time. After many adventures, both warlike and romantic, he died on the march back to Yamato, where the Emperor, his father, held court.</note> He was a great warrior, as was his son, who is said to have been a husband to the Empress Jingo—I assume a second one, because it could not have been the Emperor who was assassinated before the Empress's conquest of Korea. However, that does not matter much to my story, which is merely the legend attached to the miraculous sword known as the *Kusanagi no Tsurugi* (the grass-cutting sword). This sword is held as one of the three sacred treasures and is handed down from father to son in the Imperial Family. The sword is kept at the Atsuta Shrine in Owari Province.

Before starting, Yamato-dake no Mikoto thought he should go to Ise to worship in the temples, to pray for divine aid, and to visit an aunt who lived nearby. Yamato-dake spent five or six days with his aunt, Princess Yamato Hime, to whom he announced his intention of subduing the rebels. She presented him with her greatest treasure—the miraculous sword—and also with a flint-and-tinder box.

Before parting with her nephew, Yamato Hime no Mikoto said: ‘This sword is the most precious thing I could give you, and it will guard you safely through all dangers. Value it accordingly, for it will be one of the sacred treasures.’

After bidding farewell to Yamato Hime no Mikoto, the Prince departed, setting out for the province of Suruga on the eastern coast to see what he could learn, as it was in a state of unrest. It was there that he encountered his first danger, as his enemies laid a trap for him, knowing that he was fond of hunting.

There were some immense rush plains in Suruga Province where the village of Yaitsu Mura (‘Yaitsu’ means ‘burning fields’) now stands. The rebels decided that one of them should go and invite Yamato-dake to come out and hunt, while the others were to scatter and hide themselves in the long grass until the guide should lead him into their midst; then they would jump up and kill him. Accordingly, they sent a convincing and clever man to Yamato-dake, who told him that there were many deer on the grass plains. Would he come and hunt them? The man volunteered to act as a guide.

The invitation was tempting; and, as he had found the country less rebellious than he had expected, the Prince accepted.

When morning arrived, the Prince, in addition to carrying his hunting bow, carried the sword given to him by his aunt, Princess Yamato. # A Miraculous Sword
59

The guide intended to make the Prince hunt upwind; if they set the grass on fire properly, the flames would rush with lightning speed toward him while remaining absolutely safe for the rebels themselves.

Yamato-dake did exactly as they had expected. He came forward quietly, suspecting nothing. Suddenly, the rushes caught fire in front of him and at his sides. The Prince realized that he had been betrayed. The treacherous guide had disappeared. The Prince stood in danger of suffocation and death. The smoke, dense and choking, rushed along rapidly with a great roaring sound.

Yamato-dake tried to run for the only gap, but he was too late. Then he began cutting the grass with his sword to prevent the fire from reaching him. He discovered that whichever direction he cut with his sword, the wind shifted to that same direction. If he cut toward the north, the wind changed to the south and prevented the fire from advancing further; if he cut toward the south, the wind changed to the north, and so on. Taking advantage of this, Yamato-dake retaliated against his enemies. He took fire from his aunt's tinderbox, and where there was no fire in the rushes, he lit them, cutting through the grass at the same time in the direction he wished the fire to travel. Rushing from point to point in this way, he succeeded in his effort to turn the tables on his enemies and destroyed them all.

It is important to note that there is a sword in existence, said to be this very sword, in the Atsuta Shrine in Owari Province; a great festival in its honor is held on June 21 every year.

From that place, Yamato-dake no Mikoto went on

Finding things quiet there, he took a ship to cross to Kazusa Province, accompanied by a lady he deeply loved, who was given the title of <term>Hime</term> (Princess) because of Yamato-dake’s rank. Her name was Tachibana. They had not gone more than ten miles from shore when a terrible storm arose. The ship threatened to sink.

“This,” said Princess Tachibana, “is the work of one of the sea goddesses who thirst for men’s lives. I will give her mine, my lord; perhaps that may appease her until you have safely crossed the treacherous sea.”

Without further warning, Princess Tachibana threw herself into the sea; the waves closed over her head, to the dismay and grief of everyone, and to the breaking of Yamato-dake’s heart.

As Princess Tachibana had expected, the sea goddess was appeased. The wind died down, the water calmed, and the ship reached Kazusa Province safely. Yamato-dake traveled as far as Yezo, suppressing small rebellions along the way.

Several years later, accompanied by many of his former officers, he found himself back on the side of a hill in Sagami Province overlooking the place where poor Princess Tachibana had given up her life for him by throwing herself into the sea. The Prince gazed sadly at the sea and cried out three times, with tears flowing down his cheeks—brave though he was—“Azuma waya!” (Alas, my dearest wife!); and Eastern Japan, near the center, has since then been called “Azuma.”

## IX

# 'THE PROCESSION OF GHOSTS' <note>Somewhere between 1400 and 1550, there lived a family of celebrated painters spanning three generations, which makes it difficult to be accurate about them. There were Tosa Mitsunobu, Kano Mitsunobu, and Hasegawa Mitsunobu; sometimes Tosa Mitsunobu signed his pictures as Fujiwara Mitsunobu. When I add that there were other celebrated painters—Kano Masanobu and Kano Motonobu, besides their families, imitators, and forgers of their names—you will realize the difficulties one may encounter in determining names and dates. However, as usual, I have been safely guided by a kind friend, His Excellency Mr. Hattori, the Governor, whose knowledge of art is great. Undoubtedly, it was Tosa Mitsunobu who painted the picture known as the *Hiyakki Yakō*, or as *The One Hundred Ghosts' Procession*, which is famous and has served as a guide for drawing hobgoblins and ghosts, "spooks," "eeries," or whatever you may choose to call them. As far as I can judge, the picture was painted about the end of the first half of the fifteenth century.</note>

About four or five hundred years ago, there was an old temple not far from Fushimi, near Kyoto. It was called the Shozenji temple and had been deserted for many years because priests were afraid to live there due to the ghosts that were said to haunt it. Still, no one had ever actually seen the ghosts. No doubt the story arose because all the priests had been killed by a large band of robbers many years ago, beyond human memory—for the sake of loot, of course.

This struck such horror into the minds of everyone that the temple was allowed to rot and fall into ruin.

One year a priest, a pilgrim and a stranger, passed by the temple. Not knowing its history, he went in and sought refuge from the weather instead of continuing his journey to Fushimi. Having cold rice in his traveling bag, he felt that he could do no better than pass the night there; for, although the weather might be cold, he would at least avoid drenching the only clothes he had and would be well off in the morning.

The good man took up his quarters in one of the smaller rooms, which was in better repair than the rest of the place. After eating his meal, he said his prayers and lay down to sleep, while the rain fell in torrents on the roof and the wind howled through the creaky buildings. Try as he might, the priest could not sleep, for the cold drafts chilled him to the bone. Somewhere about midnight, the old man heard weird and unnatural noises. They seemed to come from the main building.

Prompted by curiosity, he arose; and when he reached the main building, he found <term>Hiyakki Yakō</term> (meaning a procession of one hundred ghosts)—a term, I believe, which has been generally applied to a company of ghosts. The ghosts fought, wrestled, danced, and made merry. Although greatly alarmed at first, our priest became interested. After a few moments, however, more awful spirit-like ghosts appeared. The priest ran back to the small room and barred himself in; he spent the rest of the night saying masses for the souls of the dead.

At daybreak, although the weather remained wet, the priest departed. He told the villagers what he had seen,

Having cold rice in his wallet <note>A traveling bag or pouch used by pilgrims.</note>, he felt that he could do no better than spend the night there; for, although the weather might be cold, he would at least avoid drenching the only clothes he had and would be well off in the morning.

That night the priest could not sleep, and he lay wondering what he should do the next day.

### THE PROCESSION OF GHOSTS

A little later in the night, he heard weird and unusual noises. They seemed to come from the main hall of the temple.

# ‘ The Procession of Ghosts ’

...and they spread the news so widely that within three or four days, the temple was known as the most haunted temple in the neighborhood.

It was at this time that the celebrated painter Tosa Mitsunobu heard of it. Having always been eager to paint a picture of the <term>Hiyakki Yakō</term>, he thought that a sight of the ghosts in Shozenji temple might give him the necessary material; so he set off for Fushimi and Shozenji.

Mitsunobu went straight to the temple at dusk and stayed up all night in a rather uneasy state of mind; but he saw no ghosts and heard no noise.

The next morning, he opened all the windows and doors and flooded the main temple with light. No sooner had he done this than he found the walls of the place covered, as it were, with the figures or drawings of ghosts of indescribable complexity. There were far more than two hundred, and all were different.

If only he could remember them! That was what Tosa Mitsunobu thought. Drawing his notebook and brush from his pocket, he proceeded to record them in minute detail. This occupied the better part of the day.

During his examination of the outlines of the various ghosts and goblins which he had drawn, Mitsunobu saw that the fantastic shapes had come from cracks in the damp, deserted walls; these cracks were filled with fungi and mildew, which in their turn produced the shading, coloring, and eventually the figures from which he compiled his celebrated picture <term>Hiyakki Yakō</term>.

## X

### A FAITHFUL SERVANT<note>This short tragedy, demonstrating the deep loyalty that was common 1,000 years ago, was told to me by Mr. Matsuzaki of the Kencho (Government Office).</note>

During the reign of Emperor Engi, which began in the year 901 AD, there lived a man whose name has ever since been celebrated for his beautiful writings, both poetic and otherwise. He was the Emperor's great favorite, and consequently, he was the powerful man of the day; his name was Sugawara Michizane. Needless to say, with all these factors in his favor, it was not long before he was the head of the government, living in luxury.

Things went well enough for a time, but the inevitable finally happened. Not everyone agreed with Michizane's ideas or his politics. Secret enemies lurked at every corner. Among them was one particularly wicked man named Tokihira, whose poisonous intrigues at Court were constant.

Tokihira held a government position under Michizane and hated him in his heart, thinking that if he could only arrange to get Michizane into the bad graces of the

Michizane was a man in whom little fault could be found, and so it happened that Tokihira was unable to find any reason to start malicious rumors about him; but as time went on, he became more determined to eventually do him harm.

At last, an opportunity arrived. Tokihira, who had many secret agents trying to discover something to report to the Emperor against Michizane, heard a report that Prince Toki (*Toki no Miya*) had secretly fallen in love with Michizane's beautiful daughter, and that they were holding secret meetings.

Tokihira was overjoyed at the news and went immediately to the Emperor, who received him after hearing that he had a remarkable tale of intrigue to tell.

"Your Majesty," Tokihira said, "as much as it grieves me to tell it, a serious plot is underway. Sugawara Michizane has arranged it so that Your Majesty’s younger brother, Prince Toki, has fallen in love with his daughter. As deeply as I regret to say it, they are holding secret meetings. Moreover, Michizane, Your Majesty’s Premier, is scheming so that Your Majesty may be assassinated, or at least dethroned in favor of Prince Toki, who is to marry Michizane's daughter."

Naturally, Emperor Engi was infuriated. He was a good and stable monarch and had ruled the people fairly, firmly, and well with the help of Michizane. He had regarded Michizane as a personal friend; the thought of Michizane conspiring to assassinate him, or at least scheming to place Prince Toki on the

He sent for Michizane.

Michizane protested his innocence. It was true, he said, that the Prince had fallen in love with his daughter; but that was not much to be wondered at. His daughter was beautiful; the Prince and she were much the same age, and had seen much of each other since their childhood. Now that they had grown older, they found that their friendship had turned to love. That was all. It was not easy for a Prince of royal blood to meet the lady of his heart as openly as another might; and, no doubt, they had met, for his daughter had told him so. As for the plot asserted by Tokihira, that was absolutely fanciful, and it was astonishing to hear such a dastardly accusation.

Tokihira perceived the Emperor's temper. With loud words and unscrupulous lies, he overthrew all of the unfortunate Michizane's protests; and the Emperor ordered Michizane to be sent for the rest of his life to Tsukushi, on the island of Kyushu.

Accompanied only by his faithful servant Matsuo, Michizane went into exile. Michizane's punishment, unjust as it was, ended the employment of many others. All those who had been closely associated with him were dismissed. Among them was Takebayashi Genzo, who had been one of Michizane's chief attendants. Genzo had been one of Michizane's literary pupils; consequently, it is not surprising that upon losing his employment, Genzo fled to a small town and, out of duty, took Michizane's wife and young son Kanshusai, aged

First, he told his banished master of his intention, and having obtained permission, he journeyed back to Kyoto and sought out Tokihira himself, to whom he offered his services both as a servant and as a hunter of Michizane’s son, Kanshusai. Tokihira readily hired him, thinking that now he would be sure to find the boy whom he wished to have beheaded. Tokihira had taken Michizane’s place in the Emperor’s favor and had great power; his will was almost law.

Matsuo played his part so well in Tokihira’s household and among his servants that it was not long before they all agreed that Matsuo was most faithful to his new master, and the greatest confidence was placed in him.

Shortly after this, Tokihira learned that Kanshusai was hidden under a different name in the school that belonged to Genzo. Genzo was ordered to send the boy’s head to Tokihira within forty-eight hours.

At the appointed time, Tokihira’s officials called at the school to fetch it, and they carried it back to Tokihira, saying: “Now, Lord Tokihira, there is no longer any fear for the future from Michizane’s son, for here is his head in this box. See! And here is the schoolmaster Takebayashi Genzo, who followed your lordship’s orders and cut it off.”

Tokihira was pleased, but not perfectly certain that the head was the correct one; so, knowing that Matsuo had previously been employed by Michizane and that he must know if it were Kanshusai’s head or not, he called him, ordering him to take the head out of the box and identify it.

Poor Matsuo! Imagine his feelings at having to draw his only son Kotaro’s head from the box, hold it up by the hair, and assure Lord Tokihira that it was indeed the head of Kanshusai, Michizane’s son! He did so, however, with great courage and splendid fortitude, thus saving the life of Kanshusai and fulfilling his duty to his banished master, Michizane.

Matsuo’s loyalty is still admired by those who know the story.

## XI

# PRINCE HOSOKAWA’S MOST VALUABLE TITLE-DEEDS¹

SEVERAL hundred years ago, there lived in the lands of the Hosokawas a widow and her daughter, a beautiful girl of seventeen named Kazuye. O Kazuye San’s father had been foully murdered <note>The following three words are underlined in blue ink:</note> some six months before, and both Kazuye and her mother had made up their minds to devote their fortune and their lives to bringing the criminals to justice. In these efforts they received no help, but spent all of their money, until at last they were almost forced to beg in the street for food. Day after day, however, they continued to pray in the temple for help, and never once lost heart or weakened in their purpose. O Kazuye told her mother that if she were fortunate enough to gain the affections of a man, even he would be sacrificed in the pursuit of vengeance.
One day it happened that the poverty-stricken appearance of Kazuye and her mother, returning as usual from praying in the temple, aroused the laughter of a party

After about a year had passed, a great fire broke out in the castle. It was so sudden that nothing could be done. The wind, fanning the flames, barely gave the people time to escape, let alone enough time to carry off the family valuables.

When everyone was clear of the burning mass, the <term>Daimyo</term> suddenly remembered that his title deeds would be lost and that such a disaster would be dangerous for his family. Realizing this, he jumped from his horse and was about to dash back to try to recover them; but his retainers held him back, fearing that he would die.

<meta>This page concludes the story of Okawa’s ultimate sacrifice to protect the Hosokawa family's legal documents during a castle fire.</meta>

Okawa, hearing this, thought with delight that an opportunity had now come for him to save his new master and repay him for the kindness shown to himself and Kazuye. He rushed into the burning mass and, having broken open the iron safe, seized the valuable documents. Then he found escape impossible. He was cut off by fire on all sides and plainly saw that both he and the papers would be burned. At this moment, a thought came to him. Although he must be burned, perhaps his body might save the documents. Drawing his short sword, he deliberately disemboweled himself and thrust the roll of papers into his stomach. Then he flung himself on the flaming floor and died. The fire continued. Poor Okawa was charred beyond recognition.

When the fire was over, his body was recovered, and inside the roasted corpse was found the blood-stained roll of papers on which the Hosokawa family depended. From that time on, the document has been called ‘*Hosokawa no chi daruma*’—the blood-stained document of the Hosokawas.

<summary>Okawa saves the Hosokawa family's vital title deeds by disemboweling himself and hiding the papers within his body to protect them from a fire. The documents were recovered from his charred remains and became a legendary family heirloom known as the "blood-stained document."</summary>

### XII

## THE STORY OF KATO SAYEMON<note>This was told to me by Mr. Matsuzaki. I cannot say that I think much of the story. Sayemon is presented as a hero, but to most people, he must seem like a rather cowardly and low creature. I remarked on this to Mr. Matsuzaki, saying: "I do not see how the story is finished. You make Sayemon out to be a model person, whereas to me he seems like the worst person in the story. Surely the wife and son should have been portrayed as the good people; yet you laud and praise Sayemon for leaving his family and refusing to recognize them, even though they had committed no sin against him." "I do not see the problem," said Mr. Matsuzaki. "It is the same as with the Lord Buddha. He also left his wife and devoted his life to religious affairs, just as Sayemon did." Well, I could not agree with this. Buddha was Buddha, a benefactor and helper to all of Asia. Sayemon was a poor, miserable weakling who simply sought personal peace. As far as the story goes, I defy anyone to find him a hero, or someone who in any way emulated Buddha—unless they did so from an entirely Japanese perspective. However, the story is quite celebrated and is mentioned in many Japanese books, or so Mr. Matsuzaki tells me.</note>

IN the days when Ashikaga was Shogun, there served under him a knight of good family, Kato Sayemon, of whom he was especially fond. Things went well for Sayemon. He lived in what might almost be called a palace. He possessed plenty of money. He had a charming wife who had borne him a son, and, according to old custom, he had many others who lived as wives within his mansion. There was no war in the land.

<summary>The story introduces Kato Sayemon, a wealthy and favored knight serving the Shogun Ashikaga during a time of peace. The author includes a lengthy note debating the moral character of Sayemon, who abandons his family for a religious life, comparing him unfavorably to the Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Kato Sayemon, Ashikaga Shogun, Mr. Matsuzaki, Lord Buddha, Japan, samurai, religious life, morality</keywords>

--- Page 152 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of Kato Sayemon, a knight serving the Shogun Ashikaga, as he observes a disturbing omen within his peaceful household.</meta>

Sayemon experienced no trouble in his household. Peace and contentment reigned. He enjoyed life accordingly, with feasting and so forth. "Oh, if only such a life could last!" he thought; but fate decreed otherwise.

One evening, while Sayemon was strolling through his lovely garden, watching the fireflies and listening to singing insects and piping toads—of which he was extremely fond—he happened to pass his wife’s room and look up.

There he saw his dear wife and his favorite concubine playing chess (<term>go</term> in Japanese). What struck him most was that they appeared perfectly happy and contented in each other’s company. However, while Sayemon watched, their hair seemed to rise up from behind in the shapes of snakes that fought desperately. This filled him with fear.

In amazement, Sayemon stealthily approached in order to see better, but he found the vision remained the same. His wife and the other lady, when moving their pieces, smiled at each other, showing every sign of great courtesy; nevertheless, the indistinct outlines of their hair continued to take the forms of fighting snakes. Until then, Sayemon had thought of them as almost sisters to each other, and that was indeed how they had appeared outwardly; but now that he had seen the mysterious sign of the snakes, he knew that they hated each other more than a man could understand.

He became uneasy in his mind. Until then, his life had been made doubly happy because he thought his home was peaceful; but now, he reflected, hatred and malice must be rampant in the house. Sayemon felt as if
