# The Story of Kato Sayemon

...he was like a rudderless boat, being drawn toward a waterfall from which no means of escape seemed possible.

He spent a sleepless night in meditation, during which he decided that running away would be the safest course in the end. Peace was all that he craved. To obtain it, he would devote himself to religious work for the rest of his life.

The next morning, Kato Sayemon was nowhere to be found. There was great distress in the household. Men were sent here, there, and everywhere, but Sayemon could not be found. On the fifth or sixth day after his disappearance, his wife reduced the size of the household staff, but she continued to live in the house with her little son, Ishidomaro. Even the Shogun Ashikaga was greatly troubled by Sayemon's disappearance. No news of him arrived, and time passed until a year had gone by, and then another, when Sayemon's wife resolved to take Ishidomaru, then five years old, and go in search of him.

For five weary years they wandered about, this mother and son, making inquiries everywhere; but they could not find the slightest clue until at last, one day, they were staying at a village in Kishu. There, they met an old man who told them that a year before, he had seen Kato Sayemon at the temple of Koya San. "Certainly," he said, "I knew him, for I was once a palanquin-bearer <note>A person who carries a covered litter or palanquin</note> for the Shogun, and I saw *Sayemon San* very often. I cannot say if he is still at the temple, but he was a priest there a year ago."

There was very little sleep for Ishidomaro and his mother that night. They were in a fever of excitement. Ishidomaro was now eleven years of age and was most

Unfortunately, according to ancient regulations, the temple and mountain of Koya San were for men only. No woman was allowed to ascend the mountain to worship the image of Buddha. Thus, Ishidomaro’s mother had to remain in the village while he went in search of his father.

At daybreak he started, full of hope, telling his mother not to fear. "I will bring back father this very evening," he said; "and how happy we shall all be! Farewell for now, and do not fear for me!" After saying this, Ishidomaro set off. "True," he said, "I do not know my father by sight; but he has a black mole over his left eye, as do I; besides, I feel that it is my father I am going to meet." With these and other thoughts in his mind, the boy plodded upward through the tall and gloomy forests, stopping here and there at wayside shrines to pray for success.

Higher and higher Ishidomaro climbed—Koya San is nearly 1,100 feet in height—until he reached the outer gates of the temple, whose true name is "Kongobuji," for "Koya San" means only "Mount Koya."

Having arrived at the first priest’s house, Ishidomaro saw an old man mumbling prayers.

‘Ah, my lad, I feel sorry for you,’ answered Sayemon (for it was indeed he). ‘I know of no man called Kato Sayemon in these temples.’ Delivering this speech, Sayemon showed considerable emotion. He fully recognized that the boy he was addressing was his son, and he was in great distress to deny him like this, and not to acknowledge and take him to his heart; but Sayemon had made up his mind that the rest of his life should be sacrificed for the sake of Buddha, and that all worldly things should be cast aside. Ishidomaro was not at all satisfied with this answer. He felt somehow or other that he was in the presence of his father. Moreover, the priest had a black mole over his left eye, and he, Ishidomaro, had one exactly the same.

Thus it was that Sayemon preferred to devote his life to Buddha, and (as Mr. Matsuzaki tells me) to emulate Buddha, rather than return to the ways of the world or to his family, or even to recognize his one and only son!

My sympathies are with Ishidomaro, of whom, as of his poor mother, we are told nothing further. To end in Mr. Matsuzaki’s words:

> ‘What became of Ishidomaro and his mother is not known; but it is told to this day that Kato Sayemon passed the rest of his life in peace and purity, entirely sacrificing his body and soul to Buddha, and did these things without any person to mourn over him, but in perfect contentment.’

## XIII
# GREAT FIRE CAUSED BY A LADY’S DRESS

About 120 years ago, in the Tenmei era <note>The Tenmei era occurred from 1781 to 1789.</note>, a most terrible fire broke out in the western corner of Edo—probably the worst fire known in world history, for it is said to have destroyed no fewer than 188,000 people.

At that time there lived in Edo (now Tokyo) a very rich pawnbroker, Enshu Hikoemon, the proud father of a beautiful sixteen-year-old daughter named O-Same. Her name in this instance is probably derived from the word *sameru* (to fade away), for in truth O-Same-san did fade away.

Enshu Hikoemon loved his daughter dearly; as he was a widower with no other children, his thoughts and affections were concentrated on her alone. He had long been wealthy enough to cast aside the petty thoughts and traits that had enabled him to reach his current position. From being a hard-hearted, relentless money-grubber, Enshu Hikoemon had become soft-hearted and generous—at least as far as his daughter was concerned.

Poor Hikoyemon! This was a difficult situation—his daughter in love—dying of love for an unknown priest! What was he to do? First he humored his daughter, and at last, after several days, persuaded her to accompany him to the temple. Unfortunately, they did not see the priest in question; nor did they on a second visit; and after this O Same became more dejected than ever, absolutely refusing to leave her room. Night and day her sobs were heard all over the house, and her father was utterly wretched, especially since he had now secretly discovered that the priest with whom his daughter had fallen in love was one of the most strict of Buddha's followers, and not likely to stray from the disciplinary rules of his religion.

In spite of this, Hikoyemon determined to make an effort on behalf of his daughter. He ventured to the temple alone, saw the priest, told him of his daughter's love, and asked if a union would be possible.

The priest rejected the idea, saying, "Is it not clear to you by my robes that I have devoted my love to Buddha? It is an insult that you should make such a proposal to me!"

Hikoyemon felt the loss of his beautiful daughter very much. At the funeral, there must have been half a mile of flower-bearers.

The superb dress was presented to the temple. Such dresses are carefully kept; they remind the priests to say prayers for their late owners whenever they are dusted and cleaned every two or three months.

The Vicar, or Head Priest, of this temple, however, was not a good man. Knowing its value, he stole this particular dress of O Same’s and sold it secretly to a second-hand dealer of such items.

About twelve months later, the dress was donated to the same temple again by another father whose daughter had died from a love affair, as he had bought the dress at the second-hand clothing shop. (This girl died and was buried on the same day of the same month as O Same.)

Since he was driven by greed, he sold it again. It truly seemed to be a kind of gold mine for himself and his temple. Imagine, therefore, the feelings of the priests when, in the following year—during the same month and on the exact same day that O Same and the other girl had died—another girl of the same age was buried in their cemetery. At the end of her funeral service, the dress was presented to the temple for the third time.

To say that the chief priest was astonished would be an understatement. He and the rest of them were deeply confused and troubled.

There were the honest priests, who had nothing to do with selling the garment, and the dishonest head priest, or vicar. The honest men were puzzled, while the vicar was so frightened that he decided honesty was the best policy under the circumstances. Consequently, he gathered all the priests of the temple, made a quick confession, and asked for their advice.

The priests reached one conclusion: the spirit of O Same San was within the dress, and it had to be burned. It must be destroyed with a special ceremony to appease her spirit. Accordingly, a time was set. When the day arrived, many people came to the temple. A grand ceremony was held, and finally, the valuable garment was placed on a stone carved into the shape of a lotus flower and set on fire.

The weather was calm at the time; however, as the garment caught fire, a sudden gust of wind arrived, instantly fanning the entire thing into flames. The gust increased into

The fire continued for seven days and seven nights; by the time it ended, nearly the whole southern and western portions of Yedo were destroyed, and 188,000 people had perished.

### XIV

## HISTORY OF AWOTO FUJITSUNA<note>Told to me by my friend Mr. Matsuzaki.</note>

Hojo Tokiyori—who my *Murray* guidebook says was born in 1246 A.D. and died seventeen years later, in 1263—was a Regent for a time, young as he was.

One day he went to worship at the shrine of Tsurugaoka in Kamakura. That same evening he dreamed that one of the gods appeared to him and said:

> “Hojo Tokiyori, you are very young for a ruler, and there are those who will try to deceive you, for honest men are scarce. There is one man who is of exceptional honesty, however, and if you wish to govern the people successfully, it would be wise to employ him. His name is Awoto Fujitsuna.”

Hojo Tokiyori told him of his dream. “No,” said he; “it was more than a dream: it was a vision that called upon me to appoint you to the post, which I have done.”

“Ah, indeed!” said Awoto Fujitsuna. “Then, sir, if you appoint high officials as the result of dreams and visions, it is a risky matter; for by those same dreams, we may one day be ordered to be beheaded!”

<summary>The young Regent Hojo Tokiyori appoints Awoto Fujitsuna to a government post after a god recommends him in a dream. Fujitsuna accepts but warns the Regent about the dangers of making official appointments based on visions.</summary>
<keywords>Hojo Tokiyori, Awoto Fujitsuna, Kamakura, Tsurugaoka, Regent, Murray, Mr. Matsuzaki, dreams, Japanese history</keywords>

HISTORY OF AWOTO FUJITSUNA<note>This is told to me by my friend Mr. Matsuzaki.</note>

Hojo Tokiyori—who my *Murray* guidebook says was born in 1246 A.D. and died seventeen years later, in 1263—was a Regent for a time, young as he was.

### AWOTO FUJITSUNA ORDERS EVERY ONE TO SEARCH FOR THE HALF-CENT

One night, while he was staying at his villa at Matsuoka in Kamakura, he dreamed that one of the gods appeared to him and said:

> “Hojo Tokiyori, you are very young for a ruler, and there are some who will try to deceive you, for honest men are scarce. There is one man who is of exceptional honesty, however, and if you wish to govern the people successfully, it would be advisable to employ him. His name is Awoto Fujitsuna.”

“Ah, indeed!” said Awoto Fujitsuna. “Then, sir, if you appoint high officials as the result of dreams and visions, it is a risky matter, for by those dreams we may some day be ordered to be beheaded!”

### History of Awoto Fujitsuna

Hojo Tokiyori laughed at this and said he hoped not. Awoto Fujitsuna proved to be a most excellent and trustworthy official—popular, just, and honest. No one had a word to say against him, and Hojo Tokiyori was delighted.

One day, Fujitsuna was carrying a bag of government money over a bridge. He fell, and the bag burst open. Fujitsuna collected the money, with the exception of one half-cent piece, which had somehow rolled over the edge of the bridge and fallen into the river.

Fujitsuna could have let it go and put another in its place, but that course of action would not have met the high moral standards he held in such matters. He had lost a half-cent that belonged to the government. He knew it was in the river. Consequently, he refused to move on until it was recovered. That was clearly his duty. Awoto Fujitsuna ran to the houses at either end of the bridge, telling the villagers only that he had dropped some government money into the river and asking if they would come and help him find it. Of course they would, being as ready to help as the Japanese countryfolk have been since time immemorial. Everyone followed Fujitsuna into the river—men, women, and children—and a diligent search was maintained by several hundred people for many hours without result. Finally, just as the sun was setting, an old farmer picked up the half-cent and presented it to Fujitsuna.

Fujitsuna was delighted and told the people that everything was fine now: he had recovered the money thanks to the sharp eyes of the farmer.

->12<-

# Ancient Tales and Folklore of Japan

‘But,’ they cried, ‘that is only a half-cent. Where is the rest?’

‘My friends,’ said Fujitsuna, ‘the half-cent is all that was lost; but that half-cent was not mine. It was part of the Government treasure and was entrusted to me, and it was my duty to recover it. Here are thirty yen for you who have helped me find it, to spend on sake. That is my money; and remember what I tell you—that no matter how small a thing is entrusted to you by the Government, you must not lose it, but rather give up your life and fortune.’

The villagers were greatly impressed by this honesty and reasoning.

Hojo Tokiyori, upon hearing this story, sent for and promoted Awoto Fujitsuna to a higher position than he had held before. However, despite his advancement and wealth, the minister continued to work hard, eat simple food, and wear plain clothing, living in a cottage instead of occupying a palace, and devoting his life to his country.

### XV

# A LIFE SAVED BY A SPIDER AND
# TWO DOVES

Regarding *Yoritomo*, *Murray* says that “he lived from 1147 to 1199. He was the founder of the Shogunate—the first Japanese Mayor of the Palace, if one may so phrase it. A descendant of the great house of *Minamoto*, as shrewd and ambitious as he was unscrupulous and inhuman, he was left an orphan at an early age and barely escaped death as a boy at the hands of *Kiyomori*, the then all-powerful minister who belonged to the rival house of *Taira*.”

In this excellently concise summary of *Yoritomo's* fifty-two years of life, it is easy to see that he must have had innumerable adventures. Fighting continued throughout his career; yet oddly enough, despite all of this, he died comfortably in bed.

During the first half of *Yoritomo's* life, he was once severely defeated in a battle against *Oba Kage-chika* in the *Ishibashi* mountains, in the province of *Izu*. His defeat had been so severe that *Yoritomo*, along with six of his most faithful followers—to use common language—bolted. They fled, not with great courage, but simply to save their own lives.

# A Life saved by a Spider and Two Doves

At this command, Kagetoki led the way, carefully avoiding the big tree, for he was determined to save Yoritomo’s life if he could. By some misfortune, however, he chose an abominably bad path, and Kage-chika, who was wearing a particularly heavy suit of armor, cried out, ‘Enough of your leading! Let us stick to the road where we started. It is more likely to be the one the fugitives took. In any case, this is no road at all where you are leading us, and with heavy armor on it is impossible.’

So it was that in due time they reached the huge tree. Kagetoki was very afraid that his cousin would go into the hollow and find Yoritomo, and he began to think of how he could save him.

Kage-chika was about to enter the hollow tree when a bright idea occurred to Kagetoki.

‘Wait!’ he said. ‘It is no use wasting time by going in there. Can’t you see that there is a spider’s web right across the entrance? It would have been quite impossible for anyone to get inside without breaking it.’

Kage-chika was half-inclined to agree that his cousin was right; but, still being a little suspicious of him, he reached in with his bow to feel what was inside. Just as his bow was about to strike Yoritomo’s heavy armor (which would naturally have revealed his presence), two beautiful white doves flew out from the top of the hole.

‘You are right, cousin,’ said Kage-chika, laughing when he saw the doves: ‘I am wasting time here, for no...

Thus it was that Yoritomo’s life was saved by a spider and two doves. When he became Shogun in later years, and established Kamakura as his place of residence and as the seat of government, two shrines were built in the temple of Tsuru-ga-oka, which itself is dedicated to Hachiman, the God of War. One is dedicated to the Emperor Nintoku, son of Ojin, the God of War, and the other to Yoritomo, called <term>Shirahata Jinja</term>. The shrines were erected to show Yoritomo’s gratitude to the God of War, for doves are known in Japan as the messengers of war, not of peace.

The temple, which was rebuilt in 1828 after having been destroyed by fire seven years earlier, is in the Ryobu Shinto style, with red pillars, beams, and rafters. Immediately behind the temple of Hachiman is a small hill called Shirabata-yama, from which Yoritomo is said to have often admired the view. The base of the hill is enclosed and laid out as a garden.

## XVI

# MURAKAMI YOSHITERU’S FAITHFULNESS

Murakami Yoshiteru—whom we shall call Yoshiteru for short—was one of the loyal retainers of Prince Morinaga, the third son of Emperor Godaigo, who reigned from 1319 to 1339. When I say “reigned,” I mean that Godaigo was the Emperor; however, there was a Regent at the time, Hojo Takatoki, who ruled with harshness and great selfishness.

With the exception of young Prince Morinaga, the Imperial family appeared to take things lightly. They preferred peace and comfort to unrest and conflict. Prince Morinaga was different. Fiery-tempered and proud, he believed that Hojo Takatoki was usurping the Emperor's rights. The man, he said, was by birth nothing more than one of the Emperor’s subjects and had no business being appointed Regent.

Naturally, these opinions led to trouble, and it was not long before Prince Morinaga was forced to leave the capital suddenly with his followers. There were several hundred of them—not enough to fight Hojo Takatoki at that time.

# Murakami Yoshiteru's Faithfulness

Prince Morinaga had decided that it would be better to live independently in Yamato than to be under the control of Hojo Takatoki, as his father and elder brothers were. Having gathered the most faithful of his followers—the most notable of whom was the hero of our story, Murakami Yoshiteru—the Prince left the capital in disguise and set out for Yoshino in Yamato. There, in the wild mountains, he intended to build a castle where he could live for the rest of his days independent of the Regent, whom he greatly loathed.

Prince Morinaga carried an Imperial flag with him, which he expected would win him sympathy and help even in the wild Yamato Province. Although it is only about thirty miles in a direct line from Kioto (the capital at the time) to the borders of Yamato, the entire country is mountainous and wild; roads are non-existent, and mountain paths take their place. Consequently, it was noon on the fifth day before the Prince found himself at a small border village called Imogase. There he found his way blocked, essentially, by a guard-house whose soldiers had been chosen from the Imogase villagers and were headed by a man named Shoji, a rough and disagreeable man.

When Prince Morinaga and his party of about eighty followers—dressed as *yamabushi* (fighting monks)—arrived flying the standard, they were ordered to halt by the village guard and told that they could go no further into Yamato without leaving one of their number as a hostage. The Prince was too proud to speak to the villagers and explain the situation, and unfortunately, Murakami Yoshiteru, his most trusted leader, could not be found, for he had remained several miles behind to gather straw and make a

new pair of *waraji* (straw shoes). Shoji, the leader of the Imogase villagers, was firm in his demand that one of the party should be left behind until their return. For about twenty minutes, matters stood this way. Neither side wanted to fight. At last Shoji said:

"Well, you may say that you are a prince! I am a simple villager, and I do not know. You may carry the Imperial flag; but when you are dressed like *yamabushi*, it does not look exactly as if you were a prince. Since I do not want trouble, and you want to pass without trouble—my orders being that out of all parties of more than ten armed people I am to hold one as a hostage—the only suggestion I can make is that I keep this Imperial flag as a hostage."

The prince, glad enough to avoid leaving one of his faithful followers behind, gave the standard to Shoji as a hostage, and then he and his party were allowed to pass into Yamato. They proceeded on their way. Not half an hour after they had passed, Murakami Yoshiteru arrived at the guard-house, having made himself a pair of straw shoes to take the place of his old ones; and his surprise at seeing his master's flag in such lowly hands was matched by his anger.

"What is the meaning of this?" he asked.

Shoji explained what had happened.

On hearing the story, Murakami lost control of his temper. He flew into a violent rage. He reviled Shoji and his men as a set of low blackguards who hardly had a right to look at the Imperial standard of Japan, much less dare to touch it; and with that, he began a general assault on the village guard, killing three

Two days later, the party reached Yoshino, and in the vicinity of this place they built a fortress, where they lived in peace for some months. It was not long, however, before the Regent heard of the prince’s whereabouts, and he soon sent a small army after him. For two days the fort was desperately attacked; on the third the outer gates were taken; two-thirds of the prince’s men were dead. Murakami had been wounded three times, and his life could not last long. Faithful to the end, he rushed to his prince, saying, "Master, I am mortally wounded. In less than half an hour our enemies will have conquered us, for we have only a few men left. Your Highness is unwounded, and can escape in disguise when the end comes. Give me your armor quickly, and let me pretend that I am Your Highness. I will show our enemies how a prince can die."

Changing clothes hastily and putting on the prince’s armor, Murakami—bleeding badly from his wounds and already more dead than alive with weakness from the loss of blood—regained the wall. Struggling up the last steps, he reached a point where he could see and be seen by the whole of the enemy.

# XVII

## A STORY OF THE OKI ISLANDS

The Oki Islands, located about forty-five miles from the mainland of Hoki Province, were for centuries the scene of conflict, sorrow, and exile; but today they are fairly prosperous and very peaceful. Fish, octopus, and cuttlefish are the main exports. They are a strange, wild, and rocky group of islands, difficult to access, and very few Europeans have visited them. I know of only two—the late Lafcadio Hearn and Mr. Anderson (who was there to collect animals for the Duke of Bedford). I myself sent Oto, my Japanese hunter, who was glad to return.

In the Middle Ages—that is, from about the year 1000 A.D.—there was much fighting over the islands by various chieftains, and many people were sent there in exile.

In the year 1239, Hojo Yoshitoshi defeated the Emperor Go Toba and banished him to Dogen Island.

Another Hojo chieftain banished another Emperor, Go Daigo, to Nishi-no-shima. Oribe Shima, the hero of our story, was probably banished by this same Hojo chieftain,

## A Story of Oki Islands

...long journey to the far-off province of Hoki, which, after many weeks she reached, reaching the sea at a place called Akasaki, from where on clear days the Islands of Oki can be dimly seen. Immediately she set to work and tried to persuade the fishermen to take her to the Islands; but nearly all her money was gone, and, moreover, no one was allowed to land at the Oki Islands in those days—much less to visit those who had been banished there. The fishermen laughed at Tokoyo and told her that she had better go home. The brave girl was not to be put off. She bought whatever stock of provisions she could afford, went down to the beach at night, and, selecting the lightest boat she could find, pushed it with difficulty into the water and sculled as hard as her tiny arms would allow her. Fortune sent a strong breeze, and the current also was in her favor. Next evening, more dead than alive, she found her efforts crowned with success. Her boat touched the shore of a rocky bay.

O Tokoyo sought a sheltered spot and lay down to sleep for the night. In the morning she awoke much refreshed, ate the remainder of her provisions, and started to make inquiries as to her father’s whereabouts. The first person she met was a fisherman. “No,” he said: “I have never heard of your father, and if you take my advice you will not ask for him if he has been banished, for it may lead you to trouble and him to death!”

Poor O Tokoyo wandered from one place to another, subsisting on charity, but never hearing a word of her father.

# A Story of Oki Islands

It was a creature shaped like a snake, but with legs and small scales on its back and sides. The thing was twenty-seven or twenty-eight <term>shaku</term> (about twenty-six feet) in length. Its eyes were fiery.

Tokoyo gripped her dagger with renewed determination, feeling certain that this was the evil god, the Yofuné-Nushi, who required a girl to be sacrificed to him every year. No doubt the Yofuné-Nushi took her for the girl who was his due. Well, she would show him who she was and kill him if she could, thus saving the small population of this poor island from the necessity of further annual sacrifices of a virgin.

Slowly the monster approached, and Tokoyo braced herself for the combat. When the creature was within six feet of her, she moved sideways and struck out its right eye. This so confused the evil god that he turned and tried to re-enter the cavern; but Tokoyo was too clever for him. Blinded by the loss of his right eye, as well as by the blood which flooded into his left, the monster was slow in his movements, and thus the brave and agile Tokoyo was able to do with him much as she pleased. She got to his left side, where she was able to stab him in the heart; and, knowing that he could not long survive the blow, she headed him off to prevent him from retreating too far into the cave, where she might find herself at a disadvantage in the darkness. Yofuné-Nushi, however, was unable to see his way back to the depths of his cavern and, after two or three heavy gasps, died not far from the entrance.

Tokoyo was pleased with her success. She felt that she had slain the god that cost the people of the island she had come to in search of—the life of one girl every year.

Soon assistance arrived, and everyone was carefully moved to a safe place in the village. Tokoyo was the heroine of the hour. it clear that he was suffering under the curse of someone to whom he had behaved unjustly—someone who had carved his image, cursed it, and sunk it in the sea. Now that it had been brought to the surface, he felt that the curse was over and that he would recover; and he did. Upon hearing that the heroine of the story was the daughter of his old enemy Oribe Shima, who was held in prison, he ordered his immediate release, and there was great rejoicing at the news.

The curse on the image of Hojo Takatoki had brought with it the evil god, Yofuné-Nushi, who demanded one virgin each year as a tribute. Now that Yofuné-Nushi had been killed, the islanders feared no further trouble from storms. Oribe Shima and his brave daughter O Tokoyo returned to their own home in Shima Province, where the people welcomed them with delight; their popularity soon restored their impoverished estates, where men were willing to work for free.

In the island of Kamijima (Holy Island) in the Oki Archipelago, peace reigned. No more virgins were sacrificed on June 13 to the evil god, Yofuné-Nushi, whose body was buried on the Cape at the shrine where our story begins. Another small shrine was built to commemorate the event. It was called the Tomb of the Sea Serpent.

After much traveling, the wooden statue of Hojo Takatoki found a resting place at Honsōji, in Kamakura.

# XVIII

## CAPE OF THE WOMAN’S SWORD <note>1</note>

Down in the Province of Higo is a group of large islands that, along with the mainland, frame true little inland seas, deep bays, and narrow channels. The whole of this area is called Amakusa. There is a village called Amakusa mura, a sea known as Amakusa umi, an island known as Amakusa shima, and the Cape known as Joken Zaki, which is the most prominent feature of them all, projecting into the Amakusa sea.

History relates that in the year 1577, the Daimyo of the province issued an order that everyone under him was to become a Christian or be banished.

During the next century, this decree was reversed; instead, it was ordered that the Christians should be executed. Tens of thousands of Christianized heads were collected and sent for burial to Nagasaki, Shimabara, and Amakusa.

# Cape of the Woman’s Sword

...on with my story. After all, it is possible that at the time the Amakusa people became Christians, the sword in question—being in some temple—was cast into the sea along with the gods and recovered later by a coral or pearl diver during the Bunroku period, which lasted from 1592 to 1596. A history would naturally arise from a sword recovered in such a way. But back to the story.

The Cape of Joken Zaki (the Woman’s Sword Cape) was not always called by that name. In former years, before the Bunroku period, it had been called Fudozaki (Fudo is the God of Fierceness, always represented as surrounded by fire and holding a sword) or Fudo’s Cape. The reason for the change of names was this.

The inhabitants of Amakusa lived almost entirely on what they harvested from the sea. So, when it happened that for two years of the Bunroku period no fish entered their seas or bay, they were sorely distressed; many people actually starved, and their country was in a state of desolation. Their largest and longest nets were cast and hauled in vain. They could not catch a single fish even as large as a sardine. At last, things became so bad that they could not even see schools of fish outside their bay. Peculiar rumbling sounds were occasionally heard coming from under the sea off Cape Fudo; but they thought little of these, being Japanese and accustomed to earthquakes.

All the people knew was that the fish had completely gone—where or why, they could not tell—until one day an old and much-respected fisherman said:

> ‘I fear, my friends, that the noise we so often hear off Cape Fudo has nothing to do with earthquakes, but rather that the God of the Sea has been displeased.’

One evening a few days after this, a sailing junk named the *Tsukushi-maru*, owned and commanded by a man named Tarada, anchored for the night in the lee of Fudozaki.

After stowing their sails and making everything secure, the crew brought their bedding up from below (as the weather was hot) and rolled it out on deck. Toward the middle of the night, the captain was awakened by a peculiar rumbling sound that seemed to come from the bottom of the sea. Apparently, it came from the direction where their anchor lay; the rope that held it trembled visibly. Tarada said the sound reminded him of the roaring of the falling tide in the Naruto Channel between Awa and Awaji Island. Suddenly, he saw toward the bows of the junk a beautiful maiden clothed in the finest white silk (or so he thought). She seemed, however, hardly real, as she was surrounded by a glittering haze.

Tarada was not a coward; nevertheless, he woke his men, for he did not quite like the situation. As soon as he had roused the men to their senses, he moved toward the figure, which, when only ten or twelve feet away, addressed him in a most melodious voice, saying:

> "Ah! If only I could be back in the world! That is my only wish."

Tarada, astonished and frightened, fell to his knees and was about to pray when the sound of roaring water was heard again, and the white-clad maiden disappeared into the sea.

The next morning, Tarada went ashore to ask the people of Amakusa if they had ever heard of such a thing before and to tell them of his experiences.

"No," said the village elder. "Two years ago, we never

A consultation was held by the fishermen. They concluded that the village elder was right—that someone must have been drowned in the bay, and that the body was polluting the bottom. It was her ghost that had appeared on Tarada’s ship, and the noise was naturally caused by the angry God of the Sea, who was offended that his fish were prevented from entering the bay by its uncleanness.

What was to be done was quite clear. Someone must dive to the bottom despite the depth of the water and bring the body or bones to the surface. It was a dangerous job, and not a pleasant one either—the bringing up of a corpse that had lain at the bottom for well over a year.

As no one volunteered for the dive, the villagers suggested a man who was a great swimmer—a man who had been mute all his life and consequently was a person of no value, as no one would marry him and no one cared for him. His name was Sankichi or (as they called him) Oshi-no-Sankichi, Dumb Sankichi. He was twenty-six years of age; he had always been honest; he was very religious, attending the temples and shrines

What was his poor life worth in comparison with the hundreds of fishermen who lived around the bay, whose lives depended on the presence of fish? The fishermen consulted among themselves and agreed that they would let Oshi-no-Sankichi make the attempt tomorrow; and until that time, he was the popular hero.

The next day, when the tide was low, all the villagers assembled on the beach to give Dumb Sankichi a parting cheer. He was rowed out to Tarada’s junk, and, after saying farewell to his few relatives, dived into the sea from its bows.

Sankichi swam until he reached the bottom, passing through hot and cold currents the whole way. He looked around hastily and swam about, but he found no corpse or bones. At last, he came to a projecting rock, and on top of it, he saw something like a sword wrapped in old brocade. On grasping it, he felt that it really was a sword. When he untied the string and drew the blade, it proved to be one of dazzling brightness, without a single speck of rust.

"It is said," thought Sankichi, "that Japan is the country of the sword, in which its spirit dwells. It must be the Goddess of the Sword that makes the roaring sound which frightens away the fish—whenever she comes to the surface."

## Cape of the Woman's Sword

Feeling that he had secured a rare treasure, Sankichi lost no time in returning to the surface. He was promptly hauled on board the *Tsukushi-maru* amid the cheers of the villagers and his relatives. Because he had been underwater for so long and his body was so numbed, he immediately fainted. Fires were lit, and his body was rubbed until he regained consciousness and gave an account of his dive through signs. The local head official, Naruse Tsushimanokami, examined the sword; but, despite its beauty and excellence, no name could be found on the blade, and the official expressed his opinion that the sword was a sacred treasure. He recommended the construction of a shrine dedicated to Fudo, where the sword should be kept in order to protect the village against further trouble. Money was collected. The shrine was built. Oshi-no-Sankichi was made the caretaker and lived a long and happy life.

The fish returned to the bay, for the spirit of the sword was no longer dissatisfied with being at the bottom <insert>6</insert> of the sea.

# XIX

## HOW YOGODAYU WON A BATTLE

During the reign of Emperor Shirakawa, which was between the years 1073 and 1086 A.D., there lived a general named Yogodayu. He had built a fort for himself and his small army in the wilderness of Yamato, not far from Mount Kasagi. This was the same place where, around the year 1380, the unfortunate Emperor Go-Daigo camped among the same rocky strongholds and eventually perished. Even today, as one winds in and out of the narrow gorge where the railway passes Kasagi in the Kizugawa valley, one is struck by the extreme wildness of the scenery. This was where Yogodayu built his fort. Some months later, he was attacked by his wife's brother, whom he detested, and was badly beaten—so much so that he had only about twenty warriors left alive. With these men, he escaped to Mount Kasagi and hid for two days in a cave, fearing that he would be discovered. On the third day, Yogodayu, finding that he was not being pursued, ventured out to admire the scenery. ## XX

### THE ISOLATED OR DESOLATED ISLAND

Many years ago, the Lord of <term>Kishu</term>, head of one of the three families of the <term>Tokugawas</term>, ordered his people to hold a hunting party on <term>Tomagashima</term> (Toma Island). In those days, such hunting parties were often ordered more for the purpose of improving drill and organization than for sport. It brought men together and taught others how to lead them both on land and at sea. It made men recognize their commanders and superiors, and it revealed which men were worthy of being appointed to such positions. Hunting parties of this kind were considered military maneuvers.

During this particular hunt or maneuver, the Lord of <term>Kishu</term> was to make a kind of landing by water on the island of Toma and kill all the game that his landing party could flush out.

Boats and <term>junks</term> were armed as if for war, and so were the men—except that they wore no armor.

The day for the event was fine. About sixty boats put to sea and successfully landed around eight hundred men on Toma Island; they were indeed busy chasing boar and deer all morning.

<summary>The Lord of Kishu organizes a large-scale hunting expedition on Toma Island as a military maneuver to train his men in naval landings and organizational discipline. Eight hundred men participate in the exercise, using armed junks to reach the island and hunt game throughout the morning.</summary>

## The Isolated or Desolated Island

Towards afternoon, however, a storm of great violence came on and completely stopped the sport. The men were ordered to return to the shore and regain their boats before they should be smashed on the beach.

On embarking, they put out to sea with the intention of reaching the mainland. On shore, trees were being uprooted, columns of sand flew high in the air, and the gale was indeed terrific; if it was as bad as this on shore, it must be much worse at sea. The Lord of Kishu's boats and junks <note>a type of ancient Chinese or Japanese sailing ship</note> were tossed about as if they were floating leaves.

One of the party was a notably brave man, Makino Heinei, who had been nicknamed ‘Ino shishi’ (Wild Boar) on account of his reckless bravery. Seeing that neither the junks nor the boats were making headway against the storm, he pushed the small boat off the junk, jumped into it alone, took the oars, laughed at everyone, and cried: "See here! You all seem to be too frightened to make headway. Look at what I do and follow me. I am not afraid of the waves, and none of you should be if you are to serve our Lord of Kishu faithfully."

With that, Makino Heinei shot out into the wild sea, and by extraordinary exertion managed to get some three hundred yards ahead of the rest of the fleet. Then the gale increased to such violence that he was incapable of doing anything. For fear of being blown out of the boat, he was obliged to hold tight to the mast and otherwise abandon his fate to good fortune. At times, even the heart of the Wild Boar quailed. Often his boat was lifted clean out of the water by the wind; waves towered over him; he closed his eyes and awaited his fate.

<summary>A violent storm disrupts the Lord of Kishu's hunting expedition, forcing the fleet to retreat; a recklessly brave man named Makino Heinei attempts to shame the others by rowing out alone, only to be overwhelmed by the tempest.</summary>
<keywords>Makino Heinei, Wild Boar, Ino shishi, Lord of Kishu, Tomagashima, storm, shipwreck, bravery, maritime disaster</keywords>

Finally, one squall more powerful than the rest blew his boat out of the water, and it was seen from the other boats (which lay at anchor) disappearing into the horizon. Heinei clung to the boat tightly. When the mast blew away, he held on to the ribs of the vessel. He prayed hard and earnestly. Some eight hours after the storm began, Heinei found the boat in comparatively smooth water. It was flooded and it was a wreck, but it still floated, and that was all he cared about at the moment. Moreover, Heinei felt encouraged because, between two dark clouds, he could see an opening and some stars, though at the time it was absolutely dark and the driving rain had not ceased. Suddenly, while Heinei was wondering how far he had been blown from the shore or from his friends—crack!—he felt his boat crash into a rock. The shock was so violent (for the boat was still being driven fast by the gale) that our hero lost his balance and was thrown a full ten feet away. Falling onto something soft, Heinei thought he was in the sea; but his hands suddenly realized that it was soft, wet sand. Delighted at this discovery, he looked at the clouds and the sky and concluded that it would be daylight in another hour. In the meantime, he thanked the gods for his rescue and prayed for his friends and for his lord and master.

As morning broke, Heinei arose stiff, weary, and hungry. Before the sun appeared, he realized that he was on an island. No other land was in sight, and it puzzled him greatly to guess where he could be, for from all the Kishu islands the mainland could be easily seen.

"Oh, here is a new tree! I have never seen that in—"

## The Isolated or Desolated Island

"Kishu," he said. "And this flower—that is also new—while here is a butterfly more brilliant than any I know."

Saying and thinking this, Heinei began looking for food. Being Japanese, he easily satisfied his appetite with the shellfish that were abundantly strewn everywhere after the storm.

The island on which Heinei had been cast was a fair size—about two miles across and ten miles in circumference. There was one small hill in the middle, which Heinei resolved to climb to see if he could spot Kishu from its peak. Accordingly, he set out. The undergrowth of bushes was so thick that Heinei made a detour to another bay. The trees were quite different from any he had ever seen before, and there were many kinds of palms. At last, to his delight, he found a well-worn path leading up the mountain. He took it; but when he came to a damp place in the path, he was not at all reassured, for there he saw footprints that could have been made by no one but a giant—they were fully eighteen inches long. "A warrior belonging to Kishu must fear nothing," Heinei thought, and, arming himself with a sturdy stick, he proceeded. Near the top, he found the opening to a fairly large cave, and, undaunted, he began to enter, prepared to face anything. To his surprise, an enormous man, fully eight feet tall, appeared before him, no more than ten feet from the entrance! He was a hideous, wild-looking creature, nearly black, with long, unkempt hair, flashing, angry eyes, and a mouth that stretched from ear to ear, showing two glittering rows of teeth; he wore no clothes except the skin of a wildcat tied around his loins.

As soon as he saw Heinei, he came to a standstill and said in Japanese, “Who are you? How did you get here? And what have you come for?”

Makino Heinei answered these questions as fully as he thought necessary by giving his name and adding, “I am a retainer of the Lord of Kishu, and I was blown away by the storm after we had been hunting and holding maneuvers on Toma Island.”

“And where are these places you speak of? Remember that this island is unknown to the world and has been for thousands of years. I am its sole occupant and wish to remain so. No matter how I came, I am here. My name is Tomaru, and my father was Yamaguchi Shoun, who died with his master, Toyotomi Hidetsugu, on Mount Koyasan in 1563. Both died by their own hands; and I arrived here—it does not matter how—and here I intend to remain undisturbed. I heard of your Lord of Kishu and of the Tokugawa family before I left Japan, and for that reason, I will help you by giving you the old boat in which I arrived. Come to the beach. I will send you off in the right direction, and if you continue sailing northwest, you will eventually reach Kishu. But it is a long way off—a very long way.”

With that, they walked down to the beach.

“See,” said Tomaru, “the boat is almost rotten, for it has been many years since she was placed here; but with luck, you may reach Kishu. Wait—you must have some provisions. I can only give you dried fish and fruits, but you are welcome to these. And I must give you a gift for your master, the Lord of Kishu. It is a kind of seaweed. You shall have some for yourself as well. It is—”

## XXI

# CHIKUBU ISLAND, LAKE BIWA

Many years ago, when I was a boy, there was a song about a Chinese man. It began:

> In China once there lived a man,
> And his name was Ding-dong-dang.
> His legs were long, and his feet were small,
> And this Chinese man couldn’t walk at all.

Chorus:

> Chi-chi-Maree, Chi-chi-Marah,
> Ding-dong, ding-dong, ding-dong dah,
> Kossi-kossi-ki, kossi-kossi-ka,
> Chikubu, Chikubu, Chikubu Chang.

In those days, I little thought that I would come across an island—or any other place, for that matter—that bore the name of a part of this wild and idiotic chorus, "Chikubu, Chikubu, Chikubu Chang." It sounds truly wild. Well, so it is. I have found an island on Lake Biwa which is pronounced and spelled exactly as in the chorus of this song from my youth. "Chikubu" is there, and I am puzzled to know where the composer found it. In my Japanese studies, I cannot find it.

<summary>The author recalls a nonsensical childhood song about a Chinese man that featured the name "Chikubu" in its chorus. He expresses surprise at discovering a real island of the same name on Lake Biwa and wonders about the name's origin in the song.</summary>

## Chikubu Island, Lake Biwa

However, let us get to the story. It is not a very good one; but, as it relates to the only island of importance in the lake, it is worth chronicling.

Chikubu-shima is situated about two-thirds of the way towards the northwestern end of Lake Biwa, in Omi Province. The lake is some thirty-five miles long and twelve miles wide. The island is holy, I believe, and it is said to have been created by an earthquake nearly 600 years <term>B.C.</term> Mount Fuji appeared at the same time. Thus we have (so far as we choose to believe it) the geographical pedigree of Lake Biwa and its principal island.

The nearest land to Chikubu is Tsuzurao Cape, which is about two miles away. There, some three hundred years ago, lived two sisters, O Tsuru and O Kame. They were fifteen and eleven respectively, and lived with their old and only uncle, their father and mother and all their other relations being dead. Tsuru (the crane) and Kame (the turtle) were devoted to each other; in fact, the poor girls clung to each other as the remnants of a family should cling. They loved each other. They were inseparable.

At that time there was much fear among the inhabitants of Tsuzurao Point of a large carp—a carp of such size that it was called "The Master of Lake Biwa." It was said that this fish ate dogs, cats, and sometimes people, if they were unwise enough to swim into water deep enough for him to maneuver in. His principal haunt was in the waters surrounding Chikubu Island, at the northern end of the lake.

When O Tsuru reached the age of fifteen, and her sister O Kame was eleven, O Tsuru became sick with

consumption; from bad she grew worse, and her poor little sister O Kame became quite disconsolate. She cried because of her sister's illness and went by herself to pray at all the temples in the neighborhood. Day after day she thought of nothing but her sister's illness; but all she did, poor child, was in vain. O Tsuru became worse.

In her great distress, O Kame thought that she should venture to the wild and sacred island of Chikubu, there to pray to the Goddess of Mercy, Kwannon. To do so with any chance of her prayers being heard, it was necessary that she should go alone. She would row off secretly that night.

After darkness had fallen and her uncle's household had gone to sleep, O Kame crept out and went down to the edge of the lake, where her uncle's boat and many others lay. Getting into one—the lightest she could find—she sculled toward Chikubu Island. The sky was clear and the water glistened.

In less than an hour, this devoted child of Japan was kneeling before the ever-pleasing and soothing figure of Kwannon, the goddess always ready to listen to the prayers of the unhappy; and there she prayed with all her heart, weeping at intervals in sorrow for the sickness of her sister.

When poor O Kame had finished praying, she got into her boat and began to row back to Tsuzurao. She had come within half a mile of that place when a terrible storm arose, and in the third squall, her boat capsized. O Kame was no swimmer, and as she sank into the depths of the lake, the giant carp saw her and instantly carried her off and devoured her.

# Chikubu Island, Lake Biwa

The next morning, there was consternation at Tsuzurao. When it was found that both O Kame San and one of the fishermen’s boats were missing, it was naturally assumed that she had gone out on the lake, and probably to Chikubu Island to pray to Kwannon.

Boats went out in search; but nothing could be found, except for the marks of her footsteps leading from the shore to the shrine dedicated to Kwannon. On hearing this sad news, O Tsuru, who lay near death, grew worse; but despite her sad condition, she could not bear the idea of lingering on in the world without her sister, O Kame. Consequently, she resolved to take her own life as near as she could imagine to the place where O Kame had died, so that her spirit might journey with hers until perhaps they should be reborn together. At all events, she felt it was clearly her duty to follow her sister.

When the dusk of evening arrived, O Tsuru crept out from her room and reached the beach, where she, like her little sister, took the lightest boat she could find and rowed herself out. Despite her weakness, she reached a spot where she thought the carp might have killed her sister. There, standing in the bow of the boat, she cried aloud:

> ‘Oh, mighty carp, that has devoured my sister, devour me also, so that our spirits may follow the same path and be reunited. It is for this that I cast myself into the lake!’

Saying this, O Tsuru shut her eyes and jumped into the water. Down, down, down she went, until she reached the bottom. No sooner had she landed there—feeling (strangely enough) no ill effects from being underwater—than she heard her name called.

# Ancient Tales and Folklore of Japan

‘Strange indeed,’ she thought, ‘that I should hear my name at the bottom of Lake Biwa!’

She opened her eyes and saw an old priest standing beside her. O Tsuru asked him who he was and why he had called her.

‘I was a priest,’ he explained. ‘Perhaps I am one now. In any case, I often come to the bottom of the lake. I know all about your little sister Kame—of her faithfulness and affection for you, and of yours for her. I also know about the storm that capsized her boat when she had been praying to Kwannon on Chikubu Island, and of her being taken and eaten by that horrible carp. Believe me, none of these are reasons why you should take your own life. Return to the world instead, and pray to Buddha for your sister’s blessing and for her soul. I will see that you are avenged on the carp, and I will see that you become well and strong. Take my hand, like this, and I will take you back to the shore.’

Having said this and carried Tsuru to land, the priest disappeared. For some time she lay unconscious; but when she fully came to her senses, O Tsuru found herself on Chikubu Island. Feeling considerably stronger than she had felt for some time, she went to the shrine dedicated to Kwannon and spent the rest of the night in prayer.

In the morning, after going to the beach, she saw boats in the distance coming from Tsuzurao Point; but (what was even more extraordinary) there lay, not ten feet from the shore where she stood, an enormous carp—fully nine feet long and dead!

### Chikubu Island, Lake Biwa

Among the search boats that arrived was one containing her uncle and a priest.

Tsuru told her story. The carp was buried at a small promontory on the island, which is called Miyazaki. It was named Koizuka Miya-zaki (the Carp’s Grave at Temple Cape).

O Tsuru lived to a ripe old age and was never ill again. History tells of her at the age of seventy informing Ota Nobunaga, who came to destroy temples in the neighborhood, that if he touched the shrines on Chikubu Island she herself would see to his destruction.

## XXII

### REINCARNATION

In the far northern and mountainous part of Echigo Province is a temple that, during the reign of Emperor Ichijo, had a curious story attached to it. Although Emperor Ichijo reigned as long ago as between the years 987 and 1011 A.D., the storyteller assured me that he believed the temple still exists today.

The temple's name is Kinoto, and it is situated in the hills among wild woods, which in those days must have been almost virgin forest.

The monk who presided over the Kinoto Temple was a young man, but very devout; he read sacred sermons from the holy Buddhist scriptures aloud twice a day.

One day, the good youth noticed that two monkeys had come down from the mountain and sat listening to his reading with serious faces and no mischief. He was amused and, taking no notice, continued to read. As soon as he had finished, the monkeys went off into the hills.

# Reincarnation

The monk was surprised to see the monkeys appear at both of his sermons the next day; and when they came again on the third day, he could not help asking why they came so regularly.

"We have come, holy father, because we like to hear the words and sermons of Buddha as read by you, and we greatly desire to retain all the wisdom and virtues we have heard you recite. Is it possible for you to copy out the great and holy Buddhist book?"

"It would be a very laborious task," answered the priest, highly astonished; "but, since you animals take such a rare interest in the sermons of our Great Lord Buddha, I will make an effort to satisfy your wish, hoping that you may be benefited by it."

The monkeys bowed and left the priest, pleased with themselves and the promise they had obtained, while the priest set to his gigantic labors of copying the Buddhist Bible. Some six or seven days later, about five hundred monkeys came to the temple, each bearing parchment paper, which they laid before the priest. Their leader said how deeply grateful they would be once they had the copy of the Bible, so that they might know the laws and mend their ways; and, bowing again before the priest, they retired, all except the first two monkeys. These two set diligently to work to find food for the priest while he wrote. Day after day they went into the mountains, returning with wild fruits and potatoes, honey and mushrooms; and the priest wrote steadily on, being thus attended, until he had copied five volumes of the sacred book.

When he had reached the end of the fifth volume

At last, when near the top of the mountain, his heart leapt and was filled with sorrow when he came to a hole which the monkeys had made while looking for wild potatoes—it was so deep that they had been unable to get out. No doubt both of them had died of broken hearts, fearing that the priest would think they had deserted him.

There remained nothing to do but to bury the monkeys and pray for their blessing, which he did. Shortly after this, the priest was called away from the temple to another. Since he saw no necessity to continue copying the Buddhist Bible, he put the five volumes he had copied into one of the pillars of the temple, which had a sort of shelf cupboard cut into it.

## XXIII

### THE DIVING-WOMAN OF OISO BAY

Oiso, in the Province of Sagami, has become such a celebrated place as the chosen residence of Marquis Ito and several other high-ranking Japanese personages, that a story of a somewhat romantic nature, dating back to the Ninan period, may be interesting.

During one of the earlier years of that period, which lasted from 1116 to 1169 A.D., a certain knight whose name was Takadai Jiro became ill in the town of Kamakura, where he had been on duty. He was advised to spend the hot month of August at Oiso and to give himself perfect rest, peace, and quiet there.

Having obtained permission to do this, Takadai Jiro lost no time in reaching the place and settling himself down as comfortably as possible in a small inn which faced the sea. Being a landsman who (with the exception of his service at Kamakura) had hardly ever seen the ocean, Takadai was pleased to spend his time gazing at it both by day and by night; for, like most Japanese of high birth, he was poetical and romantic.

clothes and went down to bathe. Takadai, who was about twenty-five years old, was a good swimmer and plunged into the sea without fear, swimming out for nearly half a mile. There, however, misfortune overtook him. He was seized with a violent cramp and began to sink. A fishing boat rowed by a man and carrying a diving girl happened to see him and went to the rescue; but by this time he had lost consciousness and had sunk for the third time.

The girl jumped overboard and swam to the spot where he had disappeared; after diving deep, she brought him to the surface, holding him there until the boat came up. Through the combined efforts of herself and her father, Takadai was hauled on board, but not before he had realized that the soft arm clinging around his neck belonged to a woman.

When he was fully conscious again, before they had reached the shore, Takadai saw that his rescuer was a beautiful <term>ama</term> (diving girl) no more than seventeen years old. He had never seen such beauty before—not even in the higher social circles in which he was accustomed to move. Takadai was in love with his brave savior before the boat had landed on the pebbly beach. Determined to repay the kindness he had received in some way, Takadai helped haul their boat up the steep beach and then carry their fish and nets to their little thatched cottage. There, he thanked the girl for her noble and gallant act in saving him and congratulated her father on having such a daughter. After doing this, he returned to his inn, which was no more than a few hundred yards away.

# Ancient Tales and Folklore of Japan

From that time on, Takadai’s soul knew no peace. He was possessed by the most frantic kind of love. He could not sleep at night, for he saw nothing but the face of the beautiful diving girl, whose name (he had discovered) was Kinu. Try as he might, he could not put her out of his mind for a single moment. In the daytime it was even worse, for O Kinu was nowhere to be seen; she was out at sea with her father, diving for the <term>haliotis</term> shell and others. It was usually the dusk of evening before she returned, and then, in the dim light, he could not see her clearly.

Once, indeed, Takadai tried to speak to O Kinu, but she would have nothing to say to him and continued busying herself by helping her father carry the nets and fish up to their cottage. This made Takadai feel much worse, and he went home frantic, distracted, and more in love than ever.

At last, his love grew so great that he could no longer endure it. He felt that, at the very least, it would be a relief to declare it. So, he took his most trusted servant into his confidence and sent him with a letter to the fisherman’s cottage. O Kinu San did not even write a reply, but told the old servant to thank his master on her behalf for his letter and his proposal of marriage. “Tell him also,” she said, “that no good could come of a union between someone of such high birth as he and someone as lowly as I. Such a poorly matched pair could never make a happy home.” In response to the servant’s objections, she merely added, “I have told you what to tell your master; take him the message.”

Saying this, she tore it open and read, and then, turning to the servant, continued: “It is difficult for me to understand. If you gave my message to your master correctly, he could not fail to know that I could not marry him. His position in life is far too high. Is your master quite right in his head?”

I might give you my advice, and I should do so; but, sir, in this case I must agree with my daughter that, however great the honor shown to her, she would be unwise to marry someone above her own station in life.’

Takadai’s heart was broken. There was nothing more he could say and nothing more he could do. Bowing low, he left the fisherman and retired immediately to his room in the inn, which he never left, much to the dismay of his servant.

Day by day he grew thinner, and as the day for his return from leave approached, Takadai was much more of an invalid than he had been when he first arrived at Oiso. What was he to do? The sentiment of the old proverb that ‘there are as many good fish in the sea as have ever been caught’ did not appeal to him in any way. He felt that life was no longer worth living. He resolved to end it in the sea, where his spirit might perhaps linger and occasionally catch sight of the beautiful diving girl who had bewitched his heart.

That evening, Takadai wrote a final note to Kinu, and as soon as the villagers of Oiso were asleep, he got up and went to the cottage, slipping the note under the door. Then he went to the beach; after tying a large stone to a rope and then around his neck, he got into a boat and rowed about a hundred yards from shore. There, he took the stone in his arms and jumped overboard.

The next morning, O Kinu was shocked to read in the note that Jiro Takadai intended to kill himself for love of her. She rushed down to the beach, but could see only an empty fishing boat some three or four hundred yards from the shore, to which she swam. There she found Takadai’s tobacco box and his <term>juro</term> (medicine box). O Kinu thought that Takadai must have thrown himself into the sea somewhere in this area; so she began to dive, and it was not long before she found the body. She brought it to the surface after some trouble because of the weight of the stone which his arms rigidly grasped. O Kinu took the body back to the shore, where she found Takadai’s old servant wringing his hands in grief.

The body was taken back to Kamakura, where it was buried. O Kinu was moved enough to vow that she would never marry anyone. It was true that she had not loved Takadai; but he had loved her, and had died for her. If she married, she believed his spirit would not rest in peace.

No sooner had O Kinu mentally committed to this generous path than a strange thing happened.

Sea-gulls, which were particularly rare in Oiso Bay, began to swarm into it; they settled over the exact spot where Takadai had drowned himself. In stormy weather, they hovered over it on the wing, but they never left the place. Fishermen thought it was extraordinary; but Kinu knew well enough that the spirit of Takadai must have passed into the gulls. She prayed for him regularly at the temple, and out of her small savings, she built a little tomb sacred to the memory of Takadai Jiro.

## XXIV

# THEFT AND RECOVERY OF A GOLDEN <term>KWANNON</term>

<margin><unclear>cluye</unclear></margin>
In the <term>Genroku</term> period, which lasted from 1688 to 1704, when the <term>Shogun</term> or military ruler Tsunayoshi's power was at its height, he presented a solid gold figure of <term>Kwannon</term>, the Goddess of Mercy, to each of the three leading families of the provinces of Kii, Mito, and Owari. These were considered to be of the highest and greatest value by each of these leading Lords or <term>Daimyos</term>, who kept them in their inner palaces so that they were almost impossible to reach and were considered absolutely safe from robbers; but even despite this, the Lord of Kii took additional precautions by always having a man guard his idol night and day.

At the same period lived a most redoubtable robber named Yayegumo. He was more than an ordinary robber and was what the people called a <term>fu-in-kiri</term>, which means "seal breaker" or "seal cutter." He was a first-class burglar, in fact, who never stooped to robbing the poor, but only robbed the wealthiest and most difficult palaces and castles that could be accessed, taking from

<summary>Shogun Tsunayoshi gifts precious golden Kwannon statues to the three primary Tokugawa houses, which the Lord of Kii guards with extreme care. The story introduces Yayegumo, a legendary "seal breaker" thief known for targeting only the most secure and wealthy estates.</summary>

This bold robber broke into the Lord of Kii’s Palace—no one knew how—took the statue of <term>Kwannon</term>, and left his name written on a piece of paper. The Lord of Kii, very angry, sent for the guard, whose name was Mumashima Iganosuke, and reprimanded him severely, asking him what excuse he had to make. "None, my lord: tiredness overcame me and I slept. There is but one way in which I can show my regret, and that I will do by ending my own life."

The Lord of Kii, who was a man of wisdom, answered that before he did this it would be more useful if Iganosuke would track down the robber and try to recover the statue. Iganosuke, who had always been a faithful servant, readily consented, and, having obtained indefinite leave, went away. For fully four months he was quite unsuccessful, though he had traveled over half the country. At last he heard reports of robberies in <term>Chugoku</term>, and then later in <term>Shikoku</term> Province. Hurrying down from <term>Izumo</term> to <term>Okayama</term>, he there boarded a ship bound across the <term>Inland Sea</term> for <term>Takamatsu</term>, in <term>Shikoku</term>. The weather was fine and the sea smooth, and Iganosuke was in high spirits, for he had heard that one or two of the robberies had undoubtedly been committed by <term>Yayegumo</term>, and he felt that at last he must be getting nearer the man he wished to catch—perhaps, even, he was on that very boat! Who could tell? Thinking of these possibilities, Iganosuke kept very much to himself, watching the people, whose spirits all seemed to be affected by the beautiful weather, for, though mostly strangers, they were all sociable.

Among them was a handsome young samurai who had attracted Iganosuke's attention with his refined appearance, as also by a beautiful gold pipe which he drew out from its case and smoked while chatting with his neighbor. After a while, a samurai of about sixty years of age came up to the young man and said:

"Sir, I have lost my pipe and tobacco pouch somewhere on this ship. I am a habitual smoker and am almost dying for a puff of tobacco. Might I borrow yours for a moment or two?"

The young samurai handed both his pipe and pouch to the old man with a bow, saying that doing so afforded him great pleasure.

The old samurai, after taking three puffs of the pipe, was about to empty out the ash and refill it. Doing so without thinking about what he was doing, he tapped the pipe against the outside of the ship. To his horror, the <term>gankubi</term> (the bowl) dropped off into the sea. The old man knew that the pipe was gold and of great value, and he was utterly distraught. He did not know what to say. His apologies were profuse, but they did not bring back the end of the pipe. The young samurai, of course, was much annoyed, but it would be no use getting angry. In any case, that would have been an excessively vulgar way to behave, especially toward such an old man. He said:

"Ah! The pipe was given to me by the lord of my clan for meritorious service rendered in the great hunt last year, and truly I do not know how I shall be able to face the disgrace of incurring his anger." He grew pale as he reflected on this.

# XXV

# SAIGYO HOSHI'S ROCK

About twelve miles south of Shodo Shima (Shodo Island) lies the fairly large island of Nao, or Naoshima, on the western side of the enchanting Inland Sea. I have had the good fortune to cruise over this sea at will, helped rather than hindered by the Japanese Government, owing to the kindness of Sir Ernest Satow. Naoshima has few inhabitants—no more than sixty to a hundred, I believe. At the time of our story, around the year 1156, there were only two: Sobei and his good wife, O Yone. These lived alone at a beautiful little bay, where they had built a fishing hut and cultivated some three thousand <term>tsubo</term> of land. With the produce of this land and an unlimited supply of fish, they were perfectly happy and untroubled by the conflicts of the day. These were particularly serious then, as it was the <term>Hogen</term> period (lasting from 1156 to 1160), which took its name from what was known as the <term>Hogen</term> rebellion or, to put it correctly, revolution. It was during this exciting period that the ex-Emperor Shutoku (who reigned 1124–1141), who was suspected of leading the rebellion, was banished for safety by those in power to the island of Naoshima.

At the end of the year, he died from grief. Sobei and his wife devoted all their spare time to building a small shrine to his memory. It is said to be standing to this day.

In the third year of Ninnan, the famous but eccentric priest and poet Saigyo, who was related to the Imperial family, spent seventeen days on the island, praying night and day. During this time, he sat on the favorite rock of Taro and the ex-Emperor. The rock is still known as ‘Saigyo iwa’ (Saigyo’s Rock).

## How Masakuni regained his Sight

Her prayer had been answered by Fudo San. With joy in her heart, she almost ran down the mountain, forgetting all about her own narrow escape and the long gash she had received on her head. Dr. Uozumi found it hard to keep anywhere near this healthy young woman.

Once they arrived at the house, Uozumi performed an examination of the patient and ordered remedies according to Dutch prescriptions, the medicines for which he fortunately had with him. Day after day the doctor and O Ai cared for Masakuni, and at the end of the tenth day, his left eye was perfectly cured.

Masakuni was delighted at the partial recovery of his sight and, like his daughter, attributed the good fortune of the celebrated doctor’s arrival to the mercy of Fudo San. After purifying his body and soul by living on a vegetable diet and bathing in cold water for ten days, he began making two swords, which he finished some time later. One he presented to the god Fudo, and the other to Doctor Uozumi. They were afterwards known as the celebrated swords made by the semi-blind Masakuni.

The doctor thought it a pity to allow such a skilled artist as Masakuni to remain in this remote village of Awa Province, and also felt that the beautiful O Ai should not be allowed to "rust" there; so he persuaded them to join him in Kyoto. Subsequently, he obtained a position as a lady-in-waiting in the palace of the Duke of Karasumaru for O Ai San, where she was perfectly happy.

Five years later Masakuni died, and was buried in the cemetery of Toribeyama, at the eastern end of Kyoto. So my storyteller, Fukuga, tells me.

## XXVII

### SAGAMI BAY

HATSUSHIMA ISLAND is likely unknown to all foreigners and to 9,999 out of every 10,000 Japanese; consequently, it is of little importance. Nevertheless, it has produced a rather romantic little story, which was told to me by a friend who had visited there about six years earlier.

The island is about seven miles southeast of Atami, in Sagami Bay (Izu Province). It is so isolated from the mainland that very little interaction occurs with the outside world. Indeed, it is said that the inhabitants of Hatsushima Island are a peculiar people and prefer to keep to themselves. Even today, there are only about two hundred houses, and the population cannot exceed a thousand. The main product of the island is, of course, fish; but it is also famous for its jonquil flowers (*suisenn*). Thus, it can be seen that there is hardly any trade. The little that the people buy from or sell to the mainland, they carry in their own fishing boats. In marriage as well, they keep to themselves and are generally conservative, and they are all the better for it.

The inhabitants are described as a conservative people who rarely trade or marry outside of their own small population.</summary>

Hatsushima is practically unknown to all foreigners and to 9,999 out of every 10,000 Japanese; consequently,

### O CHO SAN COMMITS SUICIDE

Nevertheless, it has produced quite a romantic story, which was told to me by a friend who had visited there about six years before.

The island is about seven miles southeast of Atami, in Sagami Bay (Izu Province). It is so isolated from the mainland that very little interaction goes on with the outside world. Indeed, it is said that the inhabitants of Hatsushima Island are a peculiar people and prefer to keep to themselves. Even today, there are only about two hundred houses, and the population cannot exceed a thousand. The main product of the island is, of course, fish; but it is also famous for its jonquil flowers (suisenn). Thus, it can be seen that there is hardly any trade. What little the people buy from or sell to the mainland, they carry in their own fishing boats. In marriage as well, they keep to themselves and are generally conservative, and are all the better for it.

# Sagami Bay

There is a well-known fisherman’s song from Hatsushima Island. It means something like the following, and the story tells the origin of that strange verse:

> Today is the tenth of June. May the rain fall in torrents!
> For I long to see my dearest O Cho San.
> Hi, Hi, Ya-re-ko-no-sa! Ya-re-ko-no-sa!

Many years ago, there lived on the island the daughter of a fisherman whose beauty was extraordinary even as a child. As she grew, Cho—for that was her name—became even more beautiful; and, despite her humble birth, she had the manners and refinement of a lady. At the age of eighteen, there was not a young man on the island who was not in love with her. Everyone was eager to seek her hand in marriage, but hardly anyone dared to ask, even through a matchmaker, as was the custom.

Among them was a handsome fisherman about twenty years old named Shinsaku. Being less bashful than the others and a little bolder, he approached Gisuke, O Cho’s brother, about the matter one day. Gisuke saw no reason why his sister shouldn't marry Shinsaku; in fact, he quite liked Shinsaku, and their families had always been friends. So he called his sister O Cho down to the beach where they were sitting and told her that Shinsaku had proposed marriage to her. He said he thought it was an excellent match that her mother would have approved of if she were alive. He added, "You must marry soon, you know. You are eighteen, and we want no unmarried women on Hatsushima, nor do we want girls brought here from the mainland to marry our bachelors."

<meta>This page follows the proposal of Shinsaku to O Cho through her brother Gisuke. O Cho has just accepted the proposal, and the story continues with the reaction of the other young men on Hatsushima Island.</meta>

"Stay, stay, my dear brother! I do not want this whole sermon on spinsterhood," cried O Cho. "I have no intention of remaining single, I can tell you; and as for Shinsaku, I would rather marry him than anyone else—so do not worry yourself further on that account. Set the date for the happy event."

Needless to say, young Gisuke was delighted, as was Shinsaku; and they decided that the marriage should take place three days from then.

Soon, when all the fishing boats had returned to the village, the news spread; and it would be difficult to describe the state of the younger men’s feelings. Until then, everyone had hoped to win the pretty O Cho San; all had lived in that happy hope and rejoiced in the uncertain state of love, which causes such happiness in its early stages. Shinsaku had previously been a general favorite. Now all of their hopes were dashed to the ground. O Cho was not for any of them. As for Shinsaku, how they suddenly hated him! "What is to be done?" they asked one another, giving little thought to the comical side of it, or the fact that in any case, O Cho could marry only one of them.

No attention was paid to the fish they had caught; their boats were scarcely pulled high enough on the beach for safety; their minds were wholly given to the question of how each and every one of them could marry O Cho San. First of all, it was decided to tell Shinsaku that they would prevent his marriage if possible. There were several fights on the quiet beach, which had never before been disturbed by a display of ill feeling. At last Gisuke, O Cho’s brother, consulted with his sister and Shinsaku; and they decided, for the peace of the island, to break

off the marriage, O Cho and her lover determined that, in any case, they would marry no one else.

However, even this great sacrifice had no effect. There were fully thirty men; in fact, all of the bachelors wanted to marry O Cho. They fought daily, and the whole island was thrown into a state of discontent. Poor O Cho San! What could she do? Had she and Shinsaku not done enough already by sacrificing their happiness for the peace of the island? There was only one more thing she could do, and, being a Japanese girl, she did it. She wrote two letters, one to her brother Gisuke and another to Shinsaku, bidding them farewell.

> "The island of Hatsushima never had trouble until I was born," she said. "For three hundred years or more our people, though poor, have lived happily and in peace. Alas! Now it is no longer so because of me. Farewell! I shall be dead. Tell our people that I have died to bring them back to their senses, for they have been foolish regarding me. Farewell!"

After leaving the two letters where Gisuke slept, O Cho slipped stealthily out of the house (it was a pouring-wet and stormy night on the 10th of June) and threw herself into the sea from some rocks near her cottage, after heavily loading her sleeves with stones so that she might rise no more.

Next morning, when Gisuke found the letters, he instinctively knew what must have happened and rushed from the house to find Shinsaku. The brother and the lover read their letters together and were stricken with grief, as, indeed, was everyone else. A search was made, and soon O Cho's straw slippers were found on the rocky point near her house. Gisuke knew she must have jumped into the sea
