here, and he and Shinsaku dived down and found her body lying at the bottom. They brought it to the surface, and she was buried just beyond the rocks where she had last stood.

From that day on, Shinsaku was unable to sleep at night. The poor fellow was completely overwhelmed with grief. He placed O Cho’s letter and straw slippers beside his bed and surrounded them with flowers. He spent his days decorating and weeping over her grave.

Finally, one evening, Shinsaku resolved to take his own life, hoping that his spirit might find O Cho, and he wandered toward her grave to say a final farewell. As he did so, he thought he saw O Cho; he called her name aloud three or four times and then, with outstretched arms, rushed toward her in delight. The noise woke Gisuke, whose house was near the grave. He came out and found Shinsaku clutching the stone pillar that was placed at the head of the grave.

Shinsaku explained that he had seen the spirit of O Cho and that he was about to follow her by taking his life; but he was talked out of this.

> “Do not do that; instead, devote your life to her memory, and I will help you build a shrine dedicated to Cho. You will join her when you die a natural death, but please her spirit here by never marrying anyone else.”

Shinsaku promised. The young men of the village now began to feel deeply sorry for Shinsaku. They thought about what selfish beasts they had been! However, they decided to change their ways and spend all their spare time building a shrine to O Cho San; and this they did. The shrine is called “The Shrine of O Cho San of Hatsushima.”

## XXVIII

### THE KING OF TORIJIMA¹

MANY years ago there lived a Daimio called Tarao. His castle and home were at Osaki, in Osumi Province, and among his retinue was a faithful and favorite servant whose name was Kume Shuzen. Kume had long been the land-steward to Lord Tarao, and indeed acted for him in everything connected with business.

One day Kume had been dispatched to the capital, Kyoto, to attend to business for his master, when the Daimio Toshiro of Hyuga quarreled with the Daimio of Osumi over some boundary question. Because Kume was not there to help his master, who was a hasty person, the two clans fought at the foot of Mount Kitamata.

<note>¹ It is impossible to say exactly which of the Torijima islands this story refers to. There are two—one a rock islet some sixty miles east of Okinawajima, the main island where the capital of all the islands, Nafa, is located; and the other or larger Torijima, between longitude 128° and 129°, and not far south of latitude 38°. My storyteller claims the tale is about the southern rocky island, which charts show as being 60 feet above water at high tide, because there is an adjacent island called Kumeshima; while I argue that it is more probably about the northern Torijima, next to which is a large island named Takuneshima, which might very well have been intended as Kumeshima. With Japanese, Chinese, and English names, these islands are very puzzling. The Japanese, though excellent mapmakers, are poor geographers, changing names as they see fit.</note>

## XXIX

### THE PERPETUAL LIFE-GIVING WINE

Between the northeastern boundary of Totomi Province and the northwestern boundary of Suruga Province stands a lofty mountain, Daimugenzan. It is a wild and rugged mountain, covered nearly three-quarters of the way up with lofty pines, yenoki, icho, camphors, and other trees. There are only a few paths, and hardly anyone goes up the hill. About halfway up through the forest is a shrine erected to Kwannon; but it is so small that no priest lives there, and the building is rotting away. No one knows why it was put up in such an inaccessible place—except, perhaps, one solitary girl and her parents, who used to go there for some reason of their own.

One day, about 1107 A.D., the girl was praying for her mother’s recovery from sickness. Okureha was her name. She lived at Tashiro, at the foot of the mountain, and was the beauty of the countryside—the daughter of a much-loved samurai of some importance. Amid the solemn silence, Okureha clapped her hands three times before Kwannon as she prayed, causing mountain echoes to resound. Having finished her prayers, Okureha began to make her

way down, when she was suddenly jumped by a rough-looking man, who grabbed her by the arm.

She cried out for help; but nothing came except the echoes of her voice, and she gave herself up for lost.

Suddenly a piercing cold breeze came along, carrying the autumn leaves in little columns. Okureha struggled violently with her attacker, who seemed to weaken against the cold wind as it struck his face. Okureha weakened too. In a few seconds the man fell down as if in a drunken sleep, and she was on the verge of falling (she did not know why) and of sleeping (she could scarcely keep her eyes open). Just then the wind blew hot instead of cold, and she felt herself awake again. On looking up she saw approaching her a beautiful girl, apparently not many years older than herself. The stranger was dressed in white, and seemed to glide. Her face was as white as the snow that capped Mount Daimugenzan; her brows were crescent-shaped, like those of Buddha; her mouth was like flowers. In a silvery voice she called to Okureha, saying:

> "Do not be surprised or afraid, my child. I saw that you were in danger, and I came to your rescue by putting that savage creature to sleep; I sent the warm breeze so that you might not fall. You need not fear that the man is dead. I can revive him if I choose, or keep him as he is if I wish. What is your name?"

Okureha fell on her knees to express her thanks, and, rising, said: "My name is Okureha. My father is the <term>samurai</term> who owns the greater part of the village of Tashiro, at the foot of the mountain. My mother being

ill, I have come up to this old shrine to pray to Kwannon for her recovery. Five times have I been up before, but I never met anyone until today, when this dreadful man attacked me. I owe my rescue entirely to you, holy lady, and I am humbly and deeply grateful. I do hope I will be able to come here and pray at this shrine again. My father and mother prayed here before I was born both to Kwannon and to the Tennin<note>Angel</note> of the mountain. They had no children, and I was sent to them after their prayers. Therefore it is right that I should come here to pray for my mother; but this horrid man has frightened me so much that I will be afraid to come alone again.”

The Mountain Goddess (for such was Okureha’s rescuer) smiled and said: “You need have no fear, my pretty child. Come here whenever you wish, and I will be your protector. Children who are as devoted to their parents as you are deserve all that is good and are holy in themselves. If you wish to please me, come again tomorrow so that we may talk; and bring me some flowers from the fields, for I never descend low enough on earth to get these, though they are my favorites—they smell so sweet. And now you had better go home. When you have had time to reach there, I will restore this horrid man to life and let him go. He is not likely to return to bother you.”

“I will be here tomorrow,” said Okureha, bowing her thanks while saying her “Sayonaras.”

Okureha San was so much impressed by the face of the Goddess that she could not sleep, and at daybreak the next morning she was out in the fields gathering flowers,

## The Perpetual Life-Giving Wine

which she took up the mountain to the shrine, where she found the goddess waiting.

They talked about many subjects and enjoyed each other’s company, and they arranged to meet often. Consequently, whenever Okureha had time, she always went up the mountain. This continued for nearly a year, until one day Okureha went up with flowers for the goddess as usual; however, she looked and felt very sad.

"Why is this?" asked the goddess. "Why are you so sad?"

"Ah, Your Holiness is right," said Okureha. "I am sad because this may be the last day I can come up here and see you. I am now seventeen years old, and my parents think I am old enough to marry. Twelve years ago, my father arranged for me to marry the son of one of his friends, Tokue of Iwasakimura, when we were old enough. Now I am told I am old enough, so I must marry. The wedding is to be in three days. After that, I will have to stay at home and work for my husband, and I fear I will not see you anymore. That is why I am sad." As she spoke, tears ran down her cheeks, and for a few moments, she could not be consoled; but the goddess soothed her, saying:

"You must not be sad, dear child. On the contrary, you are about to enter the happiest stage of life by getting married. If people did not marry and have children to inherit new spirits and life, there could be no continuation of the world. Go back happily, my child; get married and have children. You will be happy and will be doing your duty to the world and to the goddess. Before we say goodbye, I give you this small gourd of

<term>furoshu</term>.<note>furoshu: sake wine of perpetual youth</note> Take care of it on your way down the mountain, and when you are married, give some to your husband. You will both remain as you are in appearance, never growing a day older though you live for centuries, as you will; and it will also bring you perfect happiness. Now, farewell!”

Again the tears came to Okureha’s eyes as she bade farewell to her benefactress; but she mustered all her courage, and, making her last bow, took her way down the mountain, weeping as she went. Three days later, Okureha was married. It was a lucky day according to the calendars, and, moreover, it was the year that the Emperor Toba came to the throne, 1108 <term>A.D.</term>

One day, when celebrating this event at a picnic, Okureha gave her husband some of the <term>furoshu</term> <term>sake</term>, and took the rest herself, as the goddess had instructed her. They were sitting on a beautiful green grassy spot, where wild violets of delicious fragrance grew; at their feet gurgled a mountain stream of sparkling clearness. To their surprise, they found petals of cherry blossoms suddenly falling all around them. There were no cherry trees near, and at first they were much puzzled; but they saw in the blue sky one white cloud which had just sailed over them, and seated on it was the Goddess of Mount Daimugenzan. Okureha recognized her and pointed her out to her husband as their benefactress. The white cloud carried her up to the top of the mountain, where it hovered until the shades of evening hid it.

Okureha and her husband never grew older. They lived for hundreds of years as <term>Sennins</term> on Mount Daimugenzan.

## XXX

# THE HERMIT’S CAVE

MANY years ago, an old farmer named Jinnai lived in the village of Nomugi, in Hida Province, with his wife. They had a daughter whom they simply adored. Her name was Yuka. She was seven years old and an extremely beautiful child. Unfortunately, at this age, she developed a problem with her leg, which grew worse and worse until the limb became deformed. Yuka suffered no pain; but her parents were very troubled. Doctors, medicines, and the advice of many friends did not make Yuka’s leg any better.

"How sad it will be for her later on!" thought her mother and father. "Even now, it is sad that she should have a deformed leg when she plays with other children."

Since there was no help for it, Yuka and her parents had to make the best of things. In any case, Yuka was not the only one with a disability in the village. There were other cases. One of Yuka’s playmates, Tarako, had been born blind; and another, Rinkichi, was so deaf that he could hold his ear to the temple bell while the other children struck it, and he never heard the sound, though he

Nomugi village is at the foot of the great mountain Norikuradake, which rises 10,500 feet and is a wild place of volcanic origin.

Many of the children of Nomugi used to go daily and play on the grassy slope of an old dam at the end of the village. They would throw stones into the water, fish, sail boats, and pick flowers. The dam was a kind of club for the children. From morning to evening they were there, having their rice with them to eat.

One day, while they were playing like this, they were surprised by an old man with a long white beard coming toward them.

### THE OLD HERMIT ENTERTAINS THE CHILDREN

He came from the direction of the mountain. Everyone stopped their games to watch him. He came into their midst and, patting them on the head, seemed to make friends naturally. Noticing Yuka's bad leg, the old man said: "Come! How is this? Have your parents not tried to cure it?" Little Yuka answered that they had, but that they could not do any good. The old man made her lie down on the grass and began to manipulate the leg, pulling it this way and that, and rubbed in some red medicine which he took from a case. The old man then operated on Tarako the blind boy and on Kinkichi <note>The previous page identified this child as Rinkichi.</note> the deaf one.

Very little attention is paid to Japanese children. They are nearly always good and well-behaved—little adults, in fact. Therefore, they ate their suppers and went to bed as such, giving no account of their day's activities or of the strange old man.

The next day they went to the flat rock. Because it was wet, they had not started until late; but they found the old man, and, though he had no time to play with them and show the tricks he had promised, he attended to <term>Yuka</term>'s leg, and to the mute boy and the blind boy.

'Now go home,' he said, 'and come back here tomorrow. By the time you get home, <term>Yuka</term>'s leg will be healed, <term>Tarako</term> will be able to see, and <term>Rinkichi</term> will be able to hear; and I am sure your relatives will be delighted. Tomorrow, if it is fine, you must come early, and we shall have lots of fun.'

Even before they reached home, everything happened just as the old man had said. The three children were recovered. The villagers and the parents rejoiced together; but everyone was mystified as to who the <term>magician</term> could be.

‘If he returns to the mountain, as the children say, then he must live in the cave,’ said one. ‘He must be a <term>Sennin</term> <note>An immortal hermit or enlightened being with supernatural powers</note>,’ said another. ‘It is rumored that the most famous priest, <term>Kukai shonin</term>, who founded the sacred temple on <term>Mount Koyasan</term> in <term>Kii Province</term>, was able to perform these wondrous cures on children,’ added another. But, despite all the gossip and speculation, none could explain how it was possible to give sight to a boy who had been born blind. At last, someone suggested that two or three people should follow the children secretly on the following day; by hiding themselves, they might be able to see what happened. This excellent plan was adopted.

In the morning, about thirty children set off at daybreak, followed—without their knowledge—by two men from the village.

When the children arrived at the flat rock—which is said to be large enough to measure one thousand Japanese mats of six feet by three feet—they found the old man seated at one end of it. The two men who had followed them hid themselves in some fine azalea bushes.

First, they saw the old man stand up and go over to the children to hear from the three cured ones how they felt and how pleased their parents had been. <term>Tarako</term> was perhaps the most delighted of the three, for he had never seen the world before, or even his parents.

## XXXI

## YOSOJI’S CAMELLIA TREE

In the reign of Emperor Sanjo, a particularly unlucky time began. It was about the year 1013 A.D. when Sanjo ascended the throne—the first year of Chowa. A plague broke out. Two years later, the Royal Palace was burned down, and a war began with Korea, which was then known as ‘Shiragi.’

In 1016, another fire broke out in the new Palace. A year later, the Emperor abdicated the throne due to blindness and other causes. He handed over the reins of office to Prince Atsuhara, who was called Emperor Go Ichijo and ascended the throne in the first year of Kwannin, around 1017 or 1018. The period during which Emperor Go Ichijo reigned—about twenty years, up to 1036—was one of the worst in Japanese history. There were more wars, more fires, and worse plagues than ever. Generally, things were in disorder, and even Kyoto was hardly safe for people of wealth because of bands of brigands. In 1025, the most appalling outbreak of smallpox occurred; there was hardly a village or town in Japan that escaped.

<vocab>Emperor Sanjo, Chowa, Shiragi, Prince Atsuhara, Emperor Go Ichijo, Kwannin, Kyoto, smallpox</vocab>

<summary>This page describes a period of extreme civil unrest and natural disaster in 11th-century Japan, spanning the reigns of Emperors Sanjo and Go Ichijo, culminating in a devastating smallpox epidemic in 1025.</summary>
<keywords>Emperor Sanjo, Emperor Go Ichijo, Japanese history, smallpox, Kyoto, Shiragi, Chowa, Kwannin, 11th century, plague</keywords>

--- Page 344 ---
<meta>Continuing from the historical context of the 11th-century plagues, this page introduces the legend of the goddess of Mount Fuji and the story of Yosoji, a youth seeking to save his mother from smallpox.</meta>

It is at this time that our story begins. Our heroine (if she may be called such) is no less a deity than the goddess of the great mountain of Fuji, which nearly everyone in the world has heard of or seen depicted. Therefore, if the legend sounds foolish and childish, blame only my way of telling it (simply, as it was told to me), and think of the Great Mountain of Japan, about which anything should be interesting; furthermore, challenge others to find a better one. I have been able to find none myself.

During the terrible scourge of smallpox, there was a village in Suruga Province called Kamiide, which still exists but is of little importance. It suffered more severely than most other villages. Hardly an inhabitant escaped. A youth of sixteen or seventeen years was greatly tested. His mother was taken with the disease, and, since his father was dead, the responsibility of the household fell on Yosoji—for that was his name.

Yosoji obtained all the help he could for his mother, sparing nothing in the way of medicines and care; but his mother grew worse day by day, until at last her life was utterly despaired of. Having no other resource left to him, Yosoji resolved to consult a famous fortune-teller and magician, Kamo Yamakiko.

Kamo Yamakiko told Yosoji that there was only one chance that his mother could be cured, and that depended greatly on his own courage. "If," said the fortune-teller, "you will go to a small brook which flows from the southwestern side of Mount Fuji and find a small shrine near its source, where Oki-naga-suku-neo¹ is worshiped, you may be able to cure your mother by bringing her water

Yosoji, in no way discouraged, made up his mind that he would start on the following morning, and, thanking the fortune-teller, went home to prepare for an early start.

At three o’clock the next morning, he was off.

Toward midday Yosoji arrived at a place where three rough paths met and was sorely puzzled about which to take. > ‘Wait. I know what you are here for. You are a brave lad and a faithful son. I will be your guide to the stream, and—take my word for it—its waters will cure your mother. Follow me if you will, and have no fear, though the road is bad and dangerous.’

The girl turned, and Yosoji followed in amazement.

The beautiful maiden waved a wild camellia branch over her head as if with a beckoning motion, and a cloud descended from the peak of Mount Fuji, first enveloping her in mist. It then rose, revealing her figure to the weeping Yosoji, who now began to realize that he loved the departing figure, and that she was no less a figure than that of the great Goddess of Fujiyama. Yosoji fell on his knees and prayed to her, and the goddess, acknowledging his prayer, threw down the branch of wild camellia.

Yosoji carried it home and planted it, caring for it with the greatest attention. The branch grew into a tree with marvelous speed, reaching over twenty feet high in just two years. A shrine was built; people came to worship the tree; and it is said that the dewdrops from its leaves are a cure for all eye ailments.

## XXXII

### WHALES

There are many stories and superstitions regarding whales. I will take one, dating back to the 'Hoen' period (1135), which shows the veneration and the fear with which the Japanese have always held these creatures. I will include a translation by Mr. Ando, of our Consulate, of a newspaper paragraph dated February 12, 1907, showing that these superstitions are still current.

Some seven hundred and seventy-two years ago, when the 'Hoen' period began, the shrine of Atsuta at Nagoya was burned down. For some reason, this calamity was said at the time to have occurred because the head shrine-watcher, Yoda Emon, had startled one of the gods.<note>1 The gods mainly worshiped at Atsuta are the Sun Goddess Amaterasu, her brother Susa-no-o, Prince Yamato-take, his wife Miyazu-hime, and her brother Take-ino-tane; however, the most venerated object is the sword called 'Kusa-nagi no Tsurugi,' one of the three principal antique objects that form the Imperial Regalia of Japan. I have previously told a story or two about this, notably that of 'Yamato-dake no Mikoto' (p. 56 and following pages).</note>

### Whales

Province, now generally known as ‘Vries’ Island. It is the largest and most northerly of the group of islands which run in a chain towards the southeast. The nearest to Oshima is Toshi Island, often named Rishima, of which our story is told.

Yoda Emon was a man of active mind and pursuits. Perhaps that is why he startled the god who caused the fire at Atsuta. In any case, he felt his exile greatly. He could get no news of home or family, and he fretted and worried himself to such an extent that at last his nights became sleepless; he thought to himself that if some relief for his mind did not come soon, he would either have to kill himself or go mad.

At last it occurred to him that he might possibly get permission to go fishing; and the permission was granted to him, on the condition that he stayed within a mile of the shore. Day after day, Yoda took the boat which was lent to him and generally returned with a good supply of fish, singing to himself as he rowed to and from the shore. He soon managed to sleep soundly and regain his strength. After a month or two, Yoda became quite a popular person, giving his fish away for free to anyone who chose to take them, and he was soon allowed a wider range than the one-mile limit. He became an expert sailor, and if it had not been for the loss of his family, he would have been quite happy in his new home. One day, the morning being calm, Yoda ventured farther away than usual, hoping to catch some of the larger fish which were rumored to be plentiful about ten miles from Toshishima. He was lucky and caught three magnificent fish of the mackerel family, known as ‘sara.’

Unfortunately, after this, the wind, instead of blowing from the southeast as usual, came from the northwest, and instead of being able to return to Oshima, Yoda found himself being blown further from it. The wind grew stronger and stronger until a gale was blowing, and soon the currents caused a high and breaking sea. Darkness fell, and Yoda thought to himself that this was a punishment visited upon him for having caught fish. "Oh," he cried aloud, "what foolish sin have I now committed? Surely my position as a banished priest should have told me that I was sinning by catching fish!" He threw himself onto the bottom of the boat and prayed; but his prayers gained him nothing, for the wind increased in force, as did the sea. Long after midnight, a massive wave smashed the boat to splinters. Half-stunned and half-drowned, Yoda clung to the large oar and remained that way for about three hours.

At last, he felt himself bump against what he took to be a rock, and letting go of the oar, he scrambled onto it, more dead than alive. After many efforts, he was so exhausted and so numb that he sat there only half-conscious in the dark.

Towards morning, the turning tide caused the sea to calm down, and as the sun rose, Yoda found to his horror that it was no rock upon which he sat, but the back of a living whale of gigantic size. Yoda knew neither what to do nor what to think; he dared not move for fear of disturbing the whale’s rest. Not even when the animal blew water and air from its spout-hole did he

A lifeline with a buoy attached was floated toward the whale, and when it was near enough, Yoda slid off to take it and was hauled into the boat, thoroughly thankful for his rescue. As soon as Yoda was on board, the boat began to roll, for the whale lashed its tail and played about, causing a heavy sea; but, to the relief of everyone, the creature headed south for the open Pacific.

The crew on the fishing boat belonged to Toshi Island and had heard of Yoda Emon. Being good-natured men, they felt sorry for him in his exile. After his astonishing adventure with the whale, they did not mind at all taking him back to Oshima, which they reached around sunset.

Yoda immediately reported himself and was congratulated on his extraordinary escape.

After this, Yoda gave up fishing and submitted without complaint to the severe discipline of his exile. When Prince Tanin ascended the throne, an ordinance was issued granting freedom to many prisoners

"Now," thought he, "I shall be able to repay the kindness that the whale showed me in saving my life!" And he issued an order that no whales were to be chased or killed anywhere near the islands over which he had jurisdiction. At first there was some grumbling; but the Government sent messengers to Oshima to say that the Emperor approved Yoda Emon’s order, and furthermore, that during Yoda’s life, no whale was to be killed anywhere in Shichito.

In a few moments they bowed and separated. O Hanano and her maid walked away from the temple, while the youth under the cherry tree looked after them.

Tokunosuke was now furiously jealous. He came from his hiding place, and accosted the youth under the cherry tree in a rude and rough tone.

‘Who are you, you hateful rascal? Give me your name and address at once! And tell me how you dare tempt the beautiful O Hanano San to love you!’ He was about to seize his enemy by the arm when the enemy jumped suddenly back a step, and before Tokunosuke had time to catch him a sudden gust of wind blew the blossoms thickly off the cherry tree. So thick and quickly did the blossoms fall, they blinded Tokunosuke for some moments. When he could see again the handsome youth was gone; but there was a strange moaning sound inside the cherry tree, while one of the temple priests came rushing at him in great anger, crying ‘Ah! you sacrilegious villain!’

## XXXIV

# A STORY OF MOUNT KANZANREI

Far up on the northeastern coast of Korea is a high mountain called Kanzanrei. Not far from its base, where the district of Kanko Fu lies, is a village called Teiheigun, which trades in little but natural products such as mushrooms, timber, furs, fish, and a little gold.

In this village lived a pretty girl named Choyo, an orphan of some means. Her father, Choka, had been the only merchant in the district, and he had made quite a fortune for those parts, which he left to Choyo when she was about sixteen years old.

At the foot of Mount Kanzanrei lived a wood-cutter of simple and frugal habits. He lived alone in a broken-down hut, associated only with the few people to whom he sold his wood, and was generally considered to be a morose and unsociable man. He was called "the Recluse," and many wondered who he was and why he kept so much to himself, for he was not yet thirty years old and was remarkable for his good looks and strong frame. Sawada Shigeoki was his name, but the people did not know it.

<vocab>Korea, Kanzanrei, Kanko Fu, Teiheigun, Choyo, Choka, wood-cutter, Sawada Shigeoki</vocab>

# A Story of Mount Kanzanrei

One evening, as the Recluse was making his way down the rough mountain path with a large load of firewood on his back, he was resting in a particularly wild and rocky pass. The area was darkened by the huge pine trees that towered on every side, and he was startled by a rustling sound close below. He looked nervously around, for the place where he was had the reputation of being haunted by tigers—and with some truth, for several people had lately been killed by them. On this occasion, however, the sound that had startled the Recluse was caused by no tiger, but only by a pheasant that fluttered off her nest. She was imitating the movements of a wounded bird to draw the intruder’s attention away from the location of her nest. However, the Recluse thought it was strange that the bird should have acted that way, for she could neither have seen nor heard him; and so he listened intently to find the cause. He did not have many minutes to wait. Almost immediately, the Recluse heard the sounds of voices and scuffling, and, hiding himself behind the trunk of a large tree, he waited, axe in hand.

Soon he saw a girl of extraordinary beauty being carried, pushed, and dragged down the path. She was in the hands of three villainous men whom the Recluse soon recognized as bandits.

As they were coming his way, the Recluse stayed where he was, hidden behind the great pine and gripping his axe more firmly; and as the four approached him, he sprang out and blocked their way.

"Who do you have here, and what are you doing with this girl?" he cried. "Let her go, or you will suffer!"

Being three against one, the robbers were not afraid and shouted back, ‘Stay out of our way, you fool, and let us pass—unless you want to lose your life!’ But the woodcutter was not afraid. He raised his axe, and the robbers drew their swords. The woodcutter was too strong for them. In an instant, he had cut down one and pushed another over the cliff, and the third fled, only too glad to escape with his life.

The Recluse then bent down to tend to the girl, who had fainted. He fetched water and bathed her face, bringing her back to her senses; as soon as she was able to speak, he asked who she was, if she was hurt, and how she had fallen into the hands of such ruffians.

Through her sobs and weeping, the girl answered:

‘I am Choyo Choka. My home is the village of Teiheigun. Today is the anniversary of my father’s death, and I went to pray at his tomb at the foot of Gando Mountain. Since the day was fine, I decided to take a long walk and return this way. About an hour ago, I was seized by these robbers, and you know the rest. Oh, sir, I am thankful to you for your bravery in saving me. Please tell me your name.’

The woodcutter answered:

‘Ah, then you are the famous beauty of Teiheigun village, whom I have so often heard of! It is an honor indeed for me to have been able to help you. As for me, I am a woodcutter. They call me the “Recluse,” and I live at the foot of this mountain. If you will come with me, I will take you to my hut where you can rest, and then I will see you safely home.’

That night, Choyo could think of nothing but the brave and handsome woodcutter who had saved her life; indeed, she thought of him so much that before dawn broke, she found herself deeply and desperately in love.

The day passed and night fell. Choyo had told all her friends about how she had been saved and by whom. Accordingly, at daybreak the next morning, she set off carrying her gift in a basket. By good fortune, she found the Recluse at home, sharpening his axes but otherwise taking a day of rest.

"I have come, sir, to thank you again for your brave rescue of me the other day," said the love-sick Choyo, "and I have brought a small gift, which I hope you will deign to accept, however unworthy it may be."

"There is no reason to thank me for performing a common duty," said the Recluse, "but it is pleasing to be thanked by such a fair pair of lips as yours, and I feel greatly honored. The gift, however, I cannot accept; for then I should be the debtor, which is wrong for a man."

Choyo felt both flattered and rejected by this speech, and she tried again to get the Recluse to accept her gift; but, although her attempts led to friendly conversation and to playful teasing, he would not do so, and Choyo left, saying:

"Well, you have beaten me today; but I will return, and in time I shall beat you and make you accept a gift from me."

"Come here whenever you like," answered the Recluse. "I shall always be glad to see you, for you are a ray of light in my miserable hut; but you shall never place me under an obligation by making me accept a gift."

It was a strange answer, Choyo thought as she left; but she said to herself, "Oh, how handsome he is, and how I love him! And anyway, I will visit him again, often, and see who wins in the end."

Such was the confidence of a girl as beautiful as Choyo. She felt that she must eventually win.

For the next two months, she visited the Recluse often, and they sat and talked. He brought her wildflowers of great rarity and beauty from the highest mountains, and berries to eat; but never once did he court her or even accept the slightest gift from her hands. That did not stop Choyo from pursuing her love. She was determined to win in the end, and she even felt that, in a way, this strange man loved her as she loved him, but for some reason would not say so.

To the Japanese mind, he acted as Buddha did when he renounced his worldly loves. What chance is there for a sincere friendship between Japan and Korea if all men act this way?

# XXXV

## WHITE BONE MOUNTAIN

At the foot of Mount Shumongatake, in the northwestern province of Echigo, there once stood—and probably still stands today, whether in a state of decay or repair—a temple of some importance, as it was the burial ground for the ancestors of the feudal Lord Yamana. The name of the temple was Fumonji, and many high-ranking and influential priests maintained it generation after generation, thanks to the early support received from Lord Yamana’s relatives. Among the priests who presided over this temple was one named Ajari Joan, who was the adopted son of the Otomo family.

Ajari was learned and virtuous, and he had many followers; but one day, the sight of a most attractive eighteen-year-old girl named Kiku¹ upset his entire religious balance. He fell desperately in love with her, offering to sacrifice his position and reputation if she would only listen to his plea and marry him; but the lovely O Kiku San refused all his entreaties. A year later, she fell seriously ill with a fever and died, and

<note>¹ Chrysanthemum.</note>

<summary>A learned priest named Ajari Joan falls desperately in love with a young woman named Kiku, who refuses his proposals. A year later, Kiku tragically dies of a fever.</summary>
<keywords>White Bone Mountain, Mount Shumongatake, Echigo, Lord Yamana, Fumonji Temple, Ajari Joan, Kiku, unrequited love</keywords>

--- Page 388 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of Ajari Joan and O Kiku. Following Kiku's death, rumors spread of a curse, leading to Ajari's descent into madness and the eventual ruin of the Fumonji temple.</meta>

Whispers spread that Ajari the priest had cursed her in his jealousy and caused her illness and death. The rumor was not entirely without merit, for Ajari went mad within a week of O Kiku's death. He neglected his religious services and then grew worse, running wildly about the temple, shrieking at night and frightening everyone who came near. Finally, one night he dug up O Kiku's body and ate part of her flesh.

People declared that he had turned into a demon, and no one dared go near the temple; even the younger priests left, until at last he was alone. The people were so terrified that no one approached the temple, which soon fell into ruin. Thorny bushes grew on the roof, and moss grew on the previously polished and matted floors; birds built their nests inside, perched on the mortuary tablets, and made a mess of everything. The temple, which had once been a masterpiece of beauty, became a rotting ruin.

One summer evening, some six or seven months later, an old woman who owned a tea house at the foot of Mount Shumongatake was about to close her shutters when she was terrified by the sight of an approaching priest wearing a white cap. "The Devil Priest! The Devil Priest!" she cried as she slammed the last shutter in his face. "Go away, go away! We can't have you here."

"What do you mean by 'Devil Priest'? I am a traveling pilgrim priest, not a robber. Let me in at once, for I want both rest and refreshment," cried the voice from outside. The old woman looked through a crack in the shutters and saw that it was not the dreaded madman, but a venerable pilgrim priest; so she

The next afternoon the old priest, true to his word, started for the Fumonji Temple. The old lady accompanied him for the first part of the walk to the place where the path leading to the temple turned up the mountain, and there she said goodbye to him, refusing to go another step.

The sun was beginning to set as the priest came in sight of the temple, and he saw that the place was in great disorder. The gates had fallen off their hinges; withered leaves were thickly strewn everywhere and crunched under his feet; but he walked boldly on and struck a small temple bell with his staff. At the sound, many birds and bats flew from the temple, the bats flapping around his head; but there was no other sign of life. He struck the bell again with renewed force, and it boomed and clanged in echoes. At last, a thin, miserable-looking priest came out and, looking wildly about, said: "Who are you, and why have you come here? The temple has long since been deserted for some reason which I cannot understand. If you want lodging, you must go to the village. There is neither food nor bedding here."

Meanwhile, the mad priest made several rushing visits to the exterior of the temple, all the while keeping up his awful cries for O Kiku. Toward morning, he retired once more to the part of the temple where he lived, and no more noise was made. Our pilgrim then came out from his hiding place and seated himself on the rock he had occupied the evening before, determined to see if he could force a conversation with the demented man and teach him a lesson from the sacred teachings of Buddha. He sat patiently until the sun was high, but all remained silent. There was no sign of the mad priest.

Toward midday, the pilgrim heard sounds in the temple; and by and by the madman came out, looking as if he had just recovered from a drunken orgy. He appeared dazed and was quiet, and he started when he saw the old priest seated on the rock just as he had been the night before. The old man rose and, approaching him, said:

“My friend, my name is Ungai. I am a fellow priest from the Temple of Daigoji, in Wakasa Province. I came here to see you, having heard of your great wisdom; but last night I heard in the village that you had broken your vows as a priest and lost your heart to a maiden, and that from your love for her you have turned into a dangerous demon. Consequently, I have considered it my duty to come and give you a lecture, as it is impossible to let your conduct go unnoticed. Please listen to the lecture and tell me if I can help you.”

The mad priest answered quite meekly:
“You are indeed a Buddha. Please tell me what I can do to forget the past, and to become a holy and virtuous priest once more.”

Ungai answered:
“Come out here into the grounds and seat yourself on this rock.” Then he read a lecture from the Buddhist Bible, and finished by saying, “And now, if you wish to redeem your soul, you must sit on this rock until you are able to explain the following lines, which are written in this sacred book: ‘*The moon on the lake shines on the winds between the pine trees, and a long night grows quiet at midnight!*’” Having said this, Ungai bowed low and left the mad priest, Joan, seated on the rock reflecting.

For a month Ungai wandered from temple to temple, lecturing. At the end of that time he came back by way of Fumonji Temple, and thought he would go up to it and see what had happened to mad Joan. At the tea-house where he had first stayed, he asked the old landlady if she had seen or heard any more of the crazy priest.

“No,” she said: “we have neither seen nor heard of

The next morning, Ungai went to the temple and found Joan still seated exactly as he had left him on the rock, muttering the words: “*The moon on the lake shines on the winds between the pine trees, and a long night grows quiet at midnight!*” Joan’s hair and beard had become long and gray during that time, and he appeared to be miserably thin and almost transparent. Ungai was struck with pity at Joan’s righteous determination and patience, and tears came to his eyes.

“Get up, get up,” he said, “for indeed you are a holy and determined man.”

But Joan did not move. Ungai poked him with his staff to awaken him, as he thought; but, to his horror, Joan fell to pieces and disappeared like a flake of melting snow.

Ungai stayed in the temple for three days, praying for the soul of Joan. The villagers, hearing of this generous action, rebuilt the temple and made him their priest. Their temple had formerly belonged to the Mitsu sect, but now it was transferred to Ungai’s “Jo do” sect, and the title or name of “Fumonji” was changed to “Hakkotsuzan” (White Bone Mountain). The temple is said to have prospered for hundreds of years afterward.

### XXXVI

## A STORMY NIGHT'S TRAGEDY ¹

All who have read anything of Japanese history must have heard of Saigo Takamori, who lived between the years 1827 and 1877. He was a great Imperialist, fighting for the Emperor until 1876, when he gave up due to his disapproval of the Europeanization occurring in the country and the abandonment of ancient national ways. As the acting Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Army, Saigo fled to Kagoshima, where he raised a body of faithful followers; this was the beginning of the Satsuma Rebellion. The Imperialists defeated them, and in September 1877 Saigo was killed—some say in the final battle, while others say he committed ‘seppuku,’ and that his head was cut off and secretly buried so that it would not fall into the hands of his enemies. Saigo Takamori was highly honored even by the Imperialists. It is hard to call him a rebel. He did not rebel against his Emperor, but only against the repulsive idea of becoming Europeanized. Who can say that he was not right? He was a man of fine sentiment and great loyalty. Should all of us

In the first year of Meiji (1868), the Tokugawa army had been badly beaten by Saigo at Fushimi, and Field Marshal Tokugawa Keiki had the greatest difficulty reaching the sea and escaping to Edo <note>Yedo</note>. The Imperial army proceeded along the Tokaido road, determined to break up the Tokugawa forces. Their advance guard had reached Hiratsuka, near the base of Mount Fuji on the coast.

It was a spring day, the 5th of April, and the cherry trees were in full bloom. The country folk had come in to see the victorious troops, who formed the advance guard of those who had defeated the Tokugawa. There were many beggars about, along with peddlers and sellers of sweets, roasted potatoes, and various other things. Toward evening, clouds filled the sky; at five o'clock the rain began, and by six o'clock everyone was under cover.

The poor man was led in by a side door and brought into the presence of the officers. ‘Gentlemen,’ said he, ‘you have done me a very great honor and a kindness, for it is not pleasant to stand outside playing in the rain with cotton clothes on. I think I can repay you, for it is said that I play the <term>shakuhachi</term> well. Since I have been blind, it has become my only pleasure, and not only that, but also my only means of living. It is hard now in these unsettled days, when everything is upside-down, to earn a living. Not many travelers come to the inns while the Imperial troops occupy them. These are hard days, gentlemen.’

‘They may be hard days for you, poor blind fellow; but say nothing against the Imperial troops, for we must be suspicious, as there are spies of the Tokugawa. Indeed, each of us needs three eyes in his head.’

‘Well, well, I have no wish to say anything against the Imperial troops,’ said the blind man. ‘All I have to say is that it is very hard for a blind man to earn enough rice with which to fill his stomach. On average, I am called only once a week to play for private parties or to massage <note>The original text uses "shampoo," which was an archaic term for massage.</note> some person with rheumatism, which this wet weather produces—the blessing of the Gods be on it!’

In the morning, the form of a man might have been seen stealthily climbing this huge tree until he had reached the branch which hung over the inn. There he stretched himself flat and began squirming along, evidently intent on reaching the upper floor of the house. Unfortunately for him, he cracked a small branch of dead wood, and the sound caused a sentry to look up. ‘Who goes there?’ he cried, bringing his musket around; but there was no answer. The sentry shouted for help, and in less than twenty seconds the whole house was awake and outside. No escape for the man in the tree was possible. He was taken prisoner. Imagine everyone's astonishment when they found that he was the blind beggar, but now not blind at all; his eyes flashed with the fire of indignation at his captors, for the great plan of his young life was ruined.

‘Who is he?’ everyone cried, ‘and why the trickery of pretending to be blind last evening?’

‘A spy—that is what he is! A <term>Tokugawa</term> spy,’ said one. ‘Take him to Headquarters so that the chief officers may interrogate him; and be careful to hold his hands, for he has every appearance of being a <term>samurai</term> and a fighter.’

And so the prisoner was led off to the <term>Temple of Hommonji</term>, where the Staff Headquarters were temporarily located.

The prisoner was brought into the presence of Saigo Takamori and four other Imperial officers, one of whom was Katsura Kogoro. He was made to kneel. Then Saigo, who was the Chief, said, ‘Hold your head up and give us your name.’

### XXXVII

## THE KAKEMONO GHOST OF AKI PROVINCE <gloss>1</gloss>

D<sc>own</sc> the Inland Sea between Umedaichi and Kure (now a great naval port) in the province of Aki, there is a small village called Yaiyama. In this village lived a painter of some note named Abe Tenko. Abe Tenko taught more than he painted; he depended for his living mostly on the modest inheritance he had received at his father's death and on the aspiring artists who lodged in the village to take daily lessons from him. The island and rock scenery in the neighborhood provided constant study, and Tenko was never short of pupils. Among them was one who was little more than a boy, being only seventeen years old. His name was Sawara Kameju, and he was a most promising pupil. He had been sent to Tenko over a year earlier, when he was barely sixteen; because Tenko had been a friend of his father, Sawara was taken into the artist’s home and treated as if he were his own son.

Tenko had a sister who had entered the service of the Lord of Aki, with whom she had a daughter. If the child had been a son, he would have been adopted into the Aki family; however, as the child was a daughter, she was sent back to her mother's family according to Japanese custom. Consequently, Tenko took charge of the child, whose name was Kimi. Since her mother was dead, the child had lived with him for sixteen years. Our story begins with O Kimi having grown into a beautiful young woman.

O Kimi was a most devoted adopted daughter to Tenko. She managed almost all of his household affairs, and Tenko looked upon her as if she were truly his own daughter instead of an illegitimate niece, trusting her in everything.

After the arrival of the young student, O Kimi's heart caused her much distress. She fell in love with him. Sawara admired O Kimi greatly, but he never spoke a word of love, being far too absorbed in his studies. He saw Kimi as a sweet girl, taking his meals with her and enjoying her company. He would have fought for her, and he did love her; however, he never allowed himself the time to consider that she was not his sister and that he might court her. So it finally happened that one day, with the ache of love in her heart, O Kimi took advantage of her guardian's absence at the temple, where he had gone to paint something for the priests. O Kimi gathered her courage and confessed her love to Sawara. She told him that since he had come to the house, her heart had known no peace. She loved him and wished to marry him, if he did not mind.

In the old days, the Japanese were even more shockingly poor at corresponding than they are now, and even lovers or engaged couples did not write to each other, as several of my tales may show.

After Sawara had been away for a year, it seemed that he should write and say, at any rate, how he was getting on; but he did not do so. A second year passed, and still there was no news. In the meantime, there had been several admirers of O Kimi who had proposed to Tenko

Poor O Kimi San burst into tears and deep sobs, and without answering a word went to her room, where Tenko thought it best to leave her alone for the night.

In the morning she was gone; no one knew where, as there was no trace of her.

Up in Kyoto, Sawara continued his studies, true and faithful to O Kimi. After receiving Tenko’s letter approving of Myokei’s proposal for Sawara to become his son-in-law, Myokei asked Sawara if he would so honor him.

"When you marry my daughter, we shall be a family of painters, and I think you will be one of the most celebrated ones that Japan ever had."

"But, sir," cried Sawara, "I cannot do myself the honor of marrying your daughter, for I am already engaged—I have been for the last three years—to Kimi, Tenko’s daughter. It is very strange that he should not have told you!"

Myokei had nothing to say to this, but Sawara had much to think about. Perhaps he thought it was foolish of the Japanese not to correspond more freely. Accordingly, he wrote to Kimi twice, but no answer came. Then Myokei caught a chill, fell ill, and died; so Sawara returned to his village home in Aki. There, he was welcomed by Tenko, who was now lonely in his old age without O Kimi.

When Sawara heard that Kimi had gone away without leaving an address or a letter, he was very angry, for he had not been told the true reason for her departure.

"She is an ungrateful and bad girl," he said to Tenko, "and I have been lucky indeed not to marry her!"

"Yes, yes," said Tenko. "You have been lucky, but you must not be too angry. Women are strange creatures; as the saying goes, only when you see water running uphill and hens laying square eggs can you expect to see a truly honest-minded woman. But come now—I want to tell you that, since I am growing old and feeble, I wish to make you the master of my house and property here. You must take my name and marry!"

Feeling disgusted by O Kimi’s conduct, Sawara readily consented. A pretty young girl, the daughter of a wealthy farmer, was found—Kiku (the Chrysanthemum)—and she and Sawara lived happily with old Tenko, keeping his house and looking after his estate. Sawara painted in his spare time. Little by little, he became quite famous. One day, the Lord of Aki sent for him and said it was his wish that Sawara should paint the seven beautiful scenes of the Kabakarijima Islands (probably only six); the pictures were to be mounted on gold screens.

This was the first commission that Sawara had received from such a high official. He was very proud of it and went to the Upper and Lower Kabakari Islands, where he made rough sketches. He also went to the rocky islands of Shokokujima and to the small, uninhabited island of Daikokujima, where an adventure happened to him.

Strolling along the shore, he met a girl tanned by the sun and wind. She wore only a red cotton cloth around her waist, and her hair fell upon her shoulders. She had been gathering shellfish and had a basket of them under her arm. Sawara thought it strange that he should meet a woman alone in such a wild place, and even more so when she addressed him, saying, “Surely you are Sawara Kameju—are you not?”

“Yes,” answered Sawara. “I am; but it is very strange that you should know me. May I ask how you know who I am?”

“If you are Sawara, as I know you are, you should know me without asking, for I am none other than Kimi, to whom you were engaged!”

Sawara was astonished and hardly knew what to say; so he asked her questions about how she had come to this lonely island. O Kimi explained everything and ended by saying, with a smile of happiness on her face:

“And since, my dearest Sawara, I understand that what I was told is false—and that you did not marry Myokei’s daughter, and that we have been faithful to each other—we can be married and happy after all. Oh, think how happy we shall be!”

“Alas, alas, my dearest Kimi, it cannot be! I was led to believe that you had deserted our benefactor Tenko and given up all thought of me. Oh, the sadness of it—”

all the wickedness! I was persuaded that you were unfaithful, and I was made to marry another!’

O Kimi made no answer, but began to run along the shore toward a little hut which she had made her home. She ran fast, and Sawara ran after her, calling, ‘Kimi, Kimi, stop and speak to me’; but Kimi did not stop. She reached her hut and, seizing a knife, plunged it into her throat and fell back, bleeding to death. Sawara, greatly grieved, burst into tears. It was horrible to see the girl who might have been his bride lying dead at his feet, covered in blood, having suffered such a terrible death at her own hands. Deeply affected, he drew paper from his pocket and made a sketch of the body. Then he and his boatman buried O Kimi above the tide-mark near the primitive hut. Afterward, at home, with a mournful heart, he painted a picture of the dead girl and hung it in his room.

On the first night it was hung, Sawara had a dreadful dream. On awakening, he found that the figure on the <term>kakemono</term> seemed to be alive: the ghost of O Kimi stepped out of it and stood near his bed. Night after night the ghost appeared, until sleep and rest were no longer possible for Sawara. He thought there was nothing to be done but to send his wife back to her parents, which he did; and he presented the <term>kakemono</term> to the Korinji Temple, where the priests kept it with great care and prayed daily for the spirit of O Kimi San. After that, Sawara saw the ghost no more.

The <term>kakemono</term> is called the Ghost Picture of Tenko II, and it is said to be still kept in the Korinji Temple, where it was placed some 230 to 240 years ago.

## XXXVIII

### WHITE SAKE

Two thousand or more years ago, Lake Biwa in Omi Province and Mount Fuji in Suruga Province came into being in one night. Though my story relates this as fact, you are fully entitled to say, if you feel so inclined, "Wonderful indeed are the ways of Nature"; but do so respectfully, if you please, and without levity, for otherwise you will cause grave offense and will not understand the ethical ideas of Japanese folklore stories.

Well, at the time of this extraordinary geographical event, there lived a man named Yurine, who was poor even for those days. He loved sake wine and scarcely ever spent a day without drinking some of it. Yurine lived near the place which is now called Sudzukawa, a little to the north of the river known as Fujikawa.

On the day following Mount Fuji’s appearance, Yurine became ill and was consequently unable to drink his cup of sake. He became worse and worse, and at last, feeling that there was no hope for him, he decided to give himself the pleasure of drinking a cup before he died. Accordingly, he called his only son to him,

Koyuri, a boy of fourteen, and told him to go and fetch him a cup or two of the wine. Koyuri was greatly perplexed. He had no sake in the house, and there was not a single coin left with which to buy any. He did not want to tell his father this, fearing that the unpleasant state of affairs might make him worse. So he took his gourd and went wandering along the beach, wondering how he could get what his father wanted. While doing this, Koyuri heard a voice calling him by name. As he looked up toward the pines that bordered the beach, he saw a man and a woman sitting beneath an immense tree; their hair was scarlet red, and so were their bodies. At first Koyuri was afraid—he had never seen anyone like them before—but the voice was kind, and the man was signaling to him to approach. Koyuri did so in fear and trembling, but with the coolness that characterizes the Japanese boy.

As Koyuri approached the strange people, he noticed that they were drinking sake from large, flat cups known as <term>sakazuki</term>, and that on the sand beside them was an immense jar from which they took the liquor; moreover, he noticed that the sake was whiter than any he had seen before.

Thinking always of his father, Koyuri unslung his gourd, explained his father’s illness, and begged for sake. The red man took the gourd and filled it. After expressing his gratitude, Koyuri ran off delighted. “Here, father, here!” he said as he reached his hut. “I have got the sake for you, the best I have ever seen, and I am sure it tastes as good as it looks; try it and tell me!”

[Yurine drank it,] expressing great satisfaction and said that it was indeed the best he had ever tasted. The next day he wanted more. Now, there lived in the next hut to Yurine an unpleasant neighbor who was also fond of <term>saké</term>, but too poor to obtain it. His name was Mamikiko. On hearing that Yurine had been drinking <term>saké</term> for the last five days, he became furiously jealous and, calling Koyuri, asked where and how he had obtained it. The boy explained that he had gotten it from the strange people with red hair who had been living near the big pine tree for the past few days.

“Give me your gourd to taste,” cried Mamikiko, snatching it roughly. “Do you think that your father is the only man who is good enough for <term>saké</term>?” Putting the gourd to his lips, he began to drink; but he threw it down in disgust a second later and spat out what was in his mouth. “What filth is this?” he cried. “To your father you give the most excellent <term>saké</term>, while to me you give foul water! What is the meaning of it?” He gave Koyuri a sound beating and then told him to lead the way to the red people on the beach, saying, “I will beat you again if I don’t get some good <term>saké</term>; so you had better see to it!”

Koyuri led the way, weeping all the while at the loss of his <term>saké</term>, which Mamikiko had thrown away, and fearing the anger of his red friends. In the usual place, they found the strangers, who had both been drinking and

## White Saké

come here to see it. While enjoying the magnificent scene from the Suruga coast, I met this good boy, <term>Koyuri</term>, who asked for <term>saké</term> for his poor, sick, old father, and I gave him some. Now, this <term>saké</term> is not ordinary <term>saké</term>, but sacred; those who drink it live forever and retain their youth. Moreover, it cures all diseases, even in the elderly. But you must know that any medicine is sometimes a poison, and thus it is that this sweet, sacred white <term>saké</term> tastes good only to the righteous, and is bad-tasting and poisonous to the wicked. Therefore, I know that, since it tastes foul to you, you are an evil and wicked man, selfish and greedy."

And both the <term>shojos</term> laughed at <term>Mamikiko</term>, who, upon hearing that the few drops he must have swallowed would act as poison and soon kill him, began to cry with fear and to regret his behavior. He begged and implored forgiveness and that his life might be spared, and he vowed that he would reform if only given a chance. The <term>shojo</term>, taking some powder from a case, gave it to <term>Mamikiko</term> and told him to swallow it with some <term>saké</term>; "for," said he, "it is better to repent and reform even in your old age than not at all."

<term>Mamikiko</term> drank it down this time, finding the wine sweet and delicious; it strengthened him and made him feel well, and he reformed and became a good man. He became friends again with <term>Yurine</term> and treated <term>Koyuri</term> well.

Some years later, <term>Mamikiko</term> and <term>Yurine</term> built a hut at the southern base of <term>Fuji San</term>, where they brewed white <term>saké</term> from a recipe given to them by the <term>shojo</term>, and they gave it to all who suffered from <term>saké</term> poisoning. Both <term>Mamikiko</term> and <term>Yurine</term> lived for 300 years.

## XXXIX

### THE BLIND BEAUTY

NEARLY three hundred years ago (or, according to my storyteller, in the second year of <term>Kwanei</term>, which would be 1626, the period of <term>Kwanei</term> having begun in 1624 and ended in 1644), there lived at Maidzuru, in the province of Tango, a youth named Kichijiro.

Kichijiro was born in the village of Tai, where his father had been a native; but upon the death of his father, he had come with his elder brother, Kichisuke, to Maidzuru. The brother was his only living relative except for an uncle, and had taken care of him for four years, educating him from the age of eleven until fifteen. Kichijiro was very grateful and determined that, now he had reached the age of fifteen, he must no longer be a burden to his brother but must begin to make his own way in the world.

After looking about for several weeks, Kichijiro found employment with Shiwoya Hachiyemon, a merchant in Maidzuru. He worked very hard and soon gained his master's friendship; indeed, Hachiyemon thought very highly of his apprentice and favored him in many ways

### XL

## THE SECRET OF IIDAMACHI POND

In the first year of Bunkyu (1861–1864), there lived a man named Yehara Keisuke in Kasumigaseki, in the district of Kojimachi. He was a <term>hatomoto</term>—that is, a feudal vassal of the <term>Shogun</term>—and a man who commanded respect. However, beyond his rank, Yehara was well-liked for his kindness of heart and his general fairness in dealing with people. In Iidamachi lived another <term>hatomoto</term>, Hayashi Hayato. He had been married to Yehara's sister for five years. They were very happy; their daughter, now four years old, was the joy of their lives. Their cottage was somewhat run-down, but it belonged to Hayashi. It featured a pond in front and two farms; the entire property spanned about two hundred acres, of which nearly half was under cultivation. Consequently, Hayashi was able to live comfortably without working much. In the summer, he fished for carp; in the winter, he wrote extensively and was considered something of a poet.

At the time of this story, Hayashi—having finished planting his rice and sweet potatoes (<term>sato-imo</term>)—had little to do, and

<summary>This page introduces Yehara Keisuke and his brother-in-law Hayashi Hayato, a feudal vassal living a peaceful, semi-retired life in Iidamachi. Hayashi enjoys a quiet existence tending to his estate, fishing, and writing poetry with his wife and young daughter.</summary>
<keywords>Yehara Keisuke, Hayashi Hayato, hatomoto, Shogun, Iidamachi, Bunkyu era, sato-imo, samurai life</keywords>

--- Page 446 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of Hayashi Hayato and his family, following the introduction of their peaceful life on their estate in Iidamachi.</meta>

spent most of his time with his wife, fishing in his ponds, one of which contained large <term>suppon</term> (terrapin turtles) as well as <term>koi</term> (carp). Suddenly, things went wrong.

Yehara was surprised one morning to receive a visit from his sister, O Komé.

"I have come, dear brother," she said, "to beg you to help me obtain a divorce or separation from my husband."

"Divorce! Why would you want a divorce? Have you not always said you were happy with your husband, my dear friend Hayashi? For what sudden reason do you ask for a divorce? Remember, you have been married for five years now, and that is enough to prove that your life has been happy and that Hayashi has treated you well."

At first, O Komé would not give any reason why she wished to be separated from her husband; but at last, she said:

"Brother, do not think that Hayashi has been unkind. He is as kind as anyone could be, and we love each other deeply; but, as you know, Hayashi’s family has owned the land and the farms—one of which we live on—for some three hundred years. Nothing would persuade him to change his home, and I would never have wished him to do so until about twelve days ago."

"What has happened within these twelve extraordinary days?" asked Yehara.

"Dear brother, I can stand it no longer," was his sister’s answer. "Up to twelve days ago, all went well; but then a terrible thing happened. It was very dark and warm, and I was sitting outside our house looking at the clouds..."

The old woman continued:

“When Hayashi Hayato, your grandfather, was alive, we had a beautiful servant girl, seventeen years of age, called O Sumi. Your grandfather became enamored of this girl, and she of him. I was about thirty at that time and was jealous, for my beauty had faded. One day when your grandfather was out, I took Sumi to the pond and gave her a severe beating. During the struggle, she fell into the water and became entangled in the weeds; and there I left her, fully believing the water to be shallow and that she could get out. She did not succeed and was drowned. Your grandfather found her dead on his return. In those days, the police were not very thorough with their inquiries. The girl was buried, but nothing was said to me, and the matter soon blew over. Fourteen days ago was the fiftieth anniversary of this tragedy. Perhaps that is the reason for Sumi’s ghost appearing; for appear she must, or your child could not have known her name. It must be as your child says,”

# XLI

## THE SPIRIT OF YENOKI <note>Fukuga Sei said that this was an old story told to him by his nurse, who was a native of the village of Oki-yama; he also mentioned that a solid gold Buddha, eighteen inches in height, had been stolen from the temple three years ago.</note>

There is a mountain in the province of Idsumi called Oki-yama (or Oji Yama); it is connected with the Mumaru-Yama mountains. I will not vouch for my accuracy in spelling either name. Suffice it to say that the story was told to me by Fukuga Sei and translated by Mr. Ando, the Japanese translator of our Consulate at Kobe. Both of these men give the mountain’s name as Oki-yama, and say that on the top of it, from time immemorial, there has been a shrine dedicated to Fudo-myo-o (*Achala* in Sanskrit, which means ‘immovable,’ and is the god always represented as surrounded by fire and sitting uncomplainingly as an example to others; he carries a sword in one hand and a rope in the other as a warning that punishment awaits those who are unable to overcome the painful struggles of life with honor).

Well, at the top of Oki-yama (high or big mountain) is this very old temple to Fudo, and many are the

<keywords>Oki-yama, Fudo-myo-o, Achala, Idsumi province, Fukuga Sei, Mr. Ando, Kobe, Japanese folklore, Buddhism, Yenoki</keywords>

pilgrimages which are made there annually. The mountain itself is covered with forest, and there are some remarkable cryptomerias, camphor, and pine trees.

Many years ago, in the days of which I speak, there were only a few priests living up at this temple. Among them was a middle-aged man, half-priest and half-caretaker, called Yenoki. Yenoki had lived at the temple for twenty years; yet during that time, he had never set eyes on the figure of Fudo, whom he was partially assigned to guard; it was kept shut in a shrine and never seen by anyone but the head priest. One day, Yenoki’s curiosity got the better of him. Early in the morning, the door of the shrine was not quite closed. Yenoki looked in, but saw nothing. On turning toward the light again, he found that he had lost the use of the eye that had looked: he was stone-blind in his right eye.

Feeling that this divine punishment was well-deserved, and that the gods must be angry, he began purifying himself and fasted for one hundred days. Yenoki was mistaken in his method of devotion and repentance and did not pacify the gods; on the contrary, they turned him into a <term>tengu</term> (a long-nosed spirit who dwells in mountains and is the great teacher of <term>jujitsu</term>).

But Yenoki continued to call himself a priest—‘Ichigan Hoshi,’ meaning the one-eyed priest—for a year, and then died; and it is said that his spirit passed into an enormous cryptomeria tree on the east side of the mountain. After that, when sailors passed through the Chinu Sea (Osaka Bay), if there was a storm, they used to pray to the one-eyed priest for help, and if a light was seen on the top of Oki-yama, they had a sure sign

It may be said, in fact, that after the death of the one-eyed priest, more importance was attached to his spirit and to the tree in which it had taken refuge than to the temple itself. The tree was called the Lodging of the One-eyed Priest, and no one dared approach it—not even the woodcutters who were familiar with the mountains. It was a source of awe and an object of reverence.

At the foot of Oki-yama was a lonely village, separated from others by a full two <term>ri</term> (five miles), and there were only one hundred and thirty houses in it.

Every year the villagers used to celebrate the ‘<term>Bon</term>’ by engaging, after it was over, in the dance called ‘<term>Bon Odori</term>.’ Like most other things in Japan, the ‘<term>Bon</term>’ and the ‘<term>Bon Odori</term>’ were in extreme contrast. The ‘<term>Bon</term>’ was a ceremony arranged for the spirits of the dead, who are supposed to return to earth for three days annually to visit their family shrines—something like our All Saints’ Day, and in any case, quite a serious religious performance. The ‘<term>Bon Odori</term>’ is a dance that varies considerably in different provinces. It is confined mostly to villages—for one cannot count the pretty <term>geisha</term> dances in Kyoto, which are practically copies of it. It is a dance of boys and girls, one may say, and it continues nearly all night on the village green. For the three or four nights that it lasts, opportunities for flirtations of the most intense kind are plentiful. There are no chaperones (so to speak), and (to put it vulgarly) everyone "goes wild"! Previously virtuous maidens spend the night out as

So it happened that the village at the foot of Oki-yama mountain—so far away from other villages—was morally corrupt. There were no restrictions on what a girl might or might not do during the nights of the ‘<term>Bon Odori</term>.’ Things went from bad to worse until, at the time I am writing about, anarchy reigned during the festival days. At last it happened that after a particularly festive ‘Bon,’ on a beautiful moonlit night in August, the well-beloved and charming daughter of Kurahashi Yozaemon, O Kimi, aged eighteen, who had promised her lover Kurosuke that she would meet him secretly that evening, was on her way to do so. After passing the last house in her mountain village, she came to a thick copse, and standing at the edge of it was a man whom O Kimi at first took to be her lover. Upon approaching, she found that it was not Kurosuke, but a very handsome youth of twenty-three. He did not speak to her; in fact, he kept a little distance. If she advanced, he moved back. The youth was so handsome that O Kimi felt she loved him. ‘Oh, how my heart beats for him!’ she said. ‘After all, why should I not give up Kurosuke? He is not as good-looking as this man, whom I love already before I have even spoken to him. I hate Kurosuke, now that I see this man.’

...were greatly troubled in their minds. A week passed, and O Kimi San did not return.

A few days later, Tamae, the sixteen-year-old daughter of Kinsaku, who was secretly in love with the village headman’s son, was waiting for him in the temple grounds, standing there by the stone figure of Jizodo (Sanskrit, *Kshitigarbha*, Patron of Women and Children). Suddenly, a handsome youth of twenty-three years appeared near Tamae, just as had happened with O Kimi. She was greatly struck by the youth’s beauty—so much so that when he took her by the hand and led her away, she made no effort to resist, and she also disappeared.

In this way, nine girls of an amorous nature disappeared from this small village. For thirty miles around, people everywhere talked, wondered, and said unkind things.

In Oki-yama village itself, the elders said:
> ‘Yes: it must be that the immodesty of our children since the ‘Bon Odori’ has angered Yenoki San. Perhaps it is he himself who appears in the form of this handsome youth and carries off our daughters.’

Within a few days, nearly everyone agreed that they owed their losses to the Spirit of the Yenoki Tree. As soon as this idea had taken root, all the villagers locked and barred themselves in their houses both day and night. Their farms were neglected; wood was no longer being cut on the mountain; and business came to a standstill. The rumor of this state of affairs spread, and the Lord of Kishiwada, becoming uneasy, summoned Sonobé Hayama, the most celebrated swordsman in that part of Japan.

After this meeting with his master, Sonobé went home. He underwent a course of ritual purification. He fasted and bathed for a week, and then went to Oki-yama.

This was in the month of October, a time when things always look their best to me. Sonobé climbed the mountain and went first to the temple, which he reached at three o’clock in the afternoon after a difficult climb. There, he prayed before the god Fudo for a full half hour. Then he set out to cross the short valley which led up to the Oki-yama mountain and to the tree which held the spirit of the one-eyed priest, Yenoki.

It was a long and steep climb with no paths, for the mountain was avoided as much as possible even by the most adventurous woodcutters, none of whom ever dreamed of going as far as the Yenoki tree. Sonobé was in good condition and was a bold warrior. The woods were dense; there was a chilling dampness that came from the spray of a high waterfall. ### XLII

## THE SPIRIT OF THE LOTUS LILY

For some time, I have been hunting for a tale about the lotus lily. My friend Fukuga has at last found one which is said to date back some two hundred years. It applies to a castle that was then situated in what was known as Kinai, now incorporated into what may be known as the Kyoto district. Probably it refers to one of the castles in that neighborhood, though I myself know of only one, which is now called Nijo Castle.

Fukuga (who does not speak English) and my interpreter made it very difficult for me to say that the story does not really belong to a castle in the province of Izumi <note>Modern spelling of Idzumi; an ancient province in the area of modern-day Osaka.</note>, for after starting it in Kyoto they suddenly brought me to Izumi, making the hero of it the Lord of Koriyama. In any case, I was first told that disease and sickness broke out in Kinai (Kyoto). Thousands of people died from it. It spread to Izumi, where the feudal Lord of Koriyama lived, and attacked him also. Doctors were called from all parts; but it was no use. The disease spread, and, to the dismay of all,

### XLIII

## THE TEMPLE OF THE AWABI

In Noto Province, there is a small fishing village called Nanao. It is at the extreme northern end of the mainland. There is nothing opposite it until one reaches either Korea or the Siberian coast—except for the small rocky islands which are found everywhere in Japan, surrounding the mainland like an outer fringe. Nanao contains no more than five hundred souls. Many years ago, the place was devastated by an earthquake and a terrific storm, which together destroyed nearly the whole village and killed half of the people.

On the morning after this terrible disaster, it was observed that the geographical situation had changed. Opposite Nanao, some two miles from the land, a rocky island about a mile in circumference had arisen. The sea was muddy and yellow. The survivors were so overwhelmed and awed that no one ventured out in a boat for nearly a month afterward; indeed, most of the boats had been destroyed.

Being Japanese, they took things philosophically. Everyone helped one another, and within a month the village looked much as it had looked before; smaller, and less

Nanao contains no more than five hundred souls. Many years ago, the place was devastated by an earthquake and a terrific storm, which together destroyed nearly the whole village and killed half of the people.

On the morning after this terrible disaster, it was observed that the geographical situation had changed. Opposite Nanao, some two miles from the land, a rocky island about a mile in circumference had arisen. The sea was muddy and yellow. The survivors were so overwhelmed and awed that no one ventured out in a boat for nearly a month afterward; indeed, most of the boats had been destroyed. Being Japanese, they took things philosophically. Everyone helped one another, and within a month the village looked much as it had looked before; smaller and less

# The Temple of the Awabi

It was populated, perhaps, but it managed itself without help from the outside world. Indeed, all the neighboring villages had suffered in much the same way and, like ants, had set things right again.

The fishermen of Nanao arranged for their first fishing expedition to be taken together, two days before the <term>Bon</term> festival. They would first go and inspect the new island and then continue several miles out to sea to find if there were still as many <term>tai</term> fish on their favorite grounds as there used to be.

It would be a day of intense interest, and the villages along some fifty miles of the coast had all decided to make their ventures simultaneously. Each village would try its own grounds, of course, but all would start at the same time, intending to eventually report the condition of things regarding the fish to each other; for mutual assistance is a strong characteristic of the Japanese people when trouble overcomes them.

At the appointed time, two days before the festival, the fishermen started from Nanao. There were thirteen boats. They first visited the new island, which proved to be simply a large rock. There were many rockfish, such as wrasse and sea perch, around it; but beyond that, there was nothing remarkable. It had not had time to gather many shellfish on its surface, and there was as yet very little edible seaweed. So, the thirteen boats went further to sea to discover what had occurred to their old and excellent <term>tai</term> grounds.

These were found to produce just about what they used to produce in the days before the earthquake; but the fishermen were not able to stay long enough to
