make a thorough test. They had intended to be away all night; but at dusk the sky showed every sign of a storm, so they pulled up their anchors and headed for home.

As they approached the new island, they were surprised to see, on one side of it, a space of water 240 feet square lit up with a strange light. The light seemed to come from the bottom of the sea, and despite the darkness, the water was transparent. The fishermen, greatly astonished, stopped to gaze down into the blue waters. They could see fish swimming about by the thousands; but the depth was too great for them to see the bottom, and so they let their imaginations run wild with all kinds of superstitious ideas as to the cause of the light, discussing it from boat to boat. A few minutes later, they had brought in their immense paddling oars and all was quiet. Then they heard rumbling noises at the bottom of the sea, and this filled them with dismay—they feared another eruption. The oars were put out again, and to say that they moved quickly would in no way convey an idea of the speed at which the men made their boats travel over the two miles between the island and the mainland.

They reached their homes well before the storm began; but the storm lasted for two full days, and the fishermen were unable to leave the shore.

As the sea calmed down and the villagers were looking out, a new cause for astonishment appeared on the third day. Shooting out of the sea near the island rock were rays that seemed to come from a sun at the bottom of the sea. The whole village gathered on the beach to see this extraordinary spectacle, which was discussed far into the night.

# The Temple of the <term>Awabi</term>

Not even the old priest could shed any light on the matter. Consequently, the fishermen became increasingly frightened, and few of them were ready to venture to sea the next day. Although it was the season for the magnificent <term>sawara</term> (king mackerel), only one boat left the shore; it belonged to Master Kansuke, a fisherman about fifty years old, who, along with his eighteen-year-old son Matakichi—a most faithful son—was always at the forefront whenever something extraordinary needed to be done.

Kansuke had been the recognized bold fisherman of Nanao, the leader in all things for as long as most could remember, and his faithful and devoted son had followed him since the age of twelve through many perils; thus, no one was surprised to see their boat depart alone.

They went first to the <term>tai</term> grounds and fished there during the night, catching over thirty <term>tai</term> between them, which averaged about four pounds each. Toward daybreak, another storm appeared on the horizon. Kansuke weighed his anchor and started for home, hoping to retrieve a <term>hobo</term> line that he had dropped overboard near the rocky island on his way out—a line holding about two hundred hooks. They had reached the island and hauled in nearly the entire line when the rising sea caused Kansuke to lose his balance and fall overboard.

The fishermen could hardly believe the news that what they had mistaken for supernatural lights were caused by ear-shells, for the highly valued ear-shell was extremely rare in their district. However, Matakichi was a youth of such trustworthiness that even the most skeptical eventually believed him, and had it not been for the loss of Kansuke, there would have been great rejoicing in the village that evening.

Having told the villagers the news, Matakichi went to the old priest’s house at the end of the village and told him as well.

"And now that my beloved father is dead," he said, "I myself beg that you will make me one of your disciples, so that I may pray daily for my father’s spirit."

The old priest granted Matakichi’s wish and said, "Not only shall I be glad to have such a brave and devoted youth as yourself as a disciple, but I myself will also pray with you for your father’s spirit. On the twenty-first day after his death, we will take boats and pray over the spot where he drowned."

Accordingly, on the morning of the twenty-first day after the drowning of poor Kansuke, his son and the priest anchored over the place where he had been lost, and prayers for the spirit of the dead were said.

That same night, the priest awoke at midnight; he felt uneasy and thought much about the spiritual affairs of his flock.

Suddenly, he saw an old man standing near the head of his bed, who, bowing courteously, said:

> 'I am the spirit of the great ear-shell lying on the bottom of the sea near Rocky Island. I am over 1,000 years old. A few days ago, a fisherman fell from his boat into the sea, and I killed and ate him. This morning I heard your reverence, along with the son of the man I ate, praying over the place where I lay. Your sacred prayers have taught me shame, and I grieve for what I have done. To make amends, I have ordered my followers to scatter, while I have decided to kill myself so that the pearls within my shell may be given to Matakichi, the son of the man I ate. All I ask is that you pray for the well-being of my spirit. Farewell!'

After saying this, the ghost of the ear-shell vanished. Early the next morning, when Matakichi opened his shutters to dust the front of his door, he found something there that he first took to be a large rock covered with seaweed and even pink coral. Upon closer examination, Matakichi found it to be the immense ear-shell he had seen at the bottom of the sea off Rocky Island. He rushed to the temple to tell the priest, who then told Matakichi about the visitation he had received during the night.

The shell and the body contained inside it were carried to the temple with great respect and much ceremony. Prayers were said over it; and although the shell and the immense pearl were kept in the temple, the body was buried in a tomb next to Kansuke’s, with a monument erected over it and another over Kansuke’s grave. Matakichi changed his name to Nichige and lived happily.

No ear-shells have been seen near Nanao since then.

## XLIV

### HUMAN FIREFLIES

In Funakami village, Omi Province, lived an old farmer named Kanshiro. No one like him for honesty, charity, and piety had ever been known—no, not even among the priesthood. Annually, Kanshiro made pilgrimages to various parts of the country to say his prayers and do his duty toward the various deities, never thinking of his old age or his infirmities. He was not strong and suffered almost always from dysentery during the hot weather; consequently, he usually made his pilgrimages in cooler times.

In the eighth year of Kwansei, however, Kanshiro felt that he could not live another year. Feeling that he would not like to miss making another pilgrimage to the great shrines at Ise, he resolved to take all risks and go in August, the hottest month.

The people in Funakami village raised one hundred yen for the venerable man, so that he might have the honor and credit of presenting a decent sum to the great shrines.

In Funakami village, in the province of Omi, lived an old farmer named Kanshiro. No one as honest, charitable, and pious as him had ever been known—no, not even among the priests.

## XLV

# THE CHRYSANTHEMUM HERMIT

Many years ago, there lived at the foot of the Mountains of Nambu, in the <term>Adachi-gun</term> <note>Adachi District</note> of Saitama Prefecture, an old man named Kikuo, which means "Chrysanthemum Old Man."

Kikuo was a faithful retainer of Tsugaru; at that time, he was called Sawada Hayato. Kikuo was a man of great physical strength and fine appearance, and he was largely responsible for the efficiency of the small fighting force that protected the feudal lord, the castle, and the estates.

Nevertheless, a dark day came. The feudal lord’s small force was overthrown; the estates and the castle were lost. The lord and his faithful retainer, along with the few survivors, escaped to the mountains, where they continued to hope that a day might come when they would be able to have their revenge.

During this forced idleness, Kikuo, knowing his lord’s love of flowers (especially the chrysanthemum), decided to devote all his spare time to creating chrysanthemum beds. This, he thought, would ease the pain of defeat and exile.

<summary>A loyal samurai named Sawada Hayato, later known as Kikuo, escapes to the mountains with his defeated lord. To comfort his master during their exile, Kikuo begins cultivating chrysanthemum gardens.</summary>
<keywords>Kikuo, Sawada Hayato, Tsugaru, Chrysanthemum Hermit, Saitama, samurai, exile, loyalty</keywords>

--- Page 500 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of Kikuo (formerly Sawada Hayato), the loyal retainer who began growing chrysanthemums to comfort his exiled lord.</meta>

The feudal lord was greatly pleased; but his cares and anxieties were not lessened. He fell ill and died in great poverty, much to the sorrow of Kikuo and the rest of his followers. Kikuo wept night and day over the humble and lonely grave; but he busied himself once more to please the spirit of his lord by planting chrysanthemums around the tomb and tending them daily. Eventually, the border of flowers was thirty yards wide—to the amazement of all who saw it. It was because of this that Hayato received the name of Chrysanthemum-Old-Man.

The chrysanthemum is a holy flower in China. Ancient history tells of a man called Hoso (the great-grandson of the Emperor Juikai) who lived to the age of 800 years without showing the slightest sign of aging. This was attributed to his drinking the dew of the chrysanthemum. Besides his devotion to flowers, Kikuo delighted in children; he called them from the village to his poor hut, and as there was no schoolmaster, he taught them how to read, write, and <term>jujitsu</term>. The children loved him, and the good villagers revered him as if he were a kind of god.

In about his eighty-second year, Kikuo caught a cold, and the fever which came with it caused him great pain.

During the daytime, his pupils attended to his needs; but at night, the old man was alone in his cottage.

One autumn night, he awoke and found some beautiful children standing on his veranda. They did not look quite like any children he knew. They were too beautiful and noble-looking to belong to the poor people of the village.

"Kikuo Sama," cried two of them, "do not fear us,"

"though we are not real children. We are the spirits of the chrysanthemum which you love so much, and which you have cared for so well. We have come to tell you how sorry we are to see you so ill, although we have heard that in China there once lived a man named Hoso who lived for 800 years by drinking the dew that falls from the flowers. Prepare yourself, therefore, to depart."

Saying this, they all wept bitterly.

"Goodbye, then," said Kikuo. "I have no further hopes of living. May my death be easy. In the next world, I may be able to serve my old lord and master. The only thing that makes me sad to leave this world is you: I must forever regret leaving my chrysanthemums!" Saying this, he smiled at them affectionately.

"You have been very kind to us," said the Kiku spirits, "and we love you for it. Man rejoices at birth and feels sad at death; yet now you shed no tears. You say you do not mind dying except for leaving us. If you die, we shall not survive, for it would be useless misery. Believe us when we say that we shall die with you."

As the spirits of the chrysanthemums finished speaking, a gust of wind blew around the house, and they disappeared. As day dawned, the old man grew worse, and, strange to say, all the chrysanthemums began to fade—even those which were just beginning to bloom; the leaves crumpled up and dried.

## XLVI

# THE PRINCESS PEONY

Many years ago at Gamogun, in the province of Omi, there was a castle called Adzuchi-no-shiro. It was a magnificent old place, surrounded by walls and a moat filled with lotus lilies. The feudal lord was a very brave and wealthy man, Yuki Naizen-no-jo. His wife had been dead for some years. He had no son, but he had a beautiful daughter aged eighteen, who (for some reason which is not quite clear to me) was given the title of Princess. 

For a long period, there had been peace and quiet in the land; the feudal lords were on the best of terms, and everyone was happy. In these circumstances, Lord Naizen-no-jo saw a good opportunity to find a husband for his daughter, Princess Aya. After a time, the second son of the Lord of Ako, from Harima Province, was selected to the satisfaction of both fathers, though the arrangement had little to do with the couple themselves. Lord Ako's second son had looked upon his bride with approval, and she had done the same regarding him. One might say that young people are bound to approve of each other when

Princess Aya made up her mind to try and love her prospective husband. She saw nothing of him; but she thought of him, and talked of him.

One evening, when Princess Aya was walking in the magnificent gardens by the moonlight, accompanied by her maids-in-waiting, she wandered down through her favorite peony bed to the pond where she loved to gaze at her reflection on the nights of the full moon, to listen to frogs, and to watch the fireflies.

When nearing the pond, her foot slipped, and she would have fallen into the water had it not been that a young man appeared as if by magic and caught her. He disappeared as soon as he had set her on her feet again. The maids-of-honor saw her slip; they saw a glimmer of light, and that was all; but Princess Aya had seen more. She had seen the handsomest young man she could imagine. "He must have been twenty-one years old," she said to O Sadayo San, her favorite maid, "a <term>samurai</term> of the highest order. His dress was covered with my favorite peonies, and his swords were richly mounted. Oh, that I could have seen him a minute longer, to thank him for saving me from the water! Who can he be? And how could he have gotten into our gardens, through all the guards?"

So spoke the Princess to her maids, instructing them at the same time that they were to say a word to no one, for fear that her father should hear, find the young man, and behead him for trespassing.

“How is it possible for a man to get into the grounds?” said Lord Yuki Naizen-no-jo. “People say foxes and badgers sometimes take the forms of men; but even so, it is impossible for such supernatural beings to enter my castle grounds, guarded as they are at every opening.”

That evening, the poor Princess was more tired and unhappy than ever before. Thinking to cheer her up a little, the maids sent for a celebrated player of the <term>biwa</term> named Yashaskita Kengyo. Since the weather was hot, they were sitting on the gallery (<term>engawa</term>); and while the musician was playing “Dannoura,” the same handsome young <term>samurai</term> suddenly appeared from behind the peonies. This time he was visible to everyone—even the peonies embroidered on his clothing were clear.

“There he is! There he is!” they cried; at which he instantly disappeared again. The Princess was highly excited and seemed more lively than she had been for days; the old <term>Daimio</term> grew more puzzled than ever when he heard of it.

The next night, while two of the maids were playing for their mistress—O Yae San on the flute and O Yakumo on the <term>koto</term>—the figure of the young man appeared again. Although a thorough search had been made during the day in the massive peony beds with absolutely no result—not even the sign of a footprint—the matter was increasingly strange.

A consultation was held, and the lord of the castle decided to invite a veteran officer of great strength and renown, Maki Hiogo, to capture the youth.

Everyone gazed at him and wondered why Maki Hiogo did not jump up and catch him. The fact was that Maki Hiogo was so much astonished by the noble bearing of the youth that at first he did not want to touch him. Recovering himself, and thinking of his duty to his lord, he stealthily approached the young man, and, seizing him around the waist, held him tight. After a few seconds, Maki Hiogo felt a kind of wet steam falling on his face; by degrees, it made him faint; and he fell to the ground, still grasping the young <term>samurai</term>, for he had made up his mind that he would capture him.

Everyone had seen the scuffle, and some of the guards came hurrying to the place. Just as they reached the spot, Maki Hiogo came to his senses and shouted: "Come, gentlemen! I have caught him. Come and see!" But on looking at what he held in his arms, he discovered it to be only a large peony!

"Ah! It is as I said. No fox or badger spirit could pass our guards and get into this garden. It is the spirit of the peony flower that took the form of a prince." Turning to his daughter and her maids, he said: "You must take this as a compliment and pay great respect to the peony; also show kindness to the one caught by Maki Hiogo by taking care of it."

Princess Aya carried the flower back to her room, where she put it in a vase of water and placed it near her pillow. She felt as if she had her sweetheart with her. Day by day, she got better. She tended the peony herself, and, strange to say, the flower seemed to grow stronger and stronger instead of fading. At last, the Princess recovered. She became radiantly beautiful, while the peony continued to remain in perfect bloom, showing no sign of dying.

As Princess Aya was now perfectly well, her father could no longer postpone the wedding. Consequently, some days later, the Lord of Ako and his family arrived at the castle, and his second son was married to the Princess.

As soon as the wedding was over, the peony was found still in its vase—but dead and withered. After this, instead of speaking of Princess Aya or Aya Hime, the villagers always called her Botan Hime, or the Peony Princess.

# XLVII

## THE MEMORIAL CHERRY TREE <note>This story begins on February 17 in the second year of Kenkyu. Since the first year of Kenkyu was 1190 and the last was 1199, the precise date is February 17, 1192.</note>

In the compound or enclosure of the temple called Bukoji, at Takatsuji (High Cross Street), formerly called Yabugashita—which means "under the bush"—in Kyoto, an antique dealer had his little shop. His name was Kihachi.

Kihachi did not have much to sell, but what little he had was usually of high quality. Consequently, his was a place that the upper classes visited when they came to pray—to look, if not to buy—for they knew very well that if there was a fine item to be found, Kihachi would have purchased it. It was, in fact, a small and ancient version of Christie’s, except that items were not sold by auction. One day, the day this story begins, Kihachi was sitting in his shop ready either to gossip or to sell, when a young knight or court noble walked in. In those days, the Japanese called such a man a <term>Kuge</term>; he was very different from the knight of a feudal lord or of a <term>Daimio</term>, who was usually a blusterer. This particular knight had been to the temple to pray.

<summary>Kihachi, a reputable antique dealer with a shop in Kyoto's Bukoji temple grounds, receives a visit from a refined court noble. The story is set in February 1192, during the Kenkyu era.</summary>

'You have many beautiful and interesting things here,' he said. 'May I come in and look at them until this rain shower has passed? My name is Sakata, and I belong to the court.'

'Come in, come in,' said Kihachi, 'by all means. Some of my items are beautiful, and all are undoubtedly of high quality; but the nobility part with very little at present. In my trade, one wants to live two lives of a hundred years each—one hundred years of distress, revolution, and trouble, during which one may collect items cheaply; and the next hundred years of peace, during which one may sell them and enjoy the profits. My business is poor and unprofitable; yet, in spite of that, I love the things I buy, and often look at them for a long time before I put them up for sale. Where are you headed, sir? I see that you are going to travel, judging by the clothes you wear and carry.'

'That is true,' Sakata answered; 'you are very shrewd. I am traveling as far as Toba, in Yamato, to see my dearest friend, who has been taken suddenly and mysteriously ill. It is feared he may not live until I get there!'

'At Toba!' the old curio-dealer replied. 'Forgive me if I ask the name of your friend?'

'Certainly,' said Sakata. 'My friend's name is Matsui.'

'Then,' said the curio-dealer, 'he is the gentleman who is said to have killed the ghost or spirit of the old cherry tree near Toba, which grows in the grounds of the temple where he lives at present with the priests. Sakata, thanking Kihachi for this information, went on his way, and eventually found his friend Matsui being carefully nursed by the priest of the Shonen Temple, Toba, with whom he was closely connected.

Soon after the young knight had left the old curio dealer Kihachi in his shop it began to snow, and so it continued, and appeared likely to continue for some time. Kihachi, therefore, put up his shutters and retired to bed, as is often very sensibly done in Japan; and he no doubt retired with many old wood carvings to rub and give an ancient appearance to during the period of darkness.

Not very late in the evening there was a knock at the shutters. Kihachi, not wishing to get out of his warm bed, shouted: ‘Who are you? Come back in the morning. I do not feel well enough to get up tonight.’

‘But you must—you must get up! I am sent to sell you a good <term>kakemono</term>,’ <note>Picture.</note> called the voice of a young girl, so sweetly and entreatingly that the old curio dealer got up, and after much fumbling with his numbed fingers opened the door.

Snow had fallen thickly; but now it was clear moonlight, and Kihachi saw standing before him a beautiful girl of fifteen, barefooted, and holding in her hands a <term>kakemono</term> half-unfolded.

‘See,’ said she, ‘I have been sent to sell you this!’ She was the daughter of Matsui of Toba, she said.

The old man called her in and saw that the picture was of a beautiful woman standing up. It was well-executed, and the old man took a liking to it.

"I will give you one <term>rio</term> <note>A historical Japanese gold coin, often spelled ryo.</note> for it," he said; and to his astonishment, the young girl accepted his offer eagerly—so much so that he thought perhaps she had stolen it. Being a curio dealer, he said nothing about that, but paid her the money. She ran away in haste.

"Yes, she has stolen it—stolen it, undoubtedly," muttered the old man. "But what am I supposed to know about that? The <term>kakemono</term> <note>A Japanese hanging scroll painting.</note> is worth at least 50 <term>rio</term> if it is worth a cent, and such chances do not often come to me."

Kihachi was so delighted with his purchase that he lit his lamp, hung the picture in his <term>kakemono</term> corner, and sat watching it. It was indeed a well-painted, beautiful woman, and worth even more than the 50 <term>rio</term> he first thought. But, by all the saints, it seems to change! Yes, it is no longer a beautiful woman. The face has changed to that of a fearful and horrible figure. The woman's face has become haggard. It is covered with blood. The eyes open and shut, and the mouth gasps. Kihachi feels blood dripping on his head; it comes from a wound in the woman’s shoulder. To shut out such a horrific sight, he put his head under the bedclothes and remained there, sleeplessly, until dawn.

When he opened his eyes, the <term>kakemono</term> was the same as when he had bought it: a beautiful woman. He supposed that his delight in making a good bargain must have made him dream, so he thought nothing more of the horror.

Kihachi, however, was mistaken. The <term>kakemono</term> again

# The Memorial Cherry Tree

The vision kept him awake all night, showing the same bloody face and occasionally even shrieking. Kihachi got no sleep and realized that instead of a cheap bargain, he had made a very costly one; for he felt that he must go to Toba and return it to Matsui, and he knew that he could not claim any travel expenses.

After fully two days of travel, Kihachi reached the Shonen Temple near Toba, where he asked to see Matsui. He was ushered ceremoniously into his room. The invalid was feeling better; but upon being handed the <term>kakemono</term> with the figure of a lady painted on it, he turned pale, tore it to fragments, and threw it into the temple fire ('<term>irori</term>'); after which he himself jumped in with his daughter, and both were burned to death.

Kihachi was sick for many days after witnessing this sight. The story soon spread over the whole surrounding country.

Prince Nijo, the Governor of Kyoto, had a thorough inquiry made into the circumstances of the case; and it was found beyond a doubt that the trouble affecting Matsui and his family came from his having killed the spirit of the old cherry tree. The spirit—to punish him and to show that there is invisible life in old and dead things, and often of the best kind—appeared to Matsui as a beautiful woman being killed; the spirit then entered his beautiful painting and haunted him.

Prince Nijo had a fine young cherry tree planted on the spot of the old one to commemorate the event, and it is called the "Memorial Cherry Tree" to this day.

<header>XLVIII</header>

### THE ‘JIROHEI’ CHERRY TREE, KYOTO

THE Japanese say that spirits in inanimate nature generally have more vitality than ghosts of the dead. There is an old proverb which says something to the effect that ‘the spirits of trees do not love the willow’; by which, I suppose, it is meant that they do not harmonize. In Japanese pictures of ghosts, there is nearly always a willow tree. Whether Hokusai, the ancient painter, or Okyo Maruyama, a famous painter of Kyoto from a more recent date, was responsible for the pictures with ghosts and willow trees, I do not know; but Maruyama certainly painted many ghosts under willow trees—the first being modeled after his wife, who lay sick.

Exactly what this has to do with the following story I cannot see; but my storyteller began with it.

In the northern part of Kyoto is a Shinto temple called Hirano. It is famous for the fine cherry trees that grow there. Among them is an old dead tree which is called ‘Jirohei,’ and is much cared for; but the story attached to it is little known, and has not been told, I believe, to a European before.

# The ‘Jirohei’ Cherry Tree, Kyoto

During the cherry blossom season, many people go to view the trees, especially at night.

Close to the Jirohei cherry tree, many years ago, there was a large and prosperous tea-house, once owned by Jirohei, who had started in a very small way. He made money so rapidly that he attributed his success to the virtue of the old cherry tree, which he consequently venerated. Jirohei paid the greatest respect to the tree, attending to its needs. He prevented boys from climbing it and breaking its branches. The tree prospered, and so did he.

One morning, a samurai (of the violent and aggressive kind) walked up to the Hirano Temple and sat down at Jirohei’s tea-house to take a long look at the cherry blossoms. He was a powerful, dark-skinned, evil-faced man about five feet eight inches tall.

‘Are you the landlord of this tea-house?’ he asked.

‘Yes, sir,’ Jirohei answered meekly. ‘I am. What can I bring you, sir?’

‘Nothing, I thank you,’ said the samurai. ‘What a fine tree you have here opposite your tea-house!’

‘Yes, sir; it is to the beauty of the tree that I owe my prosperity. Thank you, sir, for expressing your appreciation of it.’

‘I want a branch from the tree,’ said the samurai, ‘for a geisha.’

‘Deeply as I regret it, I am obliged to refuse your request. I must refuse everyone. The temple priests gave orders to this effect before they allowed me to build this place. No matter who asks, I must refuse. Flowers may not even be picked from the tree, though they may be gathered when they fall. Please, sir, remember

‘You seem to be an unpleasantly argumentative person for your station in life,’ said the samurai. ‘When I say that I want a thing, I mean to have it; so you had better go and cut it.’

‘However much you may be determined, I must refuse,’ said Jirohei, quietly and politely.

‘And, however much you may refuse, the more determined am I to have it. I, as a samurai, said I should have it. Do you think that you can turn me from my purpose? If you do not have the politeness to get it, I will take it by force.’ Suiting his action to his words, the samurai drew a sword about three feet long and was about to cut off the best branch of all. Jirohei clung to the sleeve of his sword arm, crying:

‘I have asked you to leave the tree alone, but you would not. Please take my life instead.’

‘You are an insolent and annoying fool; I gladly follow your request’; and saying this, the samurai stabbed Jirohei slightly to make him let go of the sleeve. Jirohei did let go; but he ran to the tree, where in a further struggle over the branch—which was cut in spite of Jirohei’s defense—he was stabbed again, this time fatally. The samurai, seeing that the man must die, got away as quickly as possible, leaving the cut branch in full bloom on the ground.

Hearing the noise, the servants came out of the house, followed by Jirohei’s poor old wife.

It was seen that Jirohei himself was dead; but he clung to the tree as firmly as in life, and it was fully an hour before they were able to get him away.

# The 'Jirohei' Cherry Tree, Kyoto

From this time, things went poorly for the tea-house. Very few people came, and those who did visit were poor and spent very little money. Besides, from the day of Jirohei's murder, the tree had begun to fade and die; in less than a year, it was completely dead. The tea-house had to be closed for lack of funds to keep it open. Jirohei’s elderly wife had hanged herself on the dead tree a few days after her husband had been killed.

People said that ghosts had been seen around the tree and were afraid to go there at night. Even neighboring tea-houses suffered, as did the temple, which for a time became unpopular.

The samurai who had been the cause of all this kept his secret, telling no one but his own father what he had done; and he expressed to his father his intention of going to the temple to verify the reports about the ghosts. Thus, on the third day of March in the third year of Keio (that is, forty-two years ago), he set out one night alone and well-armed, despite his father’s attempts to stop him. He went straight to the old dead tree and hid himself behind a stone lantern.

To his astonishment, at midnight the dead tree suddenly came into full bloom, looking exactly as it had when he cut the branch and killed Jirohei.

Upon seeing this, he fiercely attacked the tree with his sharp-edged sword. He attacked it with mad fury, cutting and slashing; he heard a terrifying scream which seemed to him to come from inside the tree.

After half an hour he became exhausted, but resolved to wait until daybreak to see what damage he had caused. When day dawned, the samurai found his father lying on

## XLIX

# THE SNOW GHOST

Perhaps there are not many, even in Japan, who have heard of the ‘Yuki Onna’ (Snow Ghost). It is rarely spoken of except in the higher mountains, which are constantly covered in snow during the winter. Those who have read Lafcadio Hearn’s books will remember a story of the Yuki Onna, which is highly regarded because of its beautiful telling, but in reality is no better than the following one.

Up in the northern province of Echigo, opposite Sado Island on the Sea of Japan, snow falls heavily. Sometimes there is as much as twenty feet of it on the ground, and many people have been buried in the snow and were never found until the spring. Not many years ago, three companies of soldiers, with the exception of three or four men, were destroyed in Aomori <note>The original text uses the spelling 'Aowomori'</note>; and it was many weeks before they were dug out—dead, of course.

Mysterious disappearances naturally give rise to imaginings among a fanciful people, and from time immemorial, the Snow Ghost has been at one with the people of the North; meanwhile, those of the South say that those of the North drink so much <term>sake</term> <note>Japanese rice wine</note> that they see snow-covered trees as women.

<summary>This page introduces the legend of the Yuki Onna (Snow Ghost), noting its prevalence in the snowy northern provinces of Japan like Echigo and Aomori. The author contrasts the North's sincere belief in the ghost with the skepticism of Southerners, who attribute such sightings to intoxication.</summary>

Be that as it may, I must explain what a farmer named Kyuzaemon saw.

Kyuzaemon lived in the village of Hoi, which consisted of only eleven houses—and very poor ones at that. He was poor and doubly unfortunate, having lost both his son and his wife. He led a lonely life.

In the afternoon of January 19th, in the third year of Tem-po—that is, 1833—a tremendous snowstorm began. Kyuzaemon closed the shutters and made himself as comfortable as he could. Around eleven o'clock at night, he was awakened by a rapping at his door; it was a peculiar rap that came at regular intervals. Kyuzaemon sat up in bed, looked toward the door, and did not know what to make of it. The rapping came again, accompanied by the gentle voice of a girl. Thinking that it might be one of his neighbor's children needing help, Kyuzaemon jumped out of bed; but when he reached the door, he was afraid to open it. As the voice and rapping came again just as he reached the door, he sprang back with a cry: "Who are you? What do you want?"

"Open the door! Open the door!" came the voice from outside.

"Open the door! Is that likely until I know who you are and what you are doing out so late on such a night?"

"But you must let me in. How can I go any further in this deep snow? I do not ask for food, but only for shelter."

"I am very sorry, but I have no quilts or bedding. I cannot possibly let you stay in my house."

"I do not want quilts or bedding—only shelter," pleaded the voice.

# The Snow Ghost

'I can't let you in, anyway,' shouted Kyuzaemon. 'It is too late and against the rules and the law.'

Saying this, Kyuzaemon rebarred his door with a strong piece of wood, never once having ventured to open even a crack in the shutters to see who his visitor might be. As he turned toward his bed, with a shudder he saw the figure of a woman standing beside it, dressed in white, with her hair hanging down her back. She did not have the appearance of a ghost; her face was pretty, and she seemed to be about twenty-five years old. Kyuzaemon, taken by surprise and very much alarmed, called out:

'Who and what are you, and how did you get in? Where did you leave your <term>geta</term>?' <note>Clogs.</note>

'I can come in anywhere when I choose,' said the figure, 'and I am the woman you would not let in. I require no clogs, for I whirl along over the snow, sometimes even flying through the air. I am on my way to visit the next village, but the wind is against me. That is why I wanted you to let me rest here. If you will do so, I shall start as soon as the wind goes down; in any case, I shall be gone by the morning.'

'I would not mind letting you rest if you were an ordinary woman. I would, in fact, be glad; but I fear spirits greatly, as my forefathers have done,' said Kyuzaemon.

'Do not be afraid. You have a <term>butsudan</term>?' <note>A family altar in which the figures of various gods are placed, along with the family's memorial tablets.</note> said the figure.

'Yes: I have a <term>butsudan</term>,' said Kyuzaemon; 'but what could you want to do with that?'

It is mainly for that reason that I am about to seek him out and reason with him now."

"Am I to understand," said Kyuzaemon, "that the daughter who was married to Isaburo was the one who perished in the snow last year? If so, you must be the spirit of Oyasu, Isaburo's wife?"

"Yes, that is right," said the spirit. "I was Oyasu, the wife of Isaburo, who perished a year ago in the great snowstorm; tomorrow will be the anniversary."

## The Snow Ghost

The <term>Yuki Onna</term> (Snow Spirit) advanced; but there was no sound of footsteps as she glided to the altar.

Kyuzaemon retired to bed, where he promptly fell asleep; but shortly afterward he was disturbed by the woman's voice bidding him farewell. Before he had time to sit up, she disappeared, leaving no sign; the fire still burned in the <term>butsudan</term>.

Kyuzaemon got up at daybreak and went to the next village to see Isaburo, whom he found living with his father-in-law, Yazaemon.

"Yes," said Isaburo: "it was wrong of me to leave my late wife’s father when she died, and I am not surprised that on cold nights when it snows I have been visited continually by my wife’s spirit as a rebuke. Early this morning I saw her again, and I resolved to return. I have only been here two hours as it is."

On comparing notes, Kyuzaemon and Isaburo found that as soon as the spirit of Oyasu had left the house of Kyuzaemon, she appeared to Isaburo at about half an hour after midnight. She stayed with him until he had promised to return to her father’s house and help him in his old age.

That is roughly my story of the <term>Yuki Onna</term>. All those who die in the snow and cold become spirits of snow, appearing when there is snow; just as the spirits of those who are drowned in the sea only appear in stormy seas.

Even to the present day, in the north, priests say prayers to appease the spirits of those who have died in the snow, and to prevent them from haunting people who are connected with them.

## L

# THE SNOW TOMB <note>Told to me by Fukuchi, regarding the "fox-fires." Carefully translated by Mr. Watanabe of the Prefectural Government.</note>

Many years ago, there lived a young man of the <term>samurai</term> class who was very famous for his skill in fencing in what was called the <term>Yagyu</term> style. He was so adept that he earned no less than thirty barrels of rice and two "rations"—which, I am told, vary from one to five <term>sho</term>—a month by teaching under his master. Since one <term>sho</term> is 0.666 feet square, our young <term>samurai</term>, Rokugo Yakeiji, was well off.

The center of his success was at Minami-wari-gesui, Hongo, Edo. His teacher was Sudo Jirozaemon, and the school was at Ishiwaraku.

Rokugo was not at all arrogant about his skill. It was the young man's modesty, combined with his intelligence, that had prompted the teacher to make his pupil an assistant master. The school was one of the best in Tokyo, and there were over 100 pupils.

At this information, Rokugo was confounded, and he in turn apologized for his temper. Puzzled and ashamed, he begged his friends not to say anything more about the matter but to keep it to themselves; thereupon, he bid them farewell and left the house.

It was no longer snowing, but the snow lay thick upon the ground. Rokugo had drunk a good deal of <term>saké</term>, and his walk was not very steady as he made his way home to Warigesui.

Remembering this, Rokugo approached a little closer to the woman; and, sure enough, he could see the pattern of her dress, illuminated as if fire were underneath. The hair, too, seemed to have fire under it.

Knowing now that he was dealing with a fox, Rokugo drew his best sword—the famous one made by Moriye—and proceeded to attack carefully, for he knew he would have to hit the fox itself and not the spirit of the fox in the woman's form. (It is said that whenever a fox or a badger transforms itself into human shape, the real animal stands beside the apparition. If the apparition appears on the left side, the physical presence of the animal itself is on the right.)

Rokugo made his attack accordingly, killing the fox and consequently the apparition.

He ran to his house and called his relatives, who came flocking out with lanterns. Near a myrtle tree that was almost two hundred years old, they found the body—not of a fox or badger, but of an otter. The animal was carried home. The next day, invitations were issued to all the pupils at the fencing school to come and see it, and a great feast was given. Rokugo had wiped away a great disgrace. The pupils erected a tomb for the creature; it is known as "Yukizuka" (The Snow Tomb), and can still be seen in the Korinji Temple at Warigesui Honjo, in Tokyo.

<summary>Rokugo correctly identifies a supernatural apparition as a transformed animal and kills it, discovering it was an otter. This act restores his honor, and a tomb called the "Snow Tomb" is built for the creature at Korinji Temple.</summary>

### LI

## THE DRAGON-SHAPED PLUM TREE

IN the year 1716 of the Kyoho Era—191 years ago—there lived at Momoyama Fushimi an old gardener named Hambei, who was loved and respected for his kind nature and his great honesty. Although he was a poor man, Hambei had saved enough to live on, and he had inherited a house and garden from his father. Consequently, he was happy. His favorite pastime was tending his garden and an extraordinarily fine plum tree known in Japan as the <term>furyo</term> kind (which means ‘lying dragon’). Such trees are of great value and are much sought after for the landscaping of gardens. Curiously enough, although one may see many beautiful examples—trees growing on mountains or on wild islands—they are very rarely disturbed except near the larger commercial centers. Indeed, the Japanese have almost a veneration for some of these fantastic <term>furyo</term>-shaped trees and leave them alone, whether they are pines or plums.

Hambei loved the tree in question so much that no offer people could make would induce him to part with it. So famously beautiful were the colors and curves of this

<summary>In 1716, a respected gardener named Hambei lives a simple, happy life tending to a rare and valuable "lying dragon" plum tree. Despite its high market value, Hambei’s deep devotion to the tree’s beauty makes him refuse all offers to sell it.</summary>
<keywords>Kyoho Era, Momoyama Fushimi, Hambei, furyo, lying dragon, plum tree, Japanese gardens, 1716</keywords>

old stunted tree, large sums had many times been offered for it. Hambei loved it not only for its beauty but also because it had belonged to his father and grandfather. Now in his old age, with his wife in her dotage and his children gone, it was his chief companion. In the autumn he tended it in its untidiness of dead and dying leaves. He felt sorry and sympathetic for it in its cold and bare state in November and December; but in January he was happily engaged in watching the buds which would blossom in February. When they did bloom it was his custom to allow people to come at certain hours daily to see the tree and listen to stories of historical facts, and also to stories of romance, regarding the plum tree, of which the Japanese mind is always full. When this was over, Hambei pruned and tied the tree once more. In the hot season he lingered under it smoking his pipe, and was often rewarded for his care by two or three dozen delicious plums, which he valued and loved almost as much as if they had been his own children.

Thus, year after year, the tree had become such a companion to Hambei that a king’s ransom would not have bought it from him.

Alas! No man is destined to be left alone in this world. Someone is sure, sooner or later, to covet his property. It happened that a high official at the Emperor’s court heard of Hambei’s <term>furyo</term> tree and wanted it for his own garden. This <term>dainagon</term> sent his steward, Kotaro Naruse, to visit Hambei with the intention of purchasing it, never for a moment doubting that the old gardener would readily sell if the price offered were high enough.

Hambei was perplexed. What excuse for refusal could he make to such a high-ranking person? He made a fumbling and rather stupid remark, which the clever steward soon took advantage of.

“On no account,” said Hambei, “can I sell the old tree. I have refused many offers for it already.”

What was Hambei now to say? Such a low-born person, asked by a gallant <term>samurai</term> to grant a favor to a person no less than the <term>dainagon</term>!

“Sir,” he answered, “your request on behalf of the <term>dainagon</term> has been made so courteously that I am completely unable to refuse. You must, however, tell the <term>dainagon</term> that the tree is a gift, for I cannot sell it.”

‘Please, as is customary when making a gift, accept this small one in return.’

To the gardener’s great astonishment, the bag contained gold. He returned it to Kotaro, saying that it was impossible to accept the gift; but after being pressed again by the smooth-tongued samurai, he gave in.

The moment Kotaro left, Hambei regretted this. He felt as if he had sold his own flesh and blood—as if he had sold his daughter—to the <term>dainagon</term>.

That evening he could not sleep. Toward midnight, his wife rushed into his room and, pulling him by the sleeve, shouted:

‘You wicked old man! You villainous old rascal! At your age, too! Where did you get that girl? I have caught you! Don’t tell me lies! You are going to beat me now—I see it in your eyes. I am not surprised if you take revenge this way—you must feel like an old fool!’

Hambei thought his wife had lost her mind for good this time. He had seen no girl.

‘What is the matter with you, Oba-san?’<note>Old woman.</note> he asked. ‘I have seen no girl, and I do not know what you are talking about.’

‘Don’t tell me lies! I saw her! I saw her myself when I went down to get a cup of water!’

‘Saw, saw—what do you mean?’ said Hambei. ‘I think you have gone mad, talking about seeing girls!’

‘I did see her! I saw her weeping outside the door. And a beautiful girl she was, you old sinner—only seventeen or eighteen years old.’

# The Dragon-Shaped Plum Tree

Hambei got out of bed to see for himself whether his wife had spoken the truth or had truly gone mad.

On reaching the door he heard sobbing, and, upon opening it, he saw a beautiful girl.

"Who are you, and why are you here?" asked Hambei.

"I am the Spirit of the Plum Tree, which for so many years you have tended and loved, as did your father before you. I have heard—and grieve greatly over it—that an arrangement has been made by which I am to be moved to the <term>dainagon</term>’s gardens. It may seem like good fortune to belong to a noble family, and an honor to be taken into it. I cannot complain; yet I grieve at being moved from where I have been for so long, and from you, who have so carefully tended to my needs. Can you not let me remain here a little longer—as long as I live? I pray you, do!"

"I have made a promise to send you off on Saturday to the dainagon in Kyoto; but I cannot refuse your plea, for I love to have you here. Rest easy, and I will see what can be done," said Hambei.

The spirit dried its tears, smiled at Hambei, and disappeared, as it were, into the trunk of the tree, while Hambei’s wife stood looking on in wonder, not at all reassured that there was not some trick on her husband’s part.

At last the fatal Saturday on which the tree was to be moved arrived, and Kotaro came with many men and a cart. Hambei told him what had happened—about the tree’s spirit and what it had implored of him.

"Here! Take the money, please," said the old man. "Tell the story to the dainagon as I tell it to you, and surely he will have mercy."

<summary>Hambei meets the Spirit of the Plum Tree, who takes the form of a beautiful girl and begs him not to send her away to the dainagon's gardens. When the transport crew arrives, Hambei attempts to return the payment and asks Kotaro to plead for the tree's release.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the story of the gardener Hambei, who has attempted to return the payment for his plum tree to Kotaro, explaining that the tree's spirit appeared to him and begged to stay.</meta>

Kotaro was angry and said:
"How has this change come about? Have you been drinking too much sake, or are you trying to fool me? You must be careful, I warn you; otherwise, you shall find yourself headless. Even if the spirit of the tree did appear to you in the form of a girl, did she say that she would be sorry to leave your poor garden for a place of honor in that of the <term>dainagon</term>? You are a fool, and an insulting fool—how dare you return the dainagon’s present? How could I explain such an insult to him, and what would he think of me? Since you are not keeping your word, I will take the tree by force, or kill you in its place."

Kotaro was greatly enraged. He kicked Hambei down the steps and, drawing his sword, was about to cut off his head, when suddenly there was a little puff of wind scented with plum blossoms, and then the beautiful girl stood in front of Kotaro; she was the Spirit of the Plum Tree!

"Get out of my way, or you will get hurt," shouted Kotaro.

"No: I will not go away. You had better kill me, the spirit that has brought such trouble, instead of killing a poor, innocent old man," said the spirit.

"I don’t believe in the spirits of plum trees," said Kotaro. "That you are a spirit is evident; but you are only that of an old fox. So I will comply with your request, and at any rate, kill you first."

No sooner had he said this than he struck with his sword, and he distinctly felt that he cut through a body. The girl disappeared, and all that fell was a branch of the plum tree and most of the flowers that were blooming.

# The Dragon-Shaped Plum Tree

Kotaro now realized that what the gardener had told him was true and apologized accordingly.

"I will carry this branch to the <term>dainagon</term>," he said, "and see if he will listen to the story."

Thus, Hambei’s life was saved by the spirit of the tree.

The <term>dainagon</term> heard the story and was so moved that he sent the old gardener a kind message, telling him to keep both the tree and the money as an expression of his regret for the trouble he had caused.

Unfortunately, however, the tree withered and died soon after Kotaro’s cruel blow, despite Hambei’s care. The dead stump was venerated for many years.

In olden times, long before the misfortunes of modernization came to Japan, there lived at Kasamatsu, in Nakasatani, near Shichikwai village in the Shinji district of Hitachi Province, a hot-headed old <term>Daimyo</term>, Oda Sayemon. His castle stood on the top of a pine-clad hill about three miles from what is now known as Kamitachi station on the Nippon Railway. Sayemon was noted for his bravery as a soldier, for his terrible skill at <term>go</term> (or <term>goban</term>), and for his bad temper and violence whenever he lost—which happened every time.

His closest friends among his retainers had tried hard to improve his behavior after he lost at <term>go</term>, but it was hopeless. He struck anyone who won against him in the face with a heavy iron fan, such as was carried by warriors in those days; he would just as readily have drawn his sword and cut off his best friend’s head as allow anyone to interfere with him on those occasions. # LII THE CHESSBOARD CHERRY TREE<note>I believe this story (except for the ghost) is true, because the <term>seppuku</term> of Saito Ukon is exactly the kind of reasoning that would have occurred in that era.</note>

Playing <term>go</term> with their lord was what all his bold <term>samurai</term> dreaded most. At last, it was agreed among them that rather than suffer the gross insult of being struck by him when they won, they would let him win instead. After all, it did not matter much, as there was no money involved in the game. Thus, Sayemon’s skill grew worse and worse, for he never learned anything; yet, in his arrogance, he thought he was better than everyone else.

On the 3rd of March, in honor of his little daughter O Chio, he gave a dinner party for his retainers. The 3rd of March is Dolls’ Day (<term>Hina-no-sekku</term>)—the day on which girls bring out their dolls. People go from house to house to see them, and the little owners offer you sweet white <term>saké</term> in a doll’s cup with much ceremony. Sayemon, no doubt, chose this day of feasting as a tribute to his daughter—for he served sweet white <term>saké</term> after their food, to be drunk to the health of the dolls, instead of the regular <term>saké</term> that the guests would have liked much better. Sayemon himself absolutely disliked sweet <term>saké</term>. So as soon as the feast was over, he called Saito Ukon, one of his oldest and most faithful warriors, to come and play <term>go</term> with him, leaving the others to drink. Ukon, strangely enough, had not played with his lord before, and he was delighted that he had been chosen. He had made up his mind to die that evening after giving his master a proper lesson.

In a luxuriously decorated room, a <term>goban</term> (chessboard) was placed with two <term>go</term>-cases containing the pieces, which are made of white and black stones. The white stones are usually taken by the superior player and the black by the inferior. Without any apology or explanation,

<summary>Oda Sayemon’s retainers habitually let him win at Go to avoid his violent temper, leading to his false belief in his own skill. During the Doll Festival, Sayemon challenges his faithful warrior Saito Ukon to a game, unaware that Ukon intends to teach him a lesson even if it costs him his life.</summary>
<keywords>Oda Sayemon, Saito Ukon, Go, Hina-no-sekku, Dolls' Day, samurai, honor, arrogance, saké</keywords>

--- Page 572 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Go match between the arrogant Lord Oda Sayemon and his faithful retainer, Saito Ukon, who has resolved to teach his master a lesson in humility.</meta>

<page-num>328</page-num>

Ukon took the case containing the white stones and began to place them as if he were, without question, the superior player.

Sayemon’s temper began to flare, but he did not show it. Because his retainers had allowed him to win so many games of <term>go</term> lately, he was fully confident that he would win again, and that Ukon would also have to apologize for presuming to take the white stones.

The game ended in a win for Ukon.

"I must have another game," said Sayemon. "I was careless in that one. I will soon show you how I can beat you when I try."

Again Sayemon was beaten—this time not without losing his temper, for his face turned red, his eyes looked devilish, and with a bullying voice full of passion, he roared for a third game.

Ukon won this one as well. Sayemon’s wrath knew no bounds. Seizing his iron fan, he was about to strike Ukon a violent blow in the face. His opponent caught him by the wrist and said:

"My Lord, what are your ideas about games? Your Lordship seems to think of them strangely! It is the better player who wins, while the inferior must fail. If you fail to beat me at <term>go</term>, it is because you are the inferior player. Is your Lordship’s manner of taking defeat from a superior up to the standards of <term>bushido</term> in a <term>samurai</term>, as we are taught? Take my advice, your faithful retainer, and do not be so quick to anger—it poorly suits someone in your Lordship’s high position." And, with a look full of reproof at Sayemon, Ukon bowed almost to the ground.

<summary>Saito Ukon defeats Lord Sayemon in three consecutive games of Go, prompting a violent outburst from the lord; Ukon restrains him and delivers a stern lecture on the ethics of bushido and sportsmanship.</summary>

# The Chessboard Cherry Tree
<sig>42</sig>

“You insolent rascal!” roared Sayemon. “How dare you speak to me like that? Don’t move! Stand as you are, with your head bowed, so that I may take it off.”

“Your sword is for killing your enemies, not your retainers and friends,” said Ukon. “Sheathe your sword, my Lord. You do not need to trouble yourself to kill me, for I have already committed <term>seppuku</term><note>Disemboweled myself.</note> in order to offer you the advice I have given, and to save all others. Look here, my Lord!” Ukon opened his clothing and showed an immense cut across his stomach.

Sayemon stood for a minute, taken aback, and while he stood there, Ukon spoke to him once more, telling him how he must control his temper and treat his subjects better.

Upon hearing this advice again, Sayemon’s anger returned. Seizing his sword, he rushed at Ukon and, crying, “I will not allow myself to be advised even by your dying spirit!” made a furious strike at Ukon’s head. He missed and cut the <term>go-board</term> in two instead. Then, seeing that Ukon was dying quickly, Sayemon dropped beside him, weeping bitterly and saying:

“I deeply regret seeing you die like this, oh faithful Ukon! In losing you, I lose my oldest and most loyal retainer. You have served me faithfully and fought most gallantly in all my battles. Forgive me, I beg of you! I will take your advice. It was surely a sign from the gods that they were displeased with my conduct when they made me miss your head with my sword and cut the <term>go-board</term>.”

Ukon was pleased to find his lord repentant at last. He said:

<summary>After Lord Sayemon threatens to execute him, Ukon reveals he has already committed seppuku to prove the sincerity of his counsel; moved by this sacrifice and an accidental strike on the go-board, Sayemon finally repents of his cruel behavior.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the story of Saito Ukon and Lord Sayemon. After Ukon’s sacrifice and Sayemon’s repentance, the narrative describes the supernatural legacy of Ukon's loyalty and the miraculous cherry tree that grew from his grave.</meta>

<header>Ancient Tales and Folklore of Japan</header>

> ‘Even in death, I shall not forget the bond between master and servant. My spirit shall remain with you and watch over your well-being as long as you live.’

Then Ukon breathed his last.

Sayemon was so moved by Ukon’s faithfulness that he had him buried in his own garden, and he buried the broken <term>go-board</term> with him. From that time on, Lord Sayemon’s conduct was completely reformed. He was good and kind to all his subjects, and all his people were happy.

A few months after Ukon’s death, a cherry tree sprouted from his grave. Within three years, the tree grew to be magnificent and bloomed luxuriantly.

On March 3rd of the third year—the anniversary of Ukon’s death—Sayemon was surprised to find the tree suddenly in bloom. He was looking at it and thinking of watering it himself, as he usually did on that day, when he suddenly saw a faint figure standing by the trunk of the tree. Just as he said, ‘I know you are the spirit of the faithful Saito Ukon,’ the figure disappeared. Sayemon ran to the tree to pour water over the roots, but then he noticed that the bark for several feet up the trunk had cracked into the size and shape of the squares on a <term>go-board</term>! He was deeply impressed. For years afterward—until Sayemon’s death—Ukon’s ghost appeared every March 3rd.

A fence was built around the tree, which was considered sacred; and they say the tree can still be seen today.

# LIII

## THE PRECIOUS SWORD ‘NATORI NO HOTO’

IDE KAMMOTSU was a vassal of the Lord of Nakura town, in Kishu. His ancestors had all been brave warriors, and he had greatly distinguished himself in a battle at Shizugatake, which was named after a mountain in the province of Omi. The great Hideyoshi had successfully fought in the same place as far back as the eleventh year of the <term>Tensho Era</term> (1573–1592)—that is, 1584—against Shibata Katsuiye. Ide Kammotsu’s ancestors were loyal men. One of them, as a warrior, had a reputation second to none. He had cut off the heads of no fewer than forty-eight men with a single sword. In due time, this weapon was passed down to Ide Kammotsu and was kept by him as a most valuable family treasure. Rather early in life, Kammotsu found himself a widower. His young wife left behind a son named Fujiwaka. In time, Kammotsu, feeling lonely, married a lady named Sadako. Sadako later bore a son, who was named Goroh. Twelve or fourteen years after that, Kammotsu himself died, leaving the two

<summary>This page introduces Ide Kammotsu, a distinguished warrior of Kishu and owner of a legendary family sword that once decapitated forty-eight men. Upon his death, he leaves behind two sons, Fujiwaka and Goroh, born of different mothers.</summary>

sons in Sadako’s charge. Fujiwaka was nineteen years old at that time.

Sadako became jealous of Fujiwaka, knowing that as the eldest son, he was the heir to Kammotsu’s property. She tried every possible means to put her own son, Goroh, first.

Meanwhile, a secret romance was developing between a beautiful girl named Tae, the daughter of Iwasa Shiro, and young Fujiwaka. They had fallen in love with each other, were holding secret meetings as often as they wished, and were promising to marry. Eventually, they were discovered, and Sadako used their behavior as an excuse to drive Fujiwaka out of the house and strip him of all rights to the family property.

A faithful old nurse named Matsue, who had raised Fujiwaka from infancy, was part of the household. She was grieved by the injustice that had been done; however, she cared little for the loss of money or property compared to the loss of the sword—the miraculous sword of which the exiled son was the rightful owner. She thought day and night about how she might obtain the heirloom for young Fujiwaka.

After many days, she concluded that she must steal the sword from the <term>Ihai</term> (a memorial tablet within a shrine, inscribed with an ancestor's posthumous name, which represents the spirit of that ancestor).

One day, while her mistress and the others were away, Matsue stole the sword. No sooner had she done so than it became clear that it might be several months before she could place it in the hands of the rightful owner. For nothing had been heard of Fujiwaka.

since his stepmother had driven him out. Fearing that she might be accused, the faithful Matsue dug a hole in the garden near the <term>ayumiya</term>—a small house, such as is kept in every Japanese gentleman's garden for performing the <term>Tea Ceremony</term>—and there she placed the sword, intending to keep it hidden until such time as she should be able to present it to Fujiwaka.

Sadako, having reason to go to the <term>butsudan</term> the day after, missed the sword; and, knowing O Matsue to have been the only servant left in the house at the time, accused her of the theft of the sword.

Matsue denied the theft, thinking that in the cause of justice it was right for her to do so; but it was not easy to persuade Sadako, who had Matsue confined in an outhouse and gave orders that neither rice nor water was to be given to her until she confessed. No one was allowed to go near Matsue except Sadako herself, who kept the key to the shed, which she visited only once every four or five days.

About the tenth day, poor Matsue died from starvation. She had stuck faithfully to her resolution that she would keep the sword and deliver it someday to her young master, the lawful heir. No one knew of Matsue's death. The evening on which she died found Sadako seated in an old shed in a remote part of the garden, trying to cool herself, for it was very hot.

After she had sat for about half an hour, she suddenly saw the figure of an emaciated woman with disheveled hair. The figure appeared from behind a stone lantern, glided toward the place where Sadako was seated, and looked directly into Sadako's face.

Sadako immediately recognized Matsue and scolded her loudly for breaking out of her prison.

"Go back, you thieving woman!" she said. "I am not half finished with you yet. How dare you leave the place where you were locked up and come to confront me?"

The figure gave no answer but glided slowly along to the spot where the sword had been buried and dug it up.

Sadako watched carefully and, being no coward, rushed at the figure of Matsue, intending to seize the sword. The figure and the sword suddenly disappeared.

Sadako then ran at top speed to the shed where Matsue had been imprisoned and flung the door open violently. Before her lay Matsue, dead, evidently having been so for two or three days; her body was thin and emaciated.

Sadako realized that it must have been the ghost of O Matsue that she had seen, and she mumbled, "Namu Amida Butsu; Namu Amida Butsu," the Buddhist prayer asking for protection or mercy.

After being driven from his family home, Ide Fujiwaka had wandered to many places, begging for food. At last, he found some minor employment and was able to support himself at a very cheap inn at Umamachi, Asakusa Temple.

One midnight he awoke and found the emaciated figure of his old nurse standing at the foot of his bed, carrying in her hands the precious sword—the heirloom valued beyond all others. It was wrapped in scarlet and gold brocade, just as it had been before, and the figure of O Matsue reverently laid it at Fujiwaka’s feet.

## THE WHITE SERPENT GOD

Harada Kurando was one of the leading vassals of the Lord of Tsugaru. He was a remarkable swordsman and gave lessons in fencing. Next in seniority to Harada among the vassals was one Gundayu, who also taught fencing; but he was no match for the famous Harada and, consequently, was somewhat jealous.

One day, to encourage the art of fencing among his vassals, the Daimyo summoned all his people and ordered them to give an exhibition in his presence.

After the younger vassals had performed, the Daimyo gave an order that Harada Kurando and Hira Gundayu should have a match. To the winner, he said, he would present a gold image of the Goddess Kannon.

Both men fenced their best. There was great excitement. Gundayu had never done so well before; but Harada was too good. He won the match, receiving the gold image of Kannon from the hands of the Daimyo amid loud cheering.

faithful companions remained with him and said they would help him to ambush and attack Harada that very evening. Having arranged this cowardly plan, they proceeded to hide on the road that Harada had to travel on his way home.

For three hours they lay there with evil intentions. At last, in the moonlight, they saw Harada come staggering along; for, as was natural on such an occasion, he had been drinking <term>saké</term> freely with his friends.

When Harada’s body was found, there was great grief.

Yonosuke, Harada’s son, a boy of sixteen, vowed to avenge his father’s death and obtained special permission from the <term>Daimio</term> to kill Gundayu however and whenever he chose; Gundayu’s disappearance was sufficient evidence that he had been the murderer.

Yonosuke set out that day on his hunt for Gundayu. He wandered about the country for five long years without finding the slightest clue; but at the end of that time, by the guidance of Buddha, he located his enemy at Gifu, where Gundayu was serving as a fencing master to the local feudal lord.

Yonosuke found that it would be difficult to get to Gundayu in an ordinary way, for he hardly ever left the castle. He decided, therefore, to change his name to Ippai and to apply for a position in Gundayu’s house as a <term>chugen</term> (a samurai’s private attendant).

In this, Ippai (as we shall now call him) was particularly lucky, for since Gundayu was in need of such an attendant, he got the job.

On the 24th of June, a great celebration was held at Gundayu’s house, as it was the fifth anniversary of his service to the clan. He placed his stolen golden image of Kwannon on the <term>tokonoma</term> (the part of a Japanese room, raised five inches above the floor, where pictures and flowers are placed), and a dinner with sake was set before it. Gundayu gave a dinner for his friends, all of whom drank so heavily that they fell asleep.

The next day, the image of Kwannon had disappeared. It could not be found. A few days later, Ippai became ill, and, due to poverty, was unable to buy proper medicine; his condition went from bad to worse. His fellow servants were kind to him, but they could do nothing to improve his condition. Ippai did not seem to care; he lay in his bed and seemed almost pleased to be getting weaker and weaker. All he asked was that a branch of his favorite <term>omoto</term> (*rhodea japonica*) should be kept in a vase before his bed so that he might see it continually; and this simple request was naturally granted.

True to the spirit of a <term>samurai</term>, however, Gundayu "pulled himself together" and expressed great pleasure to the person who had brought the image of <term>Kwannon</term>. Furthermore, to celebrate the occasion, he gave a great feast that evening. Curiously enough, the <term>samurai</term> who had broken the vase and recovered the image became suddenly ill and was unable to attend.

After he had dismissed his guests, at about 10 P.M., Gundayu retired to his bed. In the middle of the night, he awoke with what he took to be a terrible nightmare. There was a choking sensation at his throat; he squirmed and twisted; gurgling noises came from his mouth to such an extent that he woke his wife, who struck a light in terror. She saw a white snake coiled tightly around her husband’s throat; his face was purple, and his eyeballs protruded two inches from his face.

She called for help, but it was too late. As the young <term>samurai</term> came rushing in, their fencing-master was black in the face and dead.

The next day, there was a close investigation. Messengers were dispatched to the Lord of Tsugaru to inquire into the history of the murdered Harada Kurando, father of Yonosuke (or "Ippai"), and into that of Gundayu, who had been in his employ for five years. Having ascertained the truth, the Lord of Gifu, moved by the zeal of Yonosuke in discharging his filial duties, returned the golden image of <term>Kwannon</term> to the bereaved Harada family; and in commemoration, he worshipped the dead snake at a shrine erected at the foot of Kodayama Mountain. The spirit is still known as <term>Hakuja no Myojin</term>, the White Serpent God.

## LV

### A FESTIVAL OF THE AWABI FISH

Manazuru-minato is situated on a small promontory of the same name. It faces Sagami Bay <note>The OCR text reads "Sagama Bay."</note>, which is famous for its beauty; behind it are mountains rising gradually, towered over in the distance by the majestic Mount Fuji. To the north on clear days, the sandy shores of Kozu and Oiso, twenty-five miles away, seem to be almost within arm's reach. Some people have compared the beauty of Manazuru-zaki, from the cape to the river, with the place in China called 'Sekiheki' <note>The Red Cliff.</note> by that country's celebrated poet, Sotoba <note>The Japanese name for the Chinese poet Su Shi, also known as Su Dongpo.</note>, who wrote 'Sekiheki no Fu,' the Ode to Sekiheki.

Many years ago, Minamoto-no-Yoritomo, after his defeat at the Battle of Ishibashiyama, fled to Manazuru-minato and stayed there for a few days while waiting for favorable weather to cross to the opposite side, the province of Awa. One can still see, I am told, the cave in which he hid, which retains its old name, 'Shitoto-iwa.' The scenery on the coast is magnificent. The rocks rise sheer out of the sea and enclose a perfect little bay on the inner side of Manazuru-zaki (Cape). There, the fishermen built a quiet little shrine, 'Kibune Jinja,' where they

worshipped the goddess who guards the fishing along their coast. They had little to complain about in the Bay of Manazuru. The waters were deep and always well-stocked with fish such as *tai* <note>Sea bream.</note>; in due season came the *sawara* (giant mackerel) and all the smaller migratory fish, including the sardine and the anchovy. The fishermen had nothing to complain about until about forty years ago, when a strange thing happened.

On the 24th of June, a person from an inland area arrived for a few days of sea-bathing. He was not a swimmer, and he drowned on the first day. His body was never recovered, though the fishermen did all they could to find it. From this event onward, for two full years, the abundance of fish in the bay decreased more and more, until it became difficult to catch enough to eat. The situation was extremely serious.

Some of the elder fishermen attributed the change to the stranger who had drowned.

"It is his unrecovered body," they said, "that has caused our sacred waters to change. The impurity has offended Gu gun O Hime, our goddess. It will never do to continue as we are. We must hold a special festival at the temple of Kibune Jinja."

Accordingly, they approached the head priest, Iwata. He was pleased with the idea, and a specific day was chosen.

On the appointed evening, hundreds of fishermen gathered together with torches in one hand and *Shirayu* or *Gohei*<gloss>1</gloss> papers fastened to a bamboo pole in the other.

# A Festival of the Awabi Fish
343

They formed into a procession and advanced toward the shrine from various directions, beating gongs. At the temple, the priest read from the sacred books and prayed to the goddess who had watched over them and their fisheries, asking her not to desert them simply because their waters had been polluted by a dead body. They promised to search for it by every means in their power and cleanse the bay.

Suddenly, while the priest was praying, a light so brilliant it nearly blinded the fishermen flashed out of the water. The priest stopped for a moment; a rumbling noise was heard at the bottom of the sea; and then a goddess of surpassing beauty (probably <term>Kwannon Gioran</term>) rose to the surface. She watched the ceremony being held on the shore for a full hour and then disappeared with another flash, leaving behind the sound of roaring waves.

The priest and the elder fishermen considered the matter and concluded that what they had seen was indeed their goddess, and that she had been pleased by their ceremony. They also believed the dead body must still be at the bottom of the bay, directly under the spot where the flashes of light and the goddess herself had appeared. It was arranged that two young virgins who could dive should be sent down to that spot to investigate, and two were accordingly chosen—Saotome and Tamajo. Wrapped in white skirts, these maidens were taken in a boat to the place where the flashes and the goddess had appeared. The girls dived, reached the bottom, and searched for the body of the man who had drowned two years before. Instead of finding it, they saw only a small but dazzling light. Curiosity led them to the spot, and there they found

hundreds upon hundreds of <term>awabi</term> (ear-shells) fastened upon a rock six feet high and twenty-five or thirty feet long. Whenever the shellfish moved, they were forced to raise their shells, and it was the glitter of the pearls inside that had attracted the maidens. This rock must have been the tomb of the drowned man, or else the home of the goddess.

Saotome and Tamajo returned to the surface, each having taken a large shell from the rock to show the priest. As they reached the shore, cheers were given in their honor, and the priest and the fishermen crowded around them.

Upon learning about the <term>awabi</term> shells, which they had never before heard of being in the bay, they concluded that it was not impurity that kept the fish away. The light reflecting from the brilliant <term>nacreous</term> shells and the pearls inside them must be the cause. We have heard many times of <term>awabi</term> flying; they must have flown here at some time within the last two years. The fishermen resolved to remove them. It was evident that the goddess had appeared in the light to show them what was keeping the fish away.

No time was lost. Many hundreds of men and women went down and cleared the place, and the fish began to return to Manazuru-minato.

At the suggestion of the priest, Iwata, a <term>matsuri</term> (festival) is held every June 24th. The fishermen light torches and go to the shrine to worship all through the night. This is called the ‘Awabi Festival’ of Kibune.

<note>The story was told to me by a man who knows nothing of <term>shellfish</term>. He told the story as if it were about the <term>osari</term>, a kind of cockle shell dug out of the sand at low tide. It is impossible that this story could have referred to any <term>shellfish</term> other than <term>haliotis</term> (the ear shell), the <term>awabi</term>, or the regular pearl oyster.</note>

Diving women have seen the "flight" of <term>haliotis</term> and described it to me. If one feels inclined to leave a rock, they all feel the same impulse and go. This is how large, old <term>haliotis</term> sometimes appear on a rock some fifteen fathoms deep when not even one was there the day before; and they depart with equal quickness. For a thousand years or more, the same rocks have been frequented by them. And divers keep their finds at the bottom of the sea a great secret—at least, so I have observed at <term>Toshi</term>.

### LVI

## THE SPIRIT OF A WILLOW TREE SAVES FAMILY HONOUR

LONG ago, there lived in Yamada village, Sarashina District, Shinano Province, one of the richest men in the northern part of Japan. For many generations, the family had been wealthy, and at last, the fortune descended in the eighty-third generation to Gobei Yuasa. The family held no official title; yet the people treated them with nearly the same respect due to a princely house. Even the boys in the street, who are not usually inclined to offer either compliments or titles of respect, bowed ceremoniously when they met Gobei Yuasa. Gobei was the soul of good nature and was sympathetic to everyone in trouble.

The riches which Gobei had inherited were mainly money and land, about which he worried very little; it would have been difficult to find a man who knew less and cared less about his business affairs than Gobei. He spent his money freely, and when he happened to think of his accounts, his easygoing nature let them all slide. His great pleasures were painting <term>kakemono</term> pictures, talking to his friends, and eating good things. He ordered his steward
