Gobei was quite celebrated as a painter and could have made a considerable amount of money by selling his <term>kakemonos</term>; but no—that would not do credit to his ancestors and his name.

One day, while things were going from bad to worse and Gobei was seated in his room painting, a friend came to gossip. He told Gobei that the village people were beginning to talk seriously about a spirit that had been seen by no fewer than three of them. At first, they had laughed at the man who saw the ghost; the second man who saw it they were not inclined to take quite seriously; but now it had been seen by one of the village elders, and so there could be no doubt about it.

"Where do they see it?" asked Gobei.

"They say that it appears under your old willow tree between eleven and twelve o’clock at night—the tree that hangs some of its boughs out of your garden into the street."

"That is odd," Gobei remarked. "I can remember hearing of no murder under that tree, nor even any spiritual connection with any of my ancestors; but there must be something to it if three of our villagers have seen it. Yet, again, where there is an old willow tree, someone is sure to say, sooner or later, that he has seen a ghost. If there is a spirit there, I wonder whose it is? I should like to paint the ghost if I could see it, so as to leave it to my descendants as the last ominous sign on the road which has led to the family’s ruin. That I shall make an effort

Never before had Gobei been seized with such energy. He dismissed his friend and went to bed at four o’clock in the afternoon so as to allow himself to be awake by ten o’clock. At that hour, his servant woke him; but even then, he could not be persuaded to get up before eleven. By twelve o’clock, midnight, Gobei was finally out in his garden, hidden in the bushes facing the willow tree. It was a bright night, and there was no sign of any ghost until after one o’clock, when clouds passed over the moon. Just as Gobei was thinking of going back to bed, he saw a thin column of white smoke rising from the ground under the willow, which gradually took the form of a charming girl.

Gobei stared in astonishment and admiration. He had never imagined that a ghost could be such a vision of beauty. He had rather expected to see a pale, wild-eyed, disheveled old woman with protruding bones—a sight that would freeze his marrow and make his teeth chatter.

Gradually, the beautiful figure approached Gobei and hung its head, as if it wished to speak to him.

‘Who and what are you?’ cried Gobei. ‘To my mind, you seem too beautiful to be the spirit of someone who is dead. If you are indeed a spirit, please tell me, if you may, whose spirit you are and why you appear under this willow tree!’

‘I am not the spirit or ghost of a human, as you say,’ answered the spirit, ‘but the spirit of this willow tree.’

Never until now has there been danger; but now, in your time, ruin has come, and it is for me to step forward and tell you how, by the foresight of your ancestor, you have been saved from disgracing the family name through bankruptcy. Please dig the strongbox up and save the name of your house. Begin as soon as you can, and be careful in the future.’

Then she vanished.

Gobei returned to his house, scarcely believing it possible that such good luck had come to him as the spirit of the willow tree planted by his wise ancestor had said. He did not go to bed, however. He summoned a few of his most faithful servants, and at daybreak began digging. What excitement there was when at nineteen feet they struck the top of an iron chest! Gobei jumped with delight; and it may almost be said that his servants did the same, for to see their honored master’s name fall into the disgrace of bankruptcy would have caused many of them to disembowel themselves.

He could hardly realize as true the good fortune which had come to him. Bag after bag was pulled out, each containing a small fortune, until finally the bottom of the box was reached. Here was found a letter about six hundred years old, saying:

> "Whichever of my descendants is forced to use the treasure to save our family reputation shall read aloud and make known that this treasure was buried by me, Fuji Yuasa, in the twenty-first generation of our family, so that in a time of need or danger a future generation will be able to rely on it and save the family name. The one whose great misfortune necessitates using the treasure must say: 'I greatly repent the folly that has brought our family's affairs so low and required the assistance of an early ancestor. I can only repay this through diligent attention to my household affairs, and also by showing high appreciation and kindness to the willow tree which has so long watched and guarded my ancestor’s treasure. These things I vow to do. I shall reform entirely.'"

Gobei Yuasa read this aloud to his servants and to his friends. He became a man of energy. His lands and farms were properly taken care of, and the Yuasa family regained its influential position.

Gobei painted a <term>kakemono</term> of the spirit of the willow tree as he had seen her, and he kept this in his own room for the rest of his life. It is the famous painting, in

### LVII

## THE CAMPHOR TREE TOMB

**Five** <term>ri</term> (ten miles) from Shirakawa, in the province of Iwaki, there is a village called Yabuki-mura. Close by is a grove about 400 feet square. The trees once included a massive camphor nearly 150 feet in height, of untold age, and venerated by villagers and strangers alike as one of the greatest trees in Japan. A shrine was built for it in the grove, which was known as the Nekoma-myojin forest; and a faithful old man, Hamada Tsushima, lived there, caring for the tree, the shrine, and the whole grove.

One day the tree was cut down; but, instead of withering or dying, it continued to grow, and it is still flourishing, even though it is lying on the ground. Poor Hamada Tsushima disembowelled himself when the sacred tree had been cut down. Perhaps it is because his spirit entered the sacred tree that the tree will not die. Here is the story:—

Lord Date Tsunamune resolved to build the finest palace that could be designed. It was to be at Shinzenza, in Shiba. He ordered that no time should be lost and directed one of his high officials, Harada Kai Naonori, to see to the matter.

Why, of course, they all agreed. That was the best way of all. They would put their stamps to the document. This they did, and after a lively evening, they departed, generally pleased with themselves.

Kinokuniya, on the other hand, went home fully contented with his evening’s business. Did he not have the permit to cut the trees in his pocket, and had he not written it himself so as to suit his own purpose? He chuckled at the thought of how neatly he had managed the business.

On the morning of the fourth day, they proceeded to erect a scaffold around the camphor tree so that they might better use their axes. As they began chopping off the lower branches, Hamada Tsushima, the keeper of the shrine, came running to them.

"Here, here! What are you doing? Cutting down the sacred camphor? Curse you! Stop, I tell you! Do you hear me? Stop at once!"

Chogoro answered:

"You do not need to stop my men in their work. They are doing what they have been ordered to do, and with every right to do it. "I know all that," said the caretaker; "but your permission is to cut down any tree except the sacred camphor."

"There you are wrong, as this letter will show you," said Chogoro; "read it yourself." And the caretaker, in great dismay, read as follows:

Hamada Tsushima, the caretaker, performed <term>harakiri</term>, disemboweling himself there and then; but not before telling Chogoro that his spirit would enter the camphor tree to take care of it and to wreak vengeance on the wicked Kinokuniya.

At last the efforts of the men brought the stately tree down with a crash; but then they found themselves unable to move it. Pull as they might, it would not budge. Each time they tried, the branches seemed to come alive; faces and eyes were stung by the hits they received from them. Pluckily they continued their efforts, but it was no use. Things grew worse. Several of the men were caught and nearly crushed to death between the branches; four had limbs broken from blows delivered in the same way. At this moment a horseman rode up and shouted:

> “My name is Matsumaye Tetsunosuke. I am one of the Lord of Sendai’s retainers. The board of councillors in Sendai has refused to allow this camphor tree to be touched. Unfortunately, you have cut it. It must now remain where it is. Our feudal lord of Sendai, Lord Date Tsunamune, will be furious. Kinokuniya the contractor planned an evil scheme and will be duly punished; while as for the Shogun’s agent, Fujieda Geki, he also must be reported. You yourselves should return to Yedo <note>Modern-day Tokyo</note>. We cannot blame you for obeying orders. But first, give me that forged permit signed by the four local fools, who, it is trusted, will destroy themselves.”

# The Camphor Tree Tomb

Chogoro and his men returned to Yedo. A few days later, the contractor fell ill, and a shampooer <note>A traditional massage therapist</note> was sent to his room. A little later, Kinokuniya was found dead; the shampooer had disappeared, even though it was impossible for him to have escaped without being seen! It is said that the spirit of Hamada Tsushima, the caretaker, had taken the form of the shampooer in order to kill the contractor. Chogoro became so uneasy in his mind that he returned to the camphor tree, where he spent all his savings to build a new shrine and appoint a caretaker. This is known as the Kusunoki Dzuka (The Camphor Tree Tomb). My storyteller tells me that the tree still lies there today.
